articles.content: Over the past 18 months, the Canadian government has committed record levels of funding to national defence . It has advanced major military procurement projects, expanded international defence partnerships and introduced new institutions, strategies and policies. These initiatives are aimed at rebuilding the Canadian Armed Forces and strengthening Canada’s defence industrial base. Yet a critical element of this effort remains largely absent: improving public understanding of the threats facing Canada and the rationale behind these investments. Without a more defence-literate population, sustaining this historical level of spending may prove just as challenging as securing the political commitments that made them possible. What is defence literacy? Defence literacy refers to the public’s understanding of two critical dimensions of national security: The threats facing Canada, ranging from conventional military activity, such as long-range missile attacks and an increased Russian and Chinese military presence in the Arctic and North Atlantic, to unconventional or grey-zone threats that extend beyond the battlefield. The policies, institutions and actions through which the government seeks to address these threats. For decades, national defence received little attention in Canadian public debate, owing in part to a relatively stable world order and American security guarantees. This false sense of security, however, has left Canadians with a significant blind spot. According to a 2021 Department of National Defence survey , four in 10 Canadians could not identify a specific threat to Canada’s security or sovereignty. Similarly, a 2026 survey commissioned by the Canadian Security Intelligence Service found that 35 per cent of Canadians could not name an agency responsible for investigating national security threats. Why it matters This deficit in defence literacy is more than just a knowledge gap. It reflects a longstanding failure to take national security seriously or fully understand its implications. Addressing this shortcoming, then, is important for at least four reasons: 1. Failing to do so undermines democratic accountability. Defence literacy should not be confused with defence advocacy: its purpose is not to persuade Canadians to support specific policies or military expenditures. Rather, it equips them with the knowledge necessary to understand, scrutinize and critically evaluate the decisions being made on defence, and hold their elected officials to account for those decisions—including at the ballot box. 2. Greater defence literacy strengthens national resilience. Grey-zone activities including foreign interference, cyberattacks and disinformation target individuals, communities and institutions beyond the traditional military sphere. The public is the target , and often the first line of defence. Canada’s ability to counter these threats depends heavily on whether Canadians can recognize, respond to, and mitigate their impact. A public that understands the threats facing the country is far better equipped to do so. 3. An informed public anchors defence investment beyond episodic responses to emerging crises. Improving Canada’s military capabilities requires sustained political commitment over decades, which is far more durable if rooted in public understanding. Crisis-driven support fades once the threat passes, whereas understanding the rationale behind defence priorities outlasts changes in government. 4. Canada’s expanding defence ambitions require thousands of new soldiers, educators, researchers, entrepreneurs and public servants, all of whom have important roles to play in strengthening national security. Introducing the broader Canadian public to these opportunities is essential to cultivating the next generation of leaders and professionals. Building a more defence-literate future Strengthening defence literacy cannot fall to government alone. It requires a whole-of-society approach bringing together academia, civil society and industry, all of which are instrumental in fostering a more informed and engaged population. Government must first communicate more openly with Canadians about the threats facing the country and the measures being taken to address them. Canada’s new National Security Strategy is a start in recognizing this need, but more must be done. Canada should learn from its Nordic allies, who treat public awareness and preparedness as central to national security. Sweden, for example, has distributed guidance to households explaining how to prepare for crises and war, while Finland has adopted a comprehensive security model emphasizing co-operation between government, businesses, civil society and citizens. Think tanks, universities and civil society organizations are also integral also in making defence and security issues accessible to the public. Through research, public conferences, media, educational initiatives and opportunities for dialogue, these institutions translate complex policy issues into informed public debate. In my work at the CDA Institute , a Canadian defence and security think tank, I see the value of these efforts firsthand, and of a further one: investing in young Canadians. Through student conferences, mentorship programmes, internships and student-led initiatives, we help cultivate the next generation of defence and security leaders. Read more: How the Canadian Armed Forces could help solve the youth employment crisis Industry, too, has a role in helping Canadians understand how investments in national defence are inextricably tied to more job creation, technological innovation and economic prosperity. As Canada undertakes its biggest increase in defence spending since the Second World War , it cannot afford to neglect the importance of an informed public. These investments only stand a chance of being sustained over time if accompanied by an equally strong commitment to helping Canadians understand why they are so important. Canada’s long-term security depends on both. Kevin Budning is the Director of Scientific Research at the CDA Institute.

articles.content: Indigenous notions of relationality and reciprocity offer a way of understanding knowledge that goes beyond what technology can produce. (Wikimedia Commons/Thomas Melad) , CC BY-NC-ND Universities, long entrusted with teaching, research and knowledge production, are confronting one of their most significant challenges: The rising use of artificial intelligence . As AI technologies advance, they can perform tasks once considered the exclusive domain of humans. The implications extend beyond concerns about plagiarism and academic misconduct. As UNESCO has acknowledged , generative AI raises questions about the importance of human participation in knowledge production. For universities, these developments invite an uncomfortable question : If AI can produce knowledge more efficiently, what makes human contributions to knowledge production valuable? The changing nature of knowledge production Recent developments in mathematics demonstrate how consequential this question might be. In September 2026, OpenAI announced that an AI system had produced a proposed solution to one aspect of the Navier–Stokes Existence and Smoothness problem, one of mathematics’ celebrated Millennium Prize problems . The Navier-Stokes problem concerns the mathematical description of fluid motion and whether certain equations can produce solutions that become unbounded. Although formal recognition of the proposed solution is pending, the announcement represents a development in AI’s capacity to contribute to mathematical discovery. Read more: AI has solved a host of big maths problems – here’s why this threatens the whole field of mathematics Achievements like this may challenge assumptions about how knowledge is produced. AI can now produce mathematical proofs and generate original research across disciplines. Universities may therefore need to reconsider what distinguishes human intellectual contributions from those of AI. These concerns are not confined to mathematics. Research demonstrates that AI may complicate conventional approaches to academic assessment, authorship and integrity. However, responding to these developments primarily through regulation and restrictions risks overlooking a more important opportunity. Fundamentally, universities should reconsider the value they assign to human lived experience as a source of knowledge. Understanding lived experience Lived experience refers to the knowledge and understanding people develop through their encounters with the world. It encompasses more than simply having experiences. It involves interpreting those experiences, assigning meaning to them and drawing upon them to understand ourselves and others . Patrick O'Leary and Ming-sum Tsui , social work researchers from Australia and Hong Kong, emphasize the importance of recognizing lived experience as a source of expertise. They argue that lived experience contributes to meaningful relationships and professional practice. Their discussion offers an important insight for universities: Knowledge is not necessarily confined to information that can be collected, analyzed and reproduced . It can also emerge from the meanings people develop through participation in the world. This distinction is especially important when considering Onkwehón:we (Indigenous) understandings of knowledge. What universities can learn from Onkwehón:we For Onkwehón:we, (a Kanien’kehá term meaning “Original Peoples”), lived experience has long been central to understanding ourselves, our world and our responsibilities. Although Onkwehón:we knowledge traditions are diverse, many emphasize that knowledge emerges through relationships among people, communities and the natural world. Onkwehón:we scholarship on relationality demonstrates how knowledge and relationships are inseparable from the people and communities in which they are developed. From this perspective, lived experience is not exclusively individual in nature. It is also collective and intergenerational. It is shaped by language, ancestral knowledge and responsibilities to others. For Onkwehón:we, knowledge may be understood through participation in relationships that extend across generations. Learning from Elders and fulfilling responsibilities within communities are not merely opportunities to acquire information. They are experiences through which knowledge becomes meaningful. Research involving Indigenous communities in Canada illustrates how relationships with the land are informed by values of respect, responsibility and reciprocity. Reciprocity is the traditional value of balanced, respectful relations with each other and with the land. These understandings challenge the assumption that knowledge can be adequately evaluated outside of the relational and experiential contexts through which it is developed. Reaffirming the purpose of universities What can universities learn from Onkwehón:we perspectives as AI becomes increasingly potent? One possibility is to place greater emphasis on lived experience within teaching, learning and research. Read more: It’s taken thousands of years, but Western science is finally catching up to Traditional Knowledge Rather than evaluating learning primarily through written work, universities could place greater emphasis upon experiential learning and community engagement. These approaches can show how knowledge shapes relationships and responsibilities. Some faculties of education, such as at Wilfrid Laurier University , already use them in parts of their programming. This would not require abandoning AI. Nor would it suggest that Indigenous knowledge traditions exist simply to resolve problems facing universities. Rather, universities can recognize that human knowledge cannot be fully understood through technology alone. Onkwehón:we scholarship already challenges universities to reconsider how their disciplinary traditions privilege certain forms of knowledge while marginalizing relational and experiential ways of knowing. Artificial intelligence makes this reconsideration increasingly urgent. An example of how scientific orientations may be reconsidered is found in the study of time. A recent study on Onkwehón:we perspectives on time explores how scientific understandings of time may be enriched by Onkwehón:we lived experiences, including seasonal cycles and relationships with the Land. Such perspectives can broaden how universities approach scientific knowledge by connecting abstract concepts with human experience. The more consequential question concerns what universities believe knowledge is for and what responsibilities accompany its creation. Onkwehón:we understandings of lived experience offer a valuable starting point. They remind us that knowledge is not simply something we produce or possess. It is also something we live, share and carry through our relationships with others . As AI begins to transform how knowledge is produced, universities have an opportunity to reaffirm the importance of human experience. Rather than an alternative to intellectual achievement, it’s an essential part of what makes knowledge meaningful. Frank Deer receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.

Learning from Elders and fulfilling responsibilities within communities are not merely opportunities to acquire information. They are experiences through which knowledge becomes meaningful. Research involving Indigenous communities in Canada illustrates how relationships with the land are informed by values of respect, responsibility and reciprocity. Reciprocity is the traditional value of balanced, respectful relations with each other and with the land. These understandings challenge the assumption that knowledge can be adequately evaluated outside of the relational and experiential contexts through which it is developed. Reaffirming the purpose of universities What can universities learn from Onkwehón:we perspectives as AI becomes increasingly potent? One possibility is to place greater emphasis on lived experience within teaching, learning and research. Read more: It’s taken thousands of years, but Western science is finally catching up to Traditional Knowledge Rather than evaluating learning primarily through written work, universities could place greater emphasis upon experiential learning and community engagement. These approaches can show how knowledge shapes relationships and responsibilities. Some faculties of education, such as at Wilfrid Laurier University , already use them in parts of their programming. This would not require abandoning AI. Nor would it suggest that Indigenous knowledge traditions exist simply to resolve problems facing universities. Rather, universities can recognize that human knowledge cannot be fully understood through technology alone. Onkwehón:we scholarship already challenges universities to reconsider how their disciplinary traditions privilege certain forms of knowledge while marginalizing relational and experiential ways of knowing. Artificial intelligence makes this reconsideration increasingly urgent. An example of how scientific orientations may be reconsidered is found in the study of time. A recent study on Onkwehón:we perspectives on time explores how scientific understandings of time may be enriched by Onkwehón:we lived experiences, including seasonal cycles and relationships with the Land. Such perspectives can broaden how universities approach scientific knowledge by connecting abstract concepts with human experience. The more consequential question concerns what universities believe knowledge is for and what responsibilities accompany its creation. Onkwehón:we understandings of lived experience offer a valuable starting point. They remind us that knowledge is not simply something we produce or possess. It is also something we live, share and carry through our relationships with others . As AI begins to transform how knowledge is produced, universities have an opportunity to reaffirm the importance of human experience. Rather than an alternative to intellectual achievement, it’s an essential part of what makes knowledge meaningful. articles.title: In the age of AI, Indigenous ways of knowing remind us why lived experience matters

articles.content: By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide . The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution . Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted. Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights. Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions . Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life, the Rohingya faced restrictions on movement, education and health care while families were restricted to a two-child limit. Returning to Myanmar just to face the same conditions of life is not an option for many Rohingya. The repatriation conundrum It’s unlikely, however, that Myanmar will agree to grant citizenship to the Rohingya. Since the 2021 coup d'état that ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her National League for Democracy, the military has had sole control of the government . Gen. Min Aung Hlaing is seen at the IX Moscow conference on international security in Moscow in June 2021. (AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko) Earlier this year, Min Aung Hlaing, the architect of the Rohingya genocide who had been commander-in-chief of the Myanmar Forces since 2011, stepped down from his role and was subsequently elected president by a military-dominated parliament . This makes the prospect of a safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to Myanmar a near impossibility. The Myanmar military and government aren’t the only entities complicating the return of the Rohingya. Since late 2023, vast swaths of Rakhine state, where most Rohingya resided until 2017, have been under control of the Arakan army. The army is the largest and most powerful non-state armed group in the country and it is vying for the independence of the Arakan region , where Rakhine is located. The Arakan army is openly hostile to the Rohingya, and those residing in the territory it controls are facing many of the same restrictions that were previously imposed by the state. The enforcement deficit The ICJ established Myanmar’s responsibility for the genocide, and consequently ordered it to provide reparations and compensation, with details still to be decided. But, in practice, there is little the court can do to compel Myanmar to take accountability and pursue justice if it refuses to do so. The ICJ has no independent enforcement mechanism ; it only relies on states’ willingness to obey international law. Only the United Nations Security Council could decide to take coercive action against Myanmar, but China and Russia, which both hold veto power, are likely to oppose it. The two states have provided Min Aung Hlaing’s regime with political, diplomatic and military support over the years. Each also has its own issues with international human rights law, namely Russia’s war in Ukraine and China’s treatment of the Uyghurs . How the ruling might help the Rohingya The ICJ ruling has brought much-needed attention to the plight of the Rohingya. Renewed interest in the Rohingya crisis is expected to draw donations that could help alleviate some of the more pressing needs. Funding for the refugee camps has dwindled in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and the dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) . Currently, the Rohingya in Bangladesh only receive US$7-$12 per person per month in food assistance. Read more: Thousands are feared dead in Myanmar’s quake. Trump’s USAID cuts will cause even more unnecessary deaths Combined with the lack of income-generating opportunities, the cuts to food rations are frequently identified by refugees as the most severe challenge they face in the camps. More attention could also result in stronger political pressure, not just on Myanmar but also on its regional partners. Malaysia, for example, began deporting refugees back to Myanmar in September 2026 . Since the government continues to deny access to international agencies for the refugees, including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees , it could not be verified whether these returns were voluntary, as Malaysia claimed. It’s unlikely the Rohingya, who make up the majority of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia, are returning of their own free will. International pressure could force Malaysia to stop the deportations and avoid causing further harm to its already vulnerable Rohingya refugee community. Not ‘illegal immigrants’ Finally, the most immediate benefit of the ruling is that, for the first time, there is a formal recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct people. The ruling directly contradicts Myanmar’s assertions that the Rohingya are “illegal immigrants from Bangladesh” who have no legitimate claim to rights and land in Rakhine. The ICJ ruling clearly affirms that the atrocities the Rohingya have suffered are indeed genocide, and while it doesn’t guarantee justice for the Rohingya, it’s a necessary precondition that opens the path to restorative justice. San Beauchemin is a member of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.

articles.content: An increasing share of Canadians are reporting financial difficulties. According to Statistics Canada , 39 per cent said it was difficult or very difficult for their household to meet its financial needs in spring 2025. Younger adults were particularly likely to experience financial difficulties. These struggles were linked to deteriorating life satisfaction and declining hope for the future. Incomes remain stagnant for many Canadians while costs climb , employment uncertainties continue and social safety net programs struggle to fill the gap. These situations show how rising economic insecurity is affecting people’s lives. Economic insecurity — sometimes described as precarity, vulnerability or financial risk — refers to how individuals balance resources and costs. To better understand how economic insecurity affects Canadians across social classes, we surveyed more than 8,000 Canadians and interviewed 127 about their experiences with economic insecurity as part of the Great Canadian Class Study . By talking to people in in-depth interviews, we learned more about the factors that lead to insecurity and how participants understood these situations. The conversations also highlighted the growing divides between younger and older adults in Canada. Economic security cuts across class We began this project to investigate whether, and how, social class shapes people’s lives in Canada. We found that social class matters in myriad ways, but not always in the ways we might expect. Growing economic insecurity helps explain why. Our recently published research in the British Journal of Sociology highlights why people’s experiences and perceptions of economic insecurity must be considered when examining social class. Our survey found that younger people, unemployed people, members of lower-income households, renters and people carrying stressful levels of credit card debt were more likely to experience insecurity. They were less able to meet their monthly expenses and did not have enough savings to cover an emergency expense. Our interviews revealed that economic insecurity was not only reflected in people’s income or assets. Some homeowners, for example, described feeling financially insecure despite owning property. The rising cost of living still left them with little money to set aside for savings or emergencies. Economic security cannot always be understood through income or wealth alone. People’s ability to manage unexpected expenses and their perceptions of their financial circumstances also matter. The growing generational divide Younger Canadians experienced the most severe effects of insecurity. Despite doing “everything right” to set themselves up for stability, many expressed resignation that they would never achieve the signifiers of middle-class status that past generations had, or the security that once came with it. Education, which has historically been seen as a route to job stability and higher incomes, instead contributed to feelings of insecurity in participants. Student debt felt insurmountable and shaped participants’ decisions about whether to pursue further schooling when rising tuition costs might not be offset by higher future earnings. Home ownership, once a traditional marker of middle-class success , was also not possible for most younger participants. Rising housing costs due to the treatment of housing as an investment opportunity , the dominance of private equity and real estate investment firms and mounting debt have made home ownership increasingly difficult to attain. For those shut out of home ownership, renting brought its own uncertainties, including rent increases, evictions and frustration at not being able to build wealth. This contrasted with the experiences of some older participants, who built their lives during a time of more opportunity and lower income inequality. Decades of good-paying jobs, a stronger social assistance system and a favourable housing market provided a stronger foundation for lifelong economic security. Homes, investments, pensions and personal savings were all sources of security that could be used to mitigate unforeseen emergencies. Addressing economic insecurity Despite its pervasiveness, there are many steps governments can take to alleviate the increasing insecurity Canadians are feeling across generations. Reinvesting in the social infrastructure that provided previous generations with a strong footing would be a good place to start. This includes expanding funding for post-secondary education to address the steady declines in government grants, strengthening rent control , building more non-market housing and instituting broader tax reforms to address growing income and wealth inequality . Our study reflects a changing Canada in which even people who grew up believing that education and hard work would lead to middle-class stability are experiencing economic insecurity. The traditional promise of meritocracy rests on the idea that people who work hard, pursue education and make responsible financial decisions can improve their circumstances. However, when those efforts no longer reliably lead to financial security, that promise becomes harder to sustain. The growing disconnect between Canadians’ expectations and their lived realities suggests that the traditional path to middle-class security is becoming increasingly difficult to follow. Michelle Maroto receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC). Andrea DeKeseredy receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC).

articles.content: In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families. “I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025 . “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change. For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom. For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages , including Nepali and English. Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue . A country of 124 mother tongues Nepal is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world , though the state has not always acknowledged it . The 2021 census recorded 124 mother tongues . Fifty years earlier, in 1971, when the Panchayat regime was promoting Nepali above all other languages, the census counted just 17 languages . Today, Nepali is the first language of just under 45 per cent of the population . I have worked in Nepal since 1991, first as a volunteer schoolteacher and later as a linguist and anthropologist. I have spent decades researching the country’s linguistic diversity . The census numbers reflect a shift I have witnessed on the ground, in communities. In 2021, for the first time, the census asked people about their ancestral language as well as their mother tongue. Nearly three million more people name Nepali as their mother tongue than they name it as their ancestral language , a sign that many families have shifted to Nepali. For other languages, the gap goes the other way. Some 300,000 more people name Nepal Bhasa, the language of the Newar community, as their ancestral language than name it as their mother tongue . Nepali is also spreading as a second language: 46 per cent of the population now speaks it that way, up from 33 per cent in 2011 . Whatever pressures Nepal’s other languages face, Nepali is certainly not a language at risk. Rights on paper On paper, Nepal’s laws side with children. The government’s School Education Sector Plan 2022-32 commits to scaling up early-grade teaching in children’s mother tongues. In practice, implementation has been sluggish and uneven. As comparative education scholar Uma Pradhan has shown , policy has long treated mother tongues as a bridge to Nepali, a stepping stone to be left behind, with the state offering little support. In a 2026 study from Tanahun , one grandparent spoke about a granddaughter in Grade 2 who was being taught only in Nepali and English: “She [does not have the] opportunity to study in [her ancestral] language; so, there is a gap.” Grade 1 students at Shree Sahara Bal Primary School in Pokhara, Nepal, in June 2013. (Photo by Jim Holmes for AusAID) , CC BY The evidence for local languages A 2024 study commissioned by UNICEF Nepal examined language use in 30 schools across all seven provinces. Its conclusion was unequivocal. When children learn in their mother tongue or a familiar language, they take a more active part in lessons and do better in assessments and exams. Many schools have rushed to switch to English-language teaching, often for financial reasons and with little teacher training. Yet students taught in Nepali outscored their English-taught peers in Nepali, in science and even in English , according to the study’s analysis of school assessment results, which was limited in scale. In Dailekh, in western Nepal, principal Sher Bahadur Rana told UNICEF that teachers once corrected children who used their own “language or dialect.” After training in multilingual teaching, he said, “we learned that children learn faster and feel more confident when we teach them in the language they speak and understand best.” Obstacles to implementation A recent review by education researchers Pariksha Onta and Amado Padilla, covering 111 studies and policy documents , points to a “persistent disconnect between constitutional commitments, classroom practice and targeted funding.” Where mother tongues are taught at all, they are usually a subject rather than the language children learn in. Textbooks in children’s mother tongues remain scarce, and most of those that do exist are translations of Nepali materials with little locally relevant content. Far too few teachers who speak local languages are recruited or trained. Parents, meanwhile, are caught in the middle. Many see English-language schools as a marker of quality and employability. And funding is lacking: in 2026–27, education and sports together received around 10.3 per cent of Nepal’s national budget , well below the international benchmark of allocating at least 15 per cent to education . Onta and Padilla’s review also highlights what works. In some Kathmandu Valley schools, children learn in Nepal Bhasa for their first three grades before Nepali and English are phased in. A strong foundation in the mother tongue supports learning in the other languages, which means families don’t have to choose between them. From paper to practice As I argued previously with colleagues Lava Deo Awasthi and Yogendra Prasad Yadava, rights “do not implement themselves.” Children should begin school in the language they understand best, with Nepali and English introduced gradually, building on that foundation. Making this work requires sustained funding, teachers trained to teach in children’s languages, and materials that reflect their lives and communities. Some municipalities have introduced local-language education programs, while Nepal’s Curriculum Development Centre has developed curricula for elementary education in more than 20 mother tongues . Language policy can sound technical, but at heart it is about whether a child’s first experience of school is a welcoming one. In Renuka Dahal’s classroom in Rautahat, where children now teach their teacher, the message is simple: their languages belong in school, and so do they. Mark Turin receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC).

articles.content: On Nov. 22, the day after COP31 climate talks collapsed in Antalya , Turkey, the global average temperature at noon UTC was estimated to be a record-setting 2.36 C above the pre-industrial average . Climate change is driving up global temperatures. Yet governments could not even agree to name the fossil fuels driving it. I have been a climate scientist since the late 1980s and have followed every UN climate summit since the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. I cannot recall a more embarrassing failure than COP31. The first draft proposed at least US$120 billion by 2035 to help countries adapt to climate change. By Nov. 19, the figure was gone. Three years ago in Dubai, governments agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. The Nov. 16 Antalya draft said so plainly. Yet, the final proposal at COP31 still omitted any mention of fossil fuels. The European Union and small island states were right to reject it. Given the recent failure, is it time for scientists and activists to boycott COP? From early success to utter failure While COP31 collapsed without an agreement, previous UN climate talks have had successes. In the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, industrialized countries agreed to reduce their collective emissions, averaged over 2008–12, to 5.2 per cent below 1990 levels. Emissions over the 2008-12 reporting period came in 9.9 per cent below 1990 levels . In Paris in 2015 , governments agreed to hold warming “well below 2 C above pre-industrial levels” while “pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5 C above pre-industrial levels.” Yet, in June 2026, a UN report found that the world is set to exceed the 1.5 C global warming target outlined in Paris. In 2015, governments invited the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) to report back in 2018 on the impacts of 1.5 C of warming and the emissions pathways that could get us there. In future emissions pathways leading to little or no overshoot of the 1.5 C target, global net carbon dioxide emissions were required to fall roughly 45 per cent from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero around 2050. Those pathways also required removing 100 to 1,000 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere over the century (so-called negative emissions) using technology that had yet to be developed. The authors spelled out the difficulties. The key government takeaway was that meeting the 1.5 C target could still be achieved. What struck me was how little those models resembled the world in which people make decisions. You can write carbon removal into a model. Somebody still has to find the land, build the equipment and pay to operate it. You don’t build a coal plant today to tear it down tomorrow. The utility has debt to repay and communities need power. What if we stayed home? Andrew Weaver on BBC News discussing COP31. Scientists, environmentalists and youth groups should boycott the next COP. I further think scientists should also consider walking away from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assessments. I was a lead author on four of them . I know what that invitation means to a young scientist, yet at some point, the scientific community needs to speak out as a collective. And those of us who have already had the privilege of working on IPCC assessments ought to speak first — and loudest. The Paris Agreement showed how readily governments can use our willingness to buy time. Ministers agreed on a temperature, asked us what it would mean if the world exceeded it, then continued exploiting fossil fuels regardless. Climate change has become a global tragedy of the commons. Fossil-fuel producers earn money selling their products while sharing the climatic cost with everyone else. Countries and tech companies are incentivized to race ahead with artificial intelligence, regardless of the environmental risks the rest of us inherit . And in our politics, climate change has become subsumed into a culture war where politics rail against green policies regardless of the facts. While Canada’s delegates were in Antalya, Ottawa committed $200 million to expand planned production at Woodfibre LNG, a liquefied natural gas export terminal in British Columbia. With decisions like that, the world is on course to even exceed 2 C of global warming. So, let governments go to the next COP and explain the empty seats. Save the airfare, the emissions and two weeks of time better spent elsewhere. Instead, use a fraction of that time to ask your representatives about the tangible action they are taking to tackle climate change. Andrew Weaver receives funding from NSERC and NRCan. He has previously served as an MLA and leader of the BC Green Party.

articles.content: Winter brings cozy sweaters, mugs of steaming cocoa and the annual search for someone to keep you warm. SZA captured the mood in “Big Boys,” the song she created for a 2022 Saturday Night Live sketch that went viral for its tongue-in-cheek call for a winter partner. It’s “cuffing season,” that time of the year when single people look for short-term partnerships to see them through the colder months. It’s also prime time for situationships — one of the most common, yet least-liked, relationship types . The season typically runs from October to Valentine’s Day, though some people start searching for a winter cuddle partner as early as summer . Initially linked to dating apps and campus culture, advertisers have embraced it as a lucrative window to sell products and activities such as skating, sleigh rides and sun-soaked getaways. But if dating apps are losing their appeal and hookup culture is facing a backlash , where does that leave cuffing season? Are you still looking for someone to get cozy with until spring, or has the whole concept become pure cringe? Dating today can feel like a mix of endless swipes, red flags and shifting expectations. From decoding mixed signals to balancing independence with intimacy, relationships in your 20s and 30s come with unique challenges. Love IRL is the latest series from Quarter Life that explores it all. These research-backed articles break down the complexities of modern love to help you build meaningful connections, no matter your relationship status. Cuffing in pop culture “Cuff” comes from African American slang and means something close to “hook up.” The term first appeared in U.S. college newspapers in 2011, the same year it was formally defined on Urban Dictionary. Two years later, rapper Fabolous released “Cuffin Season,” a track that helped carry the phrase into the mainstream. TikTok and Instagram are full of posts poking fun at cuffing as a hollow or silly approach to intimacy . Sports analogies are also used to situate cuffing season within the calendar year, which amplifies the gamification and competition associated with dating on the apps. Take this viral schedule from TikTok creator Crest : Scouting: Aug. 1-31 Drafting: Sept. 1-30 Tryouts: Oct. 1-31 Preseason: Nov. 1-30 Cuffing Season: Dec. 1-Jan. 15 Playoffs: Jan. 16-Feb. 13 Championship Game: Feb. 14 A recent Vogue story rounded up terms for the season’s stages and behaviour, including “sledging,” “winter coating” and “snowmanning.” Whether anyone actually uses these words, or whether they simply reflect a social obsession with labelling every twist of modern dating , is hard to say. What is abundantly clear is that even if cuffing rarely leads to meaningful connection, this season of casual romance has a stronghold on our culture. Why? And does the research back it up? The science of cuffing There are many scientific explanations for the rise of cuffing season, beginning with the so-called “November Theory.” According to Susan Trombetti , a matchmaker and CEO of Exclusive Matchmaking , November is the start of the holiday season and a time of increased socialization with family and friends. For some couples, that can be a happy time for deepening their bond. For others, the added stress or uncertainty can lead to a breakup, and the newly single go looking for someone to cuff. Other experts argue that we are evolutionarily inclined to seek a mate for the winter, citing drops in serotonin levels and the seasonal affective disorder associated with reduced sunlight and colder temperatures. With shorter days and fewer outdoor activities to fill them , you might find yourself craving a little more company and intimacy. Although commonly linked with Christmas and wintertime frolicking, some studies suggest it’s not just about the cold. In Australia, where Christmas falls at the start of summer, for example, sexual interest peaks in mid- to late December , just as it does in the United States and the United Kingdom. So perhaps cuffing season is less about temperature and more about the cultural weight of holidays that celebrate togetherness, stigmatize being single and mark turning points in relationships. Gen Z on cuffing As an author who has written extensively about dating apps and sexual slang and who teaches Gen Z students, I wanted to know: Is cuffing season still a thing? Read more: Cuffing season: an evolutionary explanation for why people want to settle down for the winter months Although my students see the term itself as a dated throwback, the consensus is that the winter and holiday romance ritual is alive and well. As one young woman shared: “It is absolutely still a thing, even if a little cringey.” Another student tied cuffing to its summertime counterpart, the “hot girl summer,” when women revel in their sexual freedom and live life on their own terms. She said: “Cuffing season is thrown around as a joke but the popularity of ‘hot girl summer’ means that getting together in the winter and breaking up in the summer is relevant.” Not everyone agreed. One student reasoned: “Cuffing season doesn’t exist anymore because of the social disregard for casual dating. There is no season for situationships because it’s so normalized!” Similarly, another shared: “A lot of people my age are getting tired of situationships, hookup culture and relationships that don’t really go anywhere.” Several students also noted that their generation feels less pressure to be in a relationship, a change they saw as positive. Beyond monetized romance Cuffing season reflects the dating-app ethos of an earlier time, when hookups dominated and being single carried a stigma. Yet the term is still widely used to signal the start of cute, casual fall and winter romance. A recent post on Cosmopolitan ‘s Instagram asked: “Have we officially entered cuffing season?” You may roll your eyes at the term, but casual winter coupling isn’t going anywhere. When media messaging about wholesome holiday activities for couples meet the changing calendar, people seem naturally inclined to reach for one another. Desire is seasonable, but so is the new Gingerbread Cream Cold Foam at Starbucks. What might be more novel is encouraging one another to outgrow monetized romance trends in favour of connections that are more interesting and meaningful. Treena Orchard does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) recently rejected the collective shunning of Russian athletes in international hockey. In doing so, it created a geopolitical test of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s key foreign policy tenets. The current exclusion of Russian teams stems from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 . The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), along with the International Olympic Committee and FIFA, banned Russia and its ally, Belarus, from their competitions as part of the wider global effort to penalize the Kremlin. The IIHF reiterated its position in early 2026, citing the safety and security of all participants and the “ integrity of its competitions .” In October, a three-member CAS tribunal found that unconvincing: there was insufficient evidence to establish the legal requirements for non-participation. Only substantiated security concerns could justify national exclusions. The CAS set aside the IIHF decision on procedural grounds and left it at that. Naturally, the Russian Ice Hockey Federation welcomed the decision and declared its intention to participate in the World Junior Championship in Alberta starting on Dec. 26. Banned by Canada Hockey federations in Canada and Europe expressed varying degrees of disappointment , with some countries threatening to boycott games against Russian players. Germany is threatening to abdicate its hosting duties for the May 2027 Men’s World Championship if Russia participates. Carney called the return of Russian teams “ unwelcome ” and later said the the Russian team would be barred from competing in Alberta for the World Juniors . The IIHF has since made Russia’s exclusion from the December-January World Juniors complete by yielding to the Canadian government’s restrictions. Russian officials were apoplectic and the IIHF website was hit by cyber attacks . Notably, USA Hockey has been quiet. CAS decision and Canadian foreign policy The CAS ruling and its fallout may be peripheral to what is known as great power politics , but it’s also a test of the post-rules-based global order. For Canada, the implications of disregarding the CAS ruling are considerable. For decades, Canada’s foreign policy was premised on the legitimacy of international institutions and a commitment to multilateralism . The CAS is one component of the interlocking machinery of that order. Now, major hockey countries like Canada find themselves on the horns of a dilemma: accept the CAS ruling and undermine the collective pressure campaign against Russia, or ignore the ruling and accelerate the erosion of yet another multilateral institution. Two or three years ago, Canada might have held its nose and accepted the CAS decision because of its procedural legitimacy. Trusting the global process was Canada’s overall strategy for decades but under Carney, that’s no longer the case. Yet, even in this period of “rupture ,” multilateral rules are still important. It’s not clear there’s any more wisdom in accelerating the old order’s demise than there is in practising what Carney has called “ naïve multilateralism .” Read more: Mark Carney’s Davos speech marks a major departure from Canada’s usual approach to the U.S. Canada’s bad options As host of the World Juniors, Canada was the first country with a decision to make — and future hosts are watching. Allowing the Russians to participate was likely never going to happen. Unfortunately, every option comes at a high cost. The easiest approach would have been to say it was too late to include Russia in the 2026 World Juniors. That would have eased pressure on the federal government and Hockey Canada, but it would have passed the buck to the Czech Republic, hosts of the Under-18 Women’s World Championship in January 2027 . It also wouldn’t have been the type of middle power leadership that Canada has been trying to signal. Another half-measure would have been to allow Russia’s players to compete under a neutral banner , but that doesn’t fool anyone and has even been used by Russia’s propagandists as a point of pride . The option Canada ultimately took is, ironically, right out of Donald Trump’s playbook: ignore the CAS decision and make up your own rules. Carney’s declaration that “Russians will not be there” means denying entry visas to players, coaches and staff, much like what the American president did to Iran prior to the 2026 FIFA World Cup. For Canada though, ignoring inconvenient rulings is vice masquerading as virtue. Back in from the cold? Regardless of Canada’s decision, the integration of Russia into the sporting fold is already underway in both the IOC and FIFA. The Court of Arbitration’s decision may serve as the basis for further reintegration — and Trump may accelerate the process. He’ll still be president when the United States hosts the Men’s Under-18 Hockey World Championship in April 2027 and the Summer Olympic Games in 2028. Trump’s pro-Russia tendencies may prompt him to strongarm the IIHF and IOC into bringing Russia back in from the cold. For now, the Carney government has leaned into the rupture. Ignoring the court ruling, blocking Russia’s participation and standing with Canada’s European allies is consistent with Carney’s new skepticism toward the aforementioned naive multilateralism. But it comes at a cost to whatever remains of the rules-based international order . articles.content: Carrie-Anne Moss in Crave's _YAGA_. The series, based on the play of the same name, draws on Baba Yaga from East European folklore. (Crave/Christopher Lawrence) Baba Yaga is a terrifying witch from eastern European folklore , found in folktales from Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and other Slavic countries. Yet she is more than just a scary monster. In many folktales, she offers advice and assistance to characters who are kind and clever, while punishing rude, selfish ones. Baba Yaga’s intriguing duality — her ability to be both a villain and a saviour, a figure of destruction and renewal, of darkness and light — has inspired artists and writers to produce lively adaptations that have travelled well beyond eastern European folklore and made her a favourite among audiences worldwide. The recent Crave series YAGA , starring Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams, is the latest in a long history of versions of her tales . The series, whose showrunner wrote the acclaimed play of the same name , imagines “ the myth of Baba Yaga as a contemporary mystery thriller .” As an anthropologist who has studied folklore and witchcraft, I want to examine the original Baba Yaga and how she has been received by western audiences. Trailer for ‘Yaga,’ starring Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams. Deep in a forest In folktales, Baba Yaga lives deep in the forest in a round house that spins on chicken feet, surrounded by a fence made from the bones and skulls of her victims — a grim warning of her cannibalistic nature to anyone who would dare intrude on her. She flies through the skies in a giant mortar and pestle, making a dreadful noise as she crushes her victim’s bones. Baba Yaga takes her place alongside similar villainous folktale witches; in Slavic folktales, she plays the role of the witches in tales like Hansel and Gretel, Snow White and Sleeping Beauty, whose purpose is often to both frighten and test the folktale protagonist. At the same time, her unique characteristics make her a classic figure of eastern European folklore who has become a symbol of Russian cultural identity . Beyond being a villainous witch, she can also help a sympathetic character find their missing family member, provide wealth and prosperity and even reveal the secrets of immortality. Her actions reward the kinds of behaviours that are helpful in human societies while punishing those that violate popular morality, emphasizing values that are important to storytellers and their audiences. ‘Russian Folktales’ of 1863 Oral tales of Baba Yaga date back to the days of the ancient Rus’, the ancestors of modern Russians . She first came to the attention of western readers through Alexander Afanasyev’s massive collection, Russian Folktales , published between 1855 and 1863. Almost all later adaptations of Baba Yaga stories are based on tales from this collection. Her popularity in the West increased after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. There have now been countless book and dramatic adaptations featuring Baba Yaga. Like other folkloric witches, Baba Yaga has been interpreted through a variety of lenses, each offering a perspective on why she continues to fascinate us. Russian structuralist Vladimir Propp argued that the folktale hero’s quest can be read as an initiation rite into self-knowledge and adulthood . ‘Grandmother Yaga’ Baba Yaga, whose name means “grandmother Yaga,” acts as both a challenger and a maternal figure who ushers the hero or heroine into the world of adulthood. The protagonist journeys into the dark forest where they encounter Baba Yaga, who tests their courage and wisdom by assigning impossible tasks, asking difficult questions or presenting opportunities for heroes and heroines to show their mettle. She rewards strength, courage, cleverness and facing up to her challenges, giving protagonists the ability to return home and thrive in everyday life. The protagonists come back forever changed, having gained both self-knowledge and wisdom, the very qualities that define maturity. Insights from psychology A number of scholars have offered psychological interpretations of Baba Yaga, ranging from strictly Freudian to more nuanced perspectives . Psychologist Bruno Bettelheim, who wrote about the meaning of fairy tales in his book The Uses of Enchantment , emphasized how Baba Yaga’s dual nature reflects a child’s view of its mother as a source of both love and nurture, and fear of punishment . But the fairy-tale witch might have different meanings for children of different ages. For very small children, Baba Yaga may primarily be a scary figure meant to frighten them into compliance with adult wishes. For older children, she can represent the often hostile but sometimes helpful strangers who usher them into a world of greater responsibility and self-confidence. Detail of Baba Yaga from a larger watercolour illustrating Russian fairy tale Maria Morevna. (Giles Watson/Flickr) , CC BY-SA Feminist interpretations Early feminist interpretations drew parallels between Baba Yaga and the Great Mother goddess, a feminine deity of fertility, death and regeneration alleged to have been worshipped by some prehistoric European cultures . More recent feminist interpretations focus on the witch as embodying the shadow side of the female in male-dominated societies: the woman who cannot or will not be dominated . As the opposite of what patriarchal society expects of women, she is monstrous, aggressive and frightening: she destroys men and eats children, the reverse of the alluring seductress and nurturing mother. Yet the witch is powerful exactly because she exists without the permission or control of men. Baba Yaga lives by herself deep in the forest, the heart of the natural world; she alone controls who can cross her bony fence. In a post #MeToo era in which women’s rights to bodily autonomy are once again under attack, she has become a symbol of resistance against male dominance, violence against women and environmental destruction . articles.content: “The only way we’re gonna get through this,” Lucia tells Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA6), “is by sticking together.” GTA6 is, unlike its predecessors, built around a relationship between two lead characters. The game tracks their level of intimacy on a four-point scale : running on empty , partners in crime , crazy in love and hot together . As a player, you must actively maintain the bond between them — by having them be nice to each other, go on dates and of course work together to commit crimes. And yes, they even have sex. The game has a relationship meter that allows players to watch the connection between the two rise and fall. Rob Nelson, Rockstar North’s head of development, told The Verge : “You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.” For some people, this idea, that a video game is trying to simulate a normal human relationship, will immediately set off alarm bells about the dangers of digital intimacy, especially for teenagers. I don’t think there is much to worry about. GTA6 is an immersive experience, to be sure, and players are definitely going to become invested in Lucia and Jason’s romance. But their interactions are scripted. Will artificial intimacy diminish us? Recently we have heard lots of dire warnings about what MIT researcher Sherry Turkle calls “artificial intimacy.” Turkle has recently published a book warning about the risks of emotional connections with artificial entities . In it, she says: “If these are the relationships we choose, we will be left in a world of non-relationships. Artificial intimacy is positioned to colonize and diminish the human kind.” Governments are also increasingly concerned about the risks of AI companionship, particularly for minors. China has prohibited AI companions for underage users. In the United States, several states have passed laws restricting or banning AI companions. U.S. congress is considering a federal law that would prohibit minors from using them. Tens of millions of people, including, inevitably, many teenagers, will play GTA6 in the coming months, and will experience first-hand the artificial intimacy between Jason and Lucia. They will spend hours deliberately fostering and building that intimacy. Should we be worried? A game that encourages empathy Turkle is mostly concerned about AI companions that engage users in open-ended conversations and respond directly to their emotional needs. These bots can create the impression of a reciprocal relationship with a partner who is responsive and emotionally invested. That’s a very different experience from developing a relationship between two fictional characters within a game. Also, GTA6 offers a notably positive vision of romance. Turkle argues that digital technologies allow us to experience the comforts of companionship without having to face up to the demands of human relationships. She argues that artificial intimacy is too easy, and this turns us off the messiness that comes with real attachment. GTA6 models something different. Jason and Lucia have to nurture their bond. They must talk to each other and be attentive to each other’s needs. Lucia reminds Jason: “Relationships are about communication, Jay.” And because players can switch between characters, they experience the relationship from both sides. As Rob Nelson, one of the three creative leads on GTA6 at Rockstar North, told The Guardian : “We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage empathy — for those who want it.” Arguably, Lucia and Jason show us just the sort of relationship that Turkle believes is threatened by technology. A transactional logic Though we definitely shouldn’t panic about GTA6’s digital intimacy, I do think there are aspects of the relationship that are worth noticing. The game is built around optimization. Players raise the couple’s bond meter through specific actions and the rewards are concrete. As the meter rises, the couple holds hands and kisses. At the top tier, the game unlocks the option for sex. Affection is a score, and intimacy becomes something the player earns by supplying the right inputs. Once the meter is maxed out, the couple never fights. In this way, it reproduces the sort of transactional logic that worries many critics of AI companions. In the game, these things are pretty harmless. The relationship is between two fictional characters, rather than between a user and a machine that claims to care about them. And no one profits from how attached the player becomes to Lucia or Jason. But the dynamic parallels some of the ways AI companion apps operate, and these can be more insidious. With these apps, the equivalent mechanics — reminders that your companion misses you, intimate content that is unlocked through engagement or by paying — are central to the business model. The laws of virtual romance As we debate whether and how to regulate AI companionship, the lesson here is not to target an entire class of technology. Blanket bans on AI companions are not the answer. Artificial intimacy can be harmless, or even positive, for users . Rather, we should focus on specific design features that can cause harm, particularly to young people. We should, for instance, look at the way AI companion apps are designed to maximize engagement, the way they use emotional pressure as a retention tactic and the way they present affection and sex as a reward for specific behaviours. Jason and Lucia are poised to become the digital world’s two most famous outlaws. It would be a nice irony if they end up teaching us a lesson about how to write better laws governing virtual romance. articles.content: For post-secondary students, every new academic year inevitably comes with tuition bills, textbook costs and a long list of student fees, as well as mandatory health plans . Students are locked into a number of plans covering outpatient prescription drugs, dental, extended health and virtual health care, but they’re not allowed to opt out of their school plans without comparable private insurance. These plans make Ontario college and university students under age 25 ineligible for the Ontario Health Insurance Plan Plus (OHIP+) , which covers nearly 6,000 medications at no out-of-pocket cost. Ontario’s Liberal government introduced OHIP+ in January 2018, providing free prescription drug coverage to eligible residents under 25, regardless of private insurance. In April 2019, Premier Doug Ford’s Conservative government restricted OHIP+ to cover only those who did not otherwise have private coverage . As OHIP coverage cannot be used to opt out of school plans, thousands of post-secondary students lost access to Ontario’s public drug program. To examine how Ontario post-secondary students may have been affected by this sudden change, we reviewed prescription drug plans across colleges and universities. We documented all cost-sharing components (for example, deductible, co-insurance, co-payment, dispensing fees and annual limits), specific coverage for contraceptives and exclusions . We then compared students’ coverage to the coverage available under OHIP. Variations in plans We identified substantial variation in prescription drug coverage across university and college student health plans, resulting in important inequities. There were significant disparities in cost-sharing and contraceptive coverage. Students were responsible for paying anywhere from zero per cent to 50 per cent of their prescription costs, most commonly 20 per cent. Annual coverage limits ranged from $250 to $12,500. Additionally, colleges in northern Ontario generally offered less comprehensive coverage and imposed more restrictive reimbursement criteria. Notably, none of the plans sponsored by student unions compared favourably with coverage available through OHIP. Contraceptive coverage varied considerably across institutions. Some plans covered oral contraceptives but excluded other methods such as devices and implants. Others imposed product-specific reimbursement limits, while some provided no contraceptive coverage at all. These gaps are especially concerning given that the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada identifies intrauterine devices as a first-line contraceptive option for adolescents and young adults. This illustrates the disconnect between evidence-based clinical guidelines and private insurance coverage policies. Many coverage restrictions affect conditions that already carry significant stigma, particularly among young adults. Treatments for smoking cessation, obesity, acne, infertility and erectile dysfunction were frequently excluded from coverage, subject to reimbursement caps or otherwise restricted. Such limitations may create additional barriers to care, as students may be reluctant to seek treatment because of financial concerns, stigma or both. Smoking cessation therapies were frequently excluded from student health plan coverage. In contrast, OHIP provides coverage for prescription smoking cessation medications for individuals aged 18 years and older, as well as up to one year of pharmacist-led smoking cessation counselling. In 2020, the United States Surgeon General highlighted the critical role of insurance coverage in supporting smoking cessation, stating: “Insurance coverage for smoking cessation treatment that is comprehensive, barrier-free, and widely promoted increases the use of these treatment services, leads to higher rates of successful quitting, and is cost-effective.” Impact on health and access to care Higher prescription drug costs can have important consequences for students’ health and access to care. Research from Canada and internationally consistently shows that people are more likely to use medications when they have insurance and face lower out-of-pocket costs. Conversely, losing insurance or facing higher costs can reduce medication use. A recent study in JAMA Pediatrics found that the introduction of universal coverage in Ontario in 2018 led to increases in contraceptive dispensations and decreases after restrictions were introduced. Beyond the equity and health implications of the April 2019 changes to Ontario’s public drug program, important efficiency concerns also arise. Public drug insurance programs such as OHIP are generally more efficient than private insurance mechanisms, including post-secondary student plans, in collecting revenue, sharing financial risk and administering coverage. As a result, public systems can often deliver comparable or more comprehensive coverage at a lower overall cost than fragmented private insurance arrangements. The modest reductions in government spending associated with the 2019 cuts are unlikely to offset the additional costs imposed on Ontario residents. Given the inherent and increasing inefficiencies of private insurance, including higher administrative expenses and less effective risk pooling , shifting coverage from the public to the private sector is likely to increase overall system costs and lead to higher premiums for students and their families. G. articles.content: How much public support does a company need before it can build a major development in a community? And who gets to decide if that threshold is met? These questions are emerging in New Brunswick, where two communities are approaching the prospect of AI data centre development differently. In Fundy Shores, the mayor has called for new rules governing AI data centres , even though no developer has proposed building one in his municipality yet. The municipality wants future data centre developers to obtain council approval through a rezoning process, giving residents an opportunity to weigh in before construction could proceed. In nearby Saint John, residents have been debating a proposed facility in Lorneville . At a public meeting, they raised concerns about air quality, water consumption and the benefits such a project would bring. After the meeting, one resident told reporters: “I think it demonstrates that there is no social licence for this project.” The two communities illustrate different points in the debate over social license: how to establish public support for a project before it is proposed, and what happens when residents believe that support is absent. As an environmental communication researcher, I have studied how supporters and opponents of liquefied natural gas development in British Columbia made competing claims about whose interests those projects would serve. I see similar disputes in debates over AI data centres, particularly when different parties claim to speak for the people who will live alongside a project. What is a social licence? Having a “social licence to operate” refers to the ongoing acceptance of a project by people affected by it . The term emerged in the mining industry in the 1990s, when companies recognized that even with government permits in hand, opposition from neighbours could delay or disrupt their operations. It captured the practical importance of public support, though it left open who could grant it or judge when it had been lost. Unlike a government permit, a social licence is not a formal legal authorization. It’s an informal relationship between a developer and the communities affected by its activities. Consider the debate over Enbridge’s proposed Northern Gateway pipeline . In April 2014, residents of Kitimat, B.C., where the pipeline was proposed to terminate, voted on the project. Of those who voted, 58.4 per cent opposed it . Read more: Where does all the hardware go? The hidden environmental footprint of AI data centres What followed was a political dispute about how much weight residents’ responses should carry . Opponents pointed to that result as evidence that Enbridge had failed to earn local acceptance. An idea the mining industry had used to explain why companies needed public support had given residents a way to express their opposition. Some pipeline advocates, including newspaper columnists and Conservative politicians, objected that opponents were claiming a veto over projects of national importance. A company could welcome consultation, yet disagree about what should happen when residents rejected its proposal. Whose support counts? Claims that a project has or lacks a social licence often depend on who is speaking for the community, and whose views are being counted. The public meeting in Saint John gave some residents a chance to voice their concerns, but it could not establish how the wider community felt about the proposal. The same challenge arises when projects are presented as having public support. A council resolution reflects elected representatives’ positions; a benefits agreement records what its signatories accepted while a public vote reflects the views of those who participated. Each provides evidence about a different group of people , but none necessarily represents everyone affected. This question of representation is especially important when projects affect Indigenous nations. First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities have distinct rights, governing institutions and authority to make decisions. Their views cannot be subsumed into municipal consultation or treated as another measure of local opinion. What if a community changes its mind? There is a danger to treating social licence as a one-time decision, as I mentioned in a recent interview about Fundy Shores . Before a data centre is constructed, residents have forecasts and promises to consider. Once a facility opens, they can measure those promises against their lived experiences, including how the operator responds when something goes wrong. Sherbrooke, Que., offers one example of how the experience of a project after it opens can change how a community views it. The city agreed to supply electricity to Bitfarms for a bitcoin mining facility . Soon after it opened, neighbours began complaining to the city about the noise. Bitfarms replaced the fans and installed a noise barrier, but the problem persisted. In 2021, the city and the company agreed in principle to move the operation to an industrial park . A social licence, then, is not something a developer keeps indefinitely. It largely depends on whether a project continues to meet the expectations of the people affected by it. Residents views may change as a project develops and its impacts become clearer. A council’s approval may allow construction to proceed, but it does not guarantee lasting community acceptance. Residents must have opportunities to hold operators accountable as they experience the project’s effects. Sibo Chen receives funding from Toronto Metropolitan University and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Councilof Canada. He is a member of International Environmental Communication Association as well as Vice-Chair of the Environment, Science & Risk Communication Section of the International Association for Media and Communication Research.

articles.content: Climate activists at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey , awarded Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney a Fossil of the Day award , along with other leaders from wealthy countries who skipped the summit. The satirical award is given to countries and leaders seen as doing little to support efforts to tackle climate change. The award was not the only criticism of Carney’s climate credentials. Newsweek listed the prime minister at No. 2 on a list of “climate heretics,” just behind Microsoft founder Bill Gates and ahead of United States President Donald Trump. These criticisms might seem surprising, as Carney has been seen as a climate champion. At the 2015 COP in Paris , Carney said companies need to develop plans for net-zero emissions . Yet, after becoming prime minister, he scrapped the federal consumer carbon tax and signed an agreement with Alberta to push forward a new oil pipeline. How should we make sense of the Fossil of the Day award? How did Carney go from seeming climate hero to climate villain? As sociologists, we have written about and researched environmental activism around COP summits. These gatherings are not only places for policy discussions. They provide a platform for activists to push for action and direct criticism toward obstructive governments and corporations. Fossil of the Day as a strategic event Social movements take advantage of global events such as COP to name and shame political leaders or corporations that they identify as climate villains . At COP summits, the Climate Action Network hosts the Fossil of the Day award, as well as some other awards. The ceremony resembles a TV comedy sketch, where activists describe the key climate negotiation events they wish to highlight, and set out to embarrass those obstructing progress. While this is going on, a person in a dinosaur suit dances and music from Jurassic Park plays. Meanwhile, activists sing songs with lyrics they make up for the event. Fossil of the Day is about taking advantage of a critical event. Groups like the Climate Action Network award Fossils of the Day to try to affect media coverage, influence public opinion and ultimately pressure governments to take greater action to tackle climate change. Some critical events like COP happen on a regular schedule that is known in advance. We have referred to these as regularly scheduled critical events . Groups can plan ahead and take advantage of opportunities to comment on and critique the conversations going on in official spaces of deliberation among global leaders. Relatedly, interaction ritual theory explains phenomena that often occur in the context of a common action or event . Some key elements of the process include: group assembly (bodily co-presence), mutual focus of attention and shared mood. Engagement in interaction rituals often fosters group solidarity, emotional energy, symbols of social relationship and standards of morality. We can think about the Fossil of the Day in these terms. Activists and other COP participants routinely try to attend the Fossil of the Day award. It is an opportunity to meet up and rub elbows. Participants benefit from camaraderie, some light-hearted humour, and also, in some cases, righteous anger directed at leaders, governments and other bodies who obstruct climate action. These get-togethers reinforce social ties among the participants. Canada: Climate hero to climate villain? At COP21 in Paris, then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau announced, “Canada is back!” The Trudeau government’s environment minister, Catherine McKenna, helped to negotiate the Paris Climate Agreement . One of Carney’s first acts as prime minister was to cancel the consumer carbon tax Trudeau brought in. And, among other things, Carney is now working to develop new oil and gas projects . At COP31, Carney was a no-show at the leaders summit. This past week, two former environment and climate change ministers criticized the record and direction of the current government. McKenna stated that the claim that Canada is still committed to its targets is “factually untrue.” Indeed, Canada consistently has one of the worst climate performance records . The Climate Change Performance Index, which compares the climate performance of 64 countries and the European Union, ranks Canada 62nd . This poor performance started before Carney’s tenure as prime minister , but Canada has been backsliding on the climate change file since he took office. In the view of many Canadians, Canada faces serious, and even existential, threats from the Trump-led United States. In the wake of this threat, Carney has been trying to boost economic growth and diversify international and domestic trade. Much of this has involved plans to grow the fossil fuel sector . The strategy has also been an attempt to assuage discontent fuelling separatist sentiments in oil-rich Alberta. What is not entirely clear is whether the direction of Carney’s energy and climate policies is a short-term strategy to deal with these crises, or a longer-term pivot away from climate action.
