articles.description: What would it mean to teach students who are learning academic writing to use AI in “ethical” ways — for example, large language model (LLM) chatbots like ChatGPT, a specific form of GenAI? In rhetoric and writing studies, guiding documents on the teaching of writing and literature caution against all-out bans and call for guidance on ethically incorporating LLMs into writing. My institution, the University of Victoria, is “ committed to support the use of AI in transparent, responsible, ethical and equitable ways .” In the context of teaching writing, “ethics” and AI tends to be shorthand for academic integrity, informed by questions about composing and authorship , transparency and the writing process . However, even when ethical guidance around AI use includes reflecting on when AI is appropriate at all, this often assumes, as a foregone conclusion, that ethical AI use is a possibility. AI has environmental costs , and raises profound social and human concerns . We are doing students learning academic writing a disservice if we don’t think more broadly about what “ethical” use means. Classrooms are political spaces Writing is inherently bound up with power, and many writing studies scholars and teachers see classrooms as inherently political spaces. They focus on practices that equip students to add their voices to academic conversations, without compromising their ways of knowing. For these scholars, classrooms are places to develop anti-racist , equitable and inclusive practices. Many encourage students to question power and privilege , especially in first-year writing classrooms. Students learn to build arguments, organize evidence and communicate effectively to specific audiences. They gain transferable skills and experiences that can be foundational for structuring the rest of post-secondary life. Read more: How a first-year university writing course for Indigenous students fostered skills and belonging Tyler Branson , a professor of literature who also teaches composition, describes how “we might be better off thinking of first-year writing as a course in the practice of citizenship” instead of a course in academic writing. articles.content: Canada’s efforts to reduce international student numbers have had a striking effect in Atlantic Canada. Universities in the region have lost nearly half their international students in three years. According to preliminary figures released in October , international enrolment fell by 3,020 students (18 per cent) in the past year. That brings the decline since federal restrictions began in January 2024 to almost 48 per cent. Canada’s restrictions aim to address national concerns, but their effects vary across the country. The sharp decline in Atlantic Canada raises questions about whether federal policy takes enough account of smaller provinces. Read more: International students cap falsely blames them for Canada’s housing and health-care woes A decline beyond expectations In 2024, Ottawa introduced a cap on international student study permit applications. The government cited rapid growth, housing pressures and concerns about oversight. The government subsequently set further limits on international student enrolments for 2026. There were good reasons for reform. International student recruitment had grown quickly, and governments needed to ensure that institutions could support the students they admitted. Yet the scale and distribution of the decline have surprised even federal officials. In March, Canada’s Auditor General reported that the restrictions had reduced new study permit approvals more sharply than expected. Ottawa anticipated declines of no more than 10 per cent in several smaller provinces, including all four Atlantic provinces. It even expected an increase in Newfoundland and Labrador. Instead, approvals fell by at least 59 per cent in these provinces. The federal immigration department could not explain why approval rates fell so far below expectations. Allocating study permit applications to provinces does not guarantee that students will receive permits, accept university offers or enrol. Nor can the entire enrolment decline be blamed on the federal cap. Student applications, permit approval rates, financial pressures and Canada’s appeal as a study destination also affect enrolment. The scene at Memorial University Where I work in the faculty of education at Memorial University in Newfoundland, international enrolment fell from 4,889 students in 2023 to 2,682 in fall 2026 , a decrease of more than 45 per cent. There are signs of improvement. New international enrolment increased by 14 per cent this fall. But rebuilding student numbers after several years of decline will take time. In an October update , Memorial reported that total enrolment had fallen by two per cent over the past year. This happened despite increases in new undergraduate and graduate students. Memorial’s experience shows how changes in immigration policy can make long-term university planning more difficult. Why regional differences matter Atlantic Canada faces circumstances that differ greatly from Canada’s large metropolitan centres. A recent Atlantic Economic Panel report identifies an aging population and ongoing difficulties finding workers as barriers to economic growth. It also highlights the importance of immigration in sustaining population growth and addressing labour shortages. International students are not a substitute for sound immigration or workforce development policies. Not all international graduates choose to remain in Canada. Those who wish to stay must find suitable employment and meet immigration requirements. Nevertheless, post-secondary education can provide a pathway into the Canadian workforce. International students in Atlantic Canada can develop professional networks, gain local work experience and build careers in the region. A recent study in Atlantic Canada highlights the importance of immigration in sustaining population growth and addressing labour shortages. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Andrew Vaughan Falling international enrolment also affects university finances. Statistics Canada reports that international undergraduates paid an average of $41,746 in tuition in 2025–26. Canadian undergraduates paid an average of $7,734. Although fees vary by province and program, declining international enrolment can disproportionately affect university budgets. It’s been estimated that Canadian universities lost about $1 billion in annual international tuition revenue between 2023-24 and 2025-26. Further losses are projected through 2030-31. That doesn’t mean universities should depend indefinitely on international tuition to balance their budgets. Heavy reliance on one revenue source leaves institutions vulnerable when policies change . A better way to assess the policy Addressing the enrolment decline doesn’t mean returning to the previous approach to international student recruitment. Concerns about housing, student protection and the integrity of the study permit process are important. But reducing study permit numbers should not be the only measure of success. The federal government should examine why approval rates differ so sharply among provinces. It should also consider regional needs and whether universities can adequately support international students. Provincial governments and universities have responsibilities too. These include providing housing and student services, maintaining sound recruitment practices and helping graduates find employment. Read more: Canada identifies international students as ‘ideal immigrants’ but supports are lacking Canada needs policies that balance immigration goals with the unique needs of its regions. This doesn’t mean abandoning national limits; it means examining their effects and making changes where needed. Atlantic Canada’s experience shows that reducing international student numbers is not enough to judge whether a policy works. Its impacts on universities, students and the communities they serve matter too. Dale Kirby receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.

articles.content: Tokyo then, St. John's now? A giant squid attacks a bait squid off the coast of Tokyo in 2006. (Tsunemi Kubodera/National Science Museum of Japan) , CC BY When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below , about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport , I thought to myself: “THIS I’ve gotta see!” First, the series showcases coastal Newfoundland, where I was raised and live. Second, I have studied ocean life in the island’s waters for most of my career. Third, it features the marine lab where I work , the Oceans Sciences Centre. And fourth, it stars a giant squid(-ish) animal (sorry Josh Hartnett). Giant squid have a special place in Newfoundland folklore and science, from early encounters with fishermen to some of the first scientific evidence of their existence. Unveiling the giant squid One key player in this history was the Irish clergyman Moses Harvey , who moved to Newfoundland in 1852 and undertook natural history research in what was then a British colony. Harvey’s research included revealing the existence of giant squid to the world based on a specimen that washed ashore. Fishermen had brought it to him to photograph and communicate to the science community in London. Arms, tentacles and head (buccal region, including beak visible) of a giant squid from Logy Bay, Newfoundland, photographed draped over Moses Harvey’s sponge bath in November 1873. (Variously attributed to John Maunder, Moses Harvey and Messrs. McKenny and Parsons) Fast forward to the 1960s, when the founding director of the Ocean Sciences Centre, Fred Aldrich , joined the faculty at Memorial University and soon focused his career on pursuing giant squid. Although Aldrich tried to catch a living specimen, he only obtained squid that washed up on beaches. Newfoundland is one of the global hotspots where giant squid appear more frequently, every 30 years or so (New Zealand is another, attesting to giant squid affinity for cooler waters). Below ‘s arrival roughly coincides with one of those cycles. The Rooms provincial museum in St. John’s displays a preserved version of one of these amazing animals. Giant squid: Not known to be vindictive Early in the series, we meet an (oddly) barefooted marine biologist walking through the hallways of the marine lab. This scene earned a loud “ewww” from my graduate students on the grounds of hygiene as well as occupational health and safety. The biologist turns out to be the expert on giant squid and the voice of sanity when fishermen, the military and a local developer all pursue the creature (nicknamed “Mudder” by the locals, foreshadowing why she is attacking the community) with bloodlust. This marine biologist also provides impromptu medical expertise when residents fall ill from drinking ice water tainted by the animal. (Side note, DO NOT entrust your local marine biologist with urgent medical needs — we are not that type of doctor!) I could join the Facebook crowd quibbling about who got the Newfoundland accents right and who missed the mark. Or I could ask why the Coast Guard would fully abandon people living on a small, isolated island in crisis. But Below generally did a good job on the science. The biology of the animal was reasonably plausible, including its swimming skills and even its ability to survive in ice. As a (likely necessary) stretch, I thought the intellectual prowess and directed vindictiveness of the squid in the series pushed the limits of credibility, although researchers have documented some impressive abilities in cephalopods (of which giant squid are members). Still, it was a good effort to maintain scientific plausibility and fun to see marine biota as the star attraction. Historical accuracy I took a course in marine invertebrates from Aldrich when I was an undergraduate in the early 1980s. Although he was in the late stages of his career, his enthusiasm for giant squid was still evident in his lectures. He would have loved to have seen the first live footage of giant squid in the wild collected just 20 years ago by Japanese scientists, and I think he would have enjoyed watching Below and he’d be happy I’m writing about it. I certainly enjoyed watching Below , not just because of the Newfoundland setting but because it seemed entirely appropriate for the story, which was in some ways a homage to Newfoundland and its ocean history. The plot weaved in the innate capacity of local fishers to adapt and work together to solve challenges (who can “put the arse back in a cat,” as locals would say). It addressed the collapse of the northern cod fishery that threw some 37,000 Newfoundlanders out of work. And it began with a striking scene about the government’s resettlement of more than 28,000 residents of many small coastal communities to larger centres in the 1950s and '60s. It also captured the general mistrust of government in outport communities. My CFA (come from away) graduate students also appreciated seeing the “Screeching In” ceremony , and the real sense of Newfoundland conveyed by the series. Read more: The trauma caused by resettlement in Newfoundland and Labrador must be acknowledged Stoking interest in the ocean I am not a particular fan of the horror genre, though I recognize its nod to productions from decades earlier when creatures emerged from the ocean depths to wreak havoc on an unsuspecting humanity (think Godzilla , Jaws , and Orca ). Though the genre isn’t for everyone, most people I asked said they enjoyed the series, and particularly the Newfoundland ambience. I also applaud the Below team for communicating the complexity of the ocean, and their efforts to capture the imagination and interest of the public with its many unknowns. The series also underscored the ongoing potential for ocean exploration. Scientists discover thousands of new marine species every year and could discover many more if there were more of us. Many of these discoveries come from the deep sea , where giant squid spend most of their time. Most new marine species are small animals, but, as scientists sample more ocean, a surprise discovery occasionally emerges not unlike the giant squid in Below . Perhaps given Below ’s success ( the No. 1 ranked show in Canada on Netflix the week after its release , with an 87 per cent Tomatometer on Rotten Tomatoes ), Hollywood might see some potential in telling exciting stories that bring the ocean into our living rooms. That focus could inspire a new generation of scientists. I can’t help thinking that watching Jaws and Orca when I was an impressionable teen helped to push my career interests towards the ocean, where my ancestors had also earned their living. Paul Snelgrove receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Council of Canada and the Canada First Research Excellence Fund.

articles.content: Elizabeth Holmes is questioned by Nathan Fielder in 'You Can See Everything.' (A24) This story contains a spoiler about ‘You Can See Everything .’ Canadian comedian Nathan Fielder’s runaway-hit documentary You Can See Everything reintroduces audiences to Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted of fraud in 2022 . Holmes maintains she is innocent . Through Fielder’s lens, the film prompts us to question her conduct anew by exploring the meaning of acting, drama, truth, lies and fiction. In the film, Holmes objects to a quote of hers reported by the New York Times . According to the Times , Holmes said of actors portraying her: “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” In Fielder’s documentary, Holmes’s husband reads the quote and says it doesn’t sound like something she would say . He suggests Holmes said instead: “They’re playing a character they created,” and she agrees. Partly through the film’s interviews with Holmes and her husband, as well as commentary by Fielder, viewers are led to wonder: Has she been playing a character she created, intended to deceive others? Is she now playing a role? Does she even know? Playing a role If Holmes is deliberately playing a role, we are inclined to condemn her as a fraudulent deceiver, well-deserving of her punishment; if not, we may be more inclined to see her sympathetically — flawed, caught up in a scheme largely wrought by others. ‘You Can See Everything’ trailer. It might seem that, because each person knows what they’re doing, they’re the authority on whether they are playing a role. But Fielder’s film, and his previous work that straddles the line between awkward comedy and social inquiry , challenges where the boundaries lie. In his HBO docuseries The Rehearsal , Fielder plays himself as a director helping people prepare for difficult situations by staging elaborate rehearsals of how they might unfold . The series leads the audience to question the relationship between the rehearsals and the real situation they mean to influence. Actions, imitations One way to think about this is by examining the difference between doing things and acting as though we’re doing them — for the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, the difference between an action and an imitation. To frame this issue more carefully, we can turn to a distinction Aristotle drew between “action” and “production.” For Aristotle, the arts are particular kinds of know-how. A shoemaker, for instance, knows how to produce shoes. Drama, writes Aristotle, knows how to produce the imitation ( mimēsis ) of actions . The actor’s aim is to produce a compelling imitation of someone, say, making a shoe. That imitated action is the product of the art. When done well, the audience is convinced they have seen someone do the action, perhaps briefly forgetting it was only an imitation. Often, an actor playing a shoemaker does not go so far as to make a shoe. But what if they do? ‘The Fielder Method’ The fourth episode of The Rehearsal , “The Fielder Method,” sees Fielder describe a method to train people to perform on his show. Fielder invites actors to shadow a person, called their “primary,” to learn how to imitate them in the rehearsals. He goes so far as to have them work the job of their primary or even move into a similar living arrangement. Following this method, it very well may be the case that an actor playing a shoemaker makes a real shoe. “The Fielder Method” shows that the distinction between “imitated action” and “genuine action” is porous. An audience, actor can get lost An effective imitation convinces audiences, temporarily, that we are witnessing the action, and we respond to it, at least in part, as a doing of that action. But it might suggest that understanding her properly requires us to think about the role of imitation and art in our lives, just as Fielder’s works challenge us to do. On the other hand, what exactly have we seen? Commentators have raised ethical concerns around how Fielder’s relationship to his subject shapes what we do and importantly don’t see (such as the impacts of Holmes’s fraud) — or genre questions , including whether it really should be called a documentary. Read more: Can you see everything? Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes face off in You Can See Everything A compelling imitation, Aristotle tells us , is delightful because we love to learn, and imitation teaches us. This may be why scores of audiences are going to cinemas to watch an almost three-hour-long documentary . articles.content: In its November budget , the federal government promises households “a boost today and a bridge to tomorrow.” But above all, the budget is a bet on business investment. Its centrepiece is the Productivity Mega Deduction , a tax incentive that allows businesses to write off the full cost of eligible capital investments. It’s expected to cost $36 billion over five years . By my calculations, only about 22 cents of every new dollar goes to affordability measures. These include not only direct household assistance but also housing, skills and immigration. As a tax policy researcher at McGill University, I read budgets for how policy choices show up in everyday economic life. Looking beyond the headline announcements reveals who benefits, how much they receive and when that assistance arrives. The highlights for households For many households, the biggest immediate effect is the continuation of existing support , including rent subsidies for low-income tenants, provincial funding for home care and mental health and food bank support. Four changes stand out. The Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit — formerly the GST credit — will provide another one-time top-up in early 2027, worth up to $339 for individuals and $679 for couples with two children, paid in full to most households earning under about $46,000. The new Build Canada Workers Benefit pays the lowest earners up to $675 more and reaches workers earning under $40,000 (about $52,000 for families), but from 2028 they will receive it only after filing their tax return. The federal caregiver credit becomes refundable from 2027, meaning it’s paid even to people who owe no tax. About 180,000 low-income caregivers who currently receive no benefit will be able to claim up to $1,260 annually. The most consequential change may not touch wallets at all. From the 2027 tax year, everyone will have a May 15 deadline to file and pay their taxes. This gives most taxpayers two additional weeks to pay, but self-employed people will have a month less to file. To illustrate how the changes could affect people in different circumstances, I have constructed five fictional household scenarios, based on the budget’s eligibility rules and benefit calculations. Scenario 1: A university student in Toronto Arjun, 20, rents in Toronto and earns $25,000 from part-time and summer jobs. Arjun will get the full grocery top-up of $339. Although he earns a low wage, he will not benefit from the higher workers benefit because full-time students are excluded. He could benefit from renewed rent subsidies only if he already receives them. He will also be able to visit national museums for free, as admission becomes permanently free for people under 25. What’s in it for him: a single payment of $339 and free museum admission. Scenario 2: A low-income family in Winnipeg Kwame and Sophie rent a house in Winnipeg and have two young children. Sophie earns $18,000 annually, while Kwame earns $2,000 from part-time work alongside caring for his mother, who has dementia. The family will receive the full $679 grocery top-up, and, by my calculations, $200 more from the new workers benefit, since Kwame’s $2,000 in earnings do not reduce the benefit. But from 2028, that benefit will come only after they file their tax return, not in payments during the year. The biggest gain is for Kwame. He has long been eligible for the caregiver credit but with too little income, he could never use it. Now that it is refundable, he receives the full $1,260 a year. Their children will also be able to visit the Canadian Museum for Human Rights for free. What’s in it for them: about $2,100 more in support the first year (with some of it paid later) and free museum admission for their children. Scenario 3: A business-owning household in Mississauga The Chows are homeowners in Mississauga, Ont., with a combined annual income of $120,000. The father, Tony, runs a catering business as a sole proprietor. They earn too much to qualify for the grocery top-up or the workers benefit. But Tony is the kind of business owner the budget’s centrepiece is built for. If he buys $40,000 of new kitchen equipment, the Productivity Mega Deduction lets him deduct the full cost in the year he buys it, rather than over several years. At a 30 per cent tax rate, that cuts his tax bill that year by about $12,000. The new May 15 deadline gives him two more weeks to pay, but a month less to file. What’s in it for them: about $12,000 less tax in the year Tony invests, more time to pay but less time to file. Scenario 4: A retired pensioner in Sudbury Lucien, 73, lives in Sudbury, Ont., and receives $45,000 annually in pension income. Lucien will receive the full $339 grocery supplement, but no new support through Old Age Security or the Guaranteed Income Supplement. Because little tax is withheld from his pension income, he owes approximately $4,000 annually. He must pay this in four quarterly instalments of about $1,000. Starting in 2028, the threshold for mandatory instalments rises to $7,500, allowing him to pay his tax bill in full when he files in May. What’s in it for him: a single payment of $339 and less paperwork. Scenario 5: A self-employed artist in Halifax Daniel, 34, is a self-employed illustrator in Halifax, earning $62,000 annually. The budget’s opening pages promise to make up to $45,000 of artistic earnings tax free. However, the measure is only a proposal to consult on a non-refundable Canada Creative Credit that, combined with the basic personal amount that everyone already gets, would cover up to $45,000 of artistic business income. If implemented, it could save Daniel up to approximately $4,000 annually in federal tax, based on my calculations. But details are not expected until spring 2027, and whether an illustrator’s work will qualify as “original and creative artistic works” is still to be decided. What’s in it for him: a potential tax benefit, but for now, a promise rather than a payment. Who benefits most? The budget’s assistance is primarily aimed at the lower-income households, particularly workers and caregivers. Much of it, however, is either a one-time payment or will not arrive until 2027 or later. Seniors, students and salaried middle-income families get little new support. Meanwhile, the biggest tax break goes to businesses that invest, and it pays off only for those that are profitable. The government is betting that greater business investment will raise incomes over time, and eventually benefit Canadians more broadly. But those gains are not guaranteed, and households facing high living costs need relief now. For now, they get a boost. The bridge to tomorrow is still under construction. Preetika Joshi does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Imagine you are sitting on a train, moving at a constant speed. The blinds are drawn so you can’t tell you are moving. A light bulb hangs on a chain in the centre of the car. When someone turns it on, your human eye perceives the whole carriage lighting up. What actually happens is that light first reaches the two sides of the car simultaneously. A moment later, the light reaches the front and back of the car, again simultaneously. The light has travelled at the exact same speed in all four directions. Albert Einstein wondered how this situation would be described from the perspective of someone outside the train who was not moving with the car. For a drone hovering over the train, for example, the light still reaches the two sides simultaneously but the back of the car lights up before the front. This is because the train is moving forward, so in the moment it takes the light to travel to the front and back of the car, the back has moved closer to the light source and the front has moved further away. This phenomenon, discovered by Einstein in 1905 , is called the “relativity of simultaneity.” Physicist Brian Greene explains the concept of the relativity of simultaneity (World Science Festival). On the basis of this phenomenon, scientists have argued that in reality there is no objective “now” and that time does not truly pass. Some have even suggested that the apparent passage of time may be psychological . Modern cosmological observations, however, suggest that time is more than a mere illusion. The illusion of now Einstein himself declared time to be an illusion. On the passing of his friend and fellow physicist, Michele Besso, he wrote: “Now he has departed from this strange world a little ahead of me. That means nothing. People like us, who believe in physics, know that the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion .” Along with Einstein, physicists and philosophers have often used relativity to argue there is no such thing as true simultaneity. For example, if you could say that a star several hundred light-years away is exploding “right now,” you could also stand up and walk away from it and just as well conclude that it won’t explode for another minute or so. By extension, if there is no objective now, and if all relative “nows” are on equal footing, then perhaps reality encompasses all of “ spacetime ” — every event that ever happens anywhere across the universe throughout all of eternity. Perhaps, as Einstein said, time really is nothing but a stubbornly persistent illusion. From the perspective of modern cosmology, however, it seems that an objective “now” does exist. Is the train really moving? It is tempting to say that the drone hovering in a fixed place above the train in our scenario is “at rest” and that the train is “really moving.” But we know the Earth is rapidly spinning and orbiting the Sun, which is orbiting the Milky Way, which is moving relative to nearby galaxies and so on. A composite image of the central region of our of the Milky Way galaxy using images from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, Spitzer Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory. (NASA/JPL-Caltech/ESA/CXC/STScI) Therefore, neither drone nor train can be defined as “the one that’s moving” or “the one at rest” in any absolute sense. We could define either as an equally valid relative state of rest. On the other hand, if there was an absolute state of rest and an objectively well-defined “now,” we would require a concrete scientific measurement showing that the associated space has always persisted as such, along with a way to measure velocity through it from anywhere in the universe at any time. That would make the one state of rest objectively well-defined relative to all others. Such a space could then be said to “exist” in the usual sense of the word, with Earth and all of us existing in it, and it would provide consistent definitions of “now” and of “motion.” The cosmic now Cosmology delivers this. We have already made the required measurements using the cosmic microwave background (CMB) — the cooled remains of the first light released after the Big Bang. The CMB reveals that our universe — the three-dimensional expanding space where we live and evolve — has existed for approximately 13.8 billion years. It also shows the universe to have expanded by an integrated factor of about 1,100 since it formed; and that our solar system is moving through it with a velocity of 369.82 kilometres per second towards the Crater constellation . Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist. (Wikimedia) The integrated expansion of space throughout cosmic time has been so precise in every direction we look that across the sky we can measure “ anisotropies ” that were imprinted on the CMB at the time it was formed. These are tiny differences in the CMB’s temperature from one direction to another, of about one part in 100,000, which map the slightly denser and slightly thinner regions of the early universe. It would be impossible to see this if space were not objectively defined and expansion had been different here and there. This means that Einstein’s relativity of simultaneity still applies to local phenomena as a matter of relative perspective: neither the train nor the drone gets to say they are the one that is truly at rest, and both frames of reference can be used to describe reality, just as Einstein found. However, contrary to his belief, time is more than a mere illusion. The implication from modern cosmology is that the universe exists, and events happen all across space in the course of cosmic time. These events may be described as synchronous or not, depending on one’s motion through the universe, although there is in reality one cosmic time and an objective measure of simultaneity. Daryl Janzen does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

These events may be described as synchronous or not, depending on one’s motion through the universe, although there is in reality one cosmic time and an objective measure of simultaneity. articles.content: Canadians aged 65 and older want to decide where they live and most prefer that place to be their current home . The concept of an older adult aging in the place of their choosing emphasizes that preference. Preference, however, does not guarantee that aging in that place will be possible. Feasibility depends on an older person’s circumstances and supports available where they live. John Amagoalik’s story illustrates the gap between preference and possibility when it comes to aging in place of choice. A lifelong advocate for Inuit self-determination and one of the key figures behind the creation of Nunavut , Amagoalik recently spent 16 months in an assisted-living facility in Ottawa after an infection resulted in the amputation of part of his leg. Being more than 2,000 kilometres from Iqaluit, Amagoalik told the CBC, “The worst part was the loneliness.” Friends eventually helped arrange the housing and care that has allowed him to return to his home for now. Although Amagoalik’s circumstances are particular to Nunavut, where some elders must leave the territory to access specialized services not available closer to home , his story raises a question relevant across Canada: What does it mean to say older persons have a choice about where they age if the supports they need are not available where they want to live? What determines where people age As occupational therapists and rehabilitation scientists , our research explores how engagement in everyday activities contributes to health and well-being in later life. Our work has led us to recognize that where people age is shaped not only by their preferences but also by their circumstances and supports around them. For us, this research is also personal. Our mothers continue to live independently, and both chose to move closer to family. Like many with aging parents, we think about what will allow them to continue doing so if their health, mobility or circumstances change. Having a choice about where one lives as one grows older requires realistic options. Rural communities can offer strong social connections and a sense of belonging, but as needs change, limited access to transportation, affordable and accessible housing, and other health and social services may constrain people’s ability to remain in the place they call home. Rural aging and mobility Research on rural aging has described a related tension between “aging in place” and being “stuck in place .” Remaining somewhere does not necessarily mean an older person had a meaningful choice to do so. Transportation provides a good example. Our research with older persons living in rural areas and small towns around Hamilton, Ont., identified considerable reliance on personal vehicles . If few alternatives exist, losing the ability to drive can mean losing access not only to medical appointments and groceries, but also to activities and relationships outside the home. Mobility, after all, is about much more than getting from one place to another. Being able to get around allows us to see friends and family, volunteer, exercise or simply participate in everyday activities that make life meaningful. However, what happens when driving is no longer possible and there is no realistic alternative? If managing your current home becomes difficult, is there help or a suitable and affordable option nearby? Can needed services be accessed without leaving your community? These questions also make us think differently about risk. Risk and what matters Families and health professionals understandably worry about falls , driving safety or whether an older adult can live at home alone . While those risks matter, our research has identified that focusing too much on physical safety can sometimes overshadow what older people themselves value when decisions are being made about where and how they will live. Stopping driving may reduce one kind of risk while increasing risks of isolation and loss of meaningful activities . Moving somewhere with more services may make some aspects of life easier or safer but moving away from neighbours, relationships and a place we call home has consequences for well-being. A home that no longer meets an older person’s needs can carry risk, but so can leaving it. Supporting real choice Planning ahead for mobility changes matters but so do housing, relationships, finances and ensuring support is available. However, people cannot plan around options that do not exist. Supporting real choice about aging in place also means asking: Can older community residents get where they need and want to go? Are housing, health and social supports accessible where people live? When those supports are not available, who fills the gaps? Families, friends and neighbours provide extraordinary support and can expand an older person’s choices but should not be the only infrastructure upon which aging at home depends . Aging in a place of choice cannot simply mean asking older people where they want to live. Communities and governments must ensure people have meaningful and realistic options as their health, mobility and circumstances change. Choice only means something when there are real options. Evelyne Durocher receives or has received funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, the Canadian Institute for Health Research, the Canadian Occupational Therapy Federation and the Physiotherapy Foundation of Canada.

articles.content: Open any news feed from the past few months, and the disasters arrive in a stream: smoke reaching dangerous levels throughout Canada and flash floods in Ottawa , Montréal and Toronto ; heat and drought arriving together on every continent. Driven by climate change, these events are happening more often, and rather than remaining isolated, they cause cascading, interrelated effects. Now enter the “super” or even “Godzilla” El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific. This phenomenon changes weather patterns globally, potentially bringing more extreme heat, drought and flooding. Although it’s a natural climate phenomenon, scientists are concerned about the unprecedented rate of surface warming. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has declared a greater than 83 per cent probability of strong to very strong El Niño conditions during January to March 2027 . Historical precedents are sobering, with major El Niño events of 1982-83 , 1997-98 and 2015-16 leading to extreme flooding in some regions, severe drought in others, and widespread disruption to ecosystems and economies . Now imagine if hospitals were overrun with respiratory events due to wildfire smoke, migraines, heatstroke and delirium. At the same time, the electricity grid could go down due to overwhelming demand from the use of air conditioning systems. If that scenario sounds plausible, it’s because every element has already happened in Canada, just not all at once. We call these scenarios polycrises, to represent multiple connected crises occurring simultaneously. We’ve seen these before, such as the 2013 Calgary floods , the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and the 2023 Northwest Territories wildfires that required evacuation. The toll of polycrisis on health care The health-care system deserves special consideration when preparing for polycrises. Canada’s health-care system is over capacity on a normal day, with now-familiar hallway medicine, long wait times, surgical delays, understaffing and insufficient primary and long-term care. Canadian access to care ranked ninth of 10 peer countries in a 2025 study , above only the United States. Now imagine adding severe wildfire smoke, a flood causing energy outages and a new viral illness. It’s easy to imagine health-care access and quality declining. Health care suffers at the centre of polycrises. Wildfire smoke has contributed to 1,900 premature deaths annually and $18 billion in costs in Canada. Evidence shows that smoke increases all-cause mortality and causes exacerbations of cardiovascular disease, respiratory conditions , neurologic diseases like multiple sclerosis and migraines . It can trigger stroke and delirium, affect fetal health and has been associated with developing dementia . During the 2023 wildfires, Ontario asthma-related emergency visits increased by 23.6 per cent . Floods disrupt transportation, supplies and patient discharge, while evacuations overwhelm communities, like when 20,000 Northwest Territories residents fled to Alberta in 2023. Supply-chain interruptions threaten access to medications and medical equipment, as seen during COVID-19. These crises disproportionately affect underhoused individuals , people with disabilities, lower-income households and Indigenous communities . Energy implications A strong El Niño can put the entire energy system under strain, just when the health system is most vulnerable. The effects begin months earlier. Milder winters, altered precipitation and reduced mountain snowpack diminish spring runoff and hydroelectric inflows, leaving reservoirs with less stored energy as summer demand peaks arrive. It can also influence the likelihood of extreme summer heat, which often coincides with periods of low wind output. In June 2026, Europe experienced a heat dome accompanied by a wind drought , reducing wind generation just as soaring temperatures drove up electricity demand for cooling. In extreme heat, solar power has lower capacity – known as derating – losing roughly 0.4 per cent for every degree above 25°C , and dims further under wildfire smoke. Gas turbines also lose capacity to hot-air derating on the hottest afternoons. As with the broader polycrisis, the primary issue is convergence. Demand rises precisely when many supply sources are constrained, leaving the grid with less room to absorb the next shock. The shared patient Energy poverty is where the energy system and health system share a patient. While hospitals have backup power and contingency plans, the greatest risks lie in the community. The households least able to afford cooling, air filtration or backup power are the same populations over-represented in heat and smoke morbidity. British Columbia’s 2021 heat dome led to more than 619 deaths, primarily among the elderly and those who lived in under-resourced communities . The heat dome that fills emergency departments with heatstroke and delirium is the same weather system derating the gas turbines that power hospital wards. The smoke triggering asthma exacerbations also reduces the solar output flowing into the grid. The insulin requiring refrigeration, the elevators in seniors’ residences and the oxygen concentrators in patients’ homes all depend on electricity precisely when demand is greatest. This is the defining property of a polycrisis: interconnected failures that neither the energy system nor the health-care system can prepare for alone. What resilience looks like The encouraging part is that the two systems share their defences as surely as they share their failures. Storage, demand flexibility, interties (transmission links that let grids share electricity), backup power at critical facilities and cooling centres with assured power: every investment that hardens the grid against El Niño-pattern stress also protects health outcomes. One system’s resilience budget is the other’s prevention budget. Energy-affordability support is preventive medicine delivered through a utility bill. The El Niño forecast’s real value is lead time. We must act on this warning and secure backup power, fund cooling centres, bolster critical supply chains and identify patients whose health depends on the grid. The time to prepare for a polycrisis is before the emergency is at our doorstep. This story was co-authored by Luke Killam, co-founder and CEO of GreenKey Energy, an independent energy consultancy. articles.content: Right now, Leonard Cohen is on many of his fans’ minds. The Canadian poet, novelist and singer-songwriter died Nov. 7, 2016, just one day before United States President Donald Trump was first elected . Ten years later, as the Democrat “blue wave” hopes to close the bracket on a president who once memed himself as Jesus personified , Cohen’s legacy has become effortlessly epic — even biblical — in quite a different way. Tribute gatherings Tribute gatherings for the singer abound. Cohen was the subject of a sold-out event at the Toronto International Festival of Authors at the end of October. Adam Cohen’s family tour, which began in Canada this month and reaches Europe in winter 2027, pairs his father’s music with archival photos and film . Ottawa’s Gladstone Theatre advertised their “Ten Years Gone” commemoration with a question quite suggestive to people like me who study the evolution of sacred texts: “What would Cohen say today?” Cohen’s ‘contemporary psalms’ As an answer, I highlight an under-celebrated part of Cohen’s poetry and song. As I detail in my 2023 book Prophets of Love: The Unlikely Kinship of Leonard Cohen and the Apostle Paul , all of Cohen’s work is infused with biblical allusions. But some of Cohen’s work does more than echo biblical themes. It takes on biblical format, in the tradition of poetic prayer known in Hebrew as tehillim . Tehillim, or Psalms, inform the Jewish liturgical tradition of addressing God directly, not only in praise, but also in lament, desperation and challenge . This is most explicit in what publisher McClelland and Stewart called Cohen’s “contemporary psalms” in his Book of Mercy . In 1984, as Cohen turned 50, his life provided the material for the 50 psalms of lament, complaint, joy, doubt, adoration and desperation that made up this poetry collection. Like the biblical Psalms, these short poems are numbered rather than titled. Cohen described the collection as “meant for people like myself who could use it, at a particular time,” as “a book of prayer.” Many interpreters continue to analyze this collection as Tehillim . Writing liturgy Although modest about himself in public, Cohen never lacked ambition for his poetry. Rabbi Mordecai Finley , who has read Cohen’s poems aloud for High Holy Days, recalls Cohen confiding that he felt he was always writing not just poetry, but liturgy. Ben Sales points out that Cohen’s song “If It Be Your Will” echoes the Friday evening prayer service welcoming Shabbat, and “Who By Fire” is a nearly word-for-word arrangement of the High Holiday prayer, the “Unetaneh Tokef .” Cohen’s “ Anthem ,” with its famous line “that’s how the light gets in,” inspires ponderings from both Christians and Jews . And “ Hallelujah ,” — a biblical term heard in church services — is a star example of a Cohen song as religious anthem, despite its references to surprisingly carnal biblical texts . I believe Cohen’s grappling with the divine, whether overt, or nestled within his sensual poetry, might prove to be his most enduring memorial. Multiple traditions and levels Cohen biographer and author Harry Freedman reports that Cohen studied in India, referenced the Kabbalah frequently and knew the lore of the Christian Desert Mothers and Fathers . Both Kabbalah and early Christian ascetics blur the boundaries between the erotic and the divine. Cohen’s way of addressing the sensual and the spiritual simultaneously allows the same song to reach different people — or reach the same person at different times. He could also speak from multiple traditions. Cohen was an ordained Rinzai Zen monk , the grandson of a famous rabbi and Talmud scholar. As an impressionable child he went to mass with his Irish nanny in Montréal, a city of churches. In I’m Your Man , music journalist Sylvie Simmons chronicles how Cohen was a deeply knowledgeable Jew who moved comfortably between the Torah, Talmud, Tao Te Ching, Sufi mysticism and the New Testament. No religious tourist Fewer Canadians remember the literary critic Northrop Frye than know Cohen. But the poet turned out to be the perfect example of the professor’s point: the educated imagination lives and breathes the vocabulary of the sacred. Cohen was no religious tourist. Rather, the singer “spoke multiple religions” fluently, always from his Jewish roots. At this 10th yahrzeit of his passing, it’s worth considering to whom (besides his audiences) he addressed his final performances. In “Traveling Light,” from You Want it Darker , he sang: “But if the road leads back to you, Must I forget the things I knew …Traveling light, like we used to do.” Grappling with God Like the ultimate Psalmist, King David, dethroned and on the run , Cohen was at a low point in his career when he wrote Book of Mercy . In those dark days of seeming failure, before Jennifer Warnes’s Famous Blue Raincoat revived his career, Book of Mercy was the middle-aged Jewish poet’s attempt to leave at least something of permanence: “We talk in this manner, we sing the time-honoured songs, and we compose new ones, as we were commanded,” he wrote in “25.” Yet, for me, it is Cohen’s final albums 20 and 30 years later, as his life neared its end, that most resemble the Psalms in how they grapple with God. Psalms for every human experience Through the years, Cohen addressed God right before our eyes in the person of a lover. At the end of his life, he boldly exposed the relationship that had been there all along — perhaps most notably in the song “You Want it Darker.” Here, he addressed God as “My lord,” incorporated elements of the Jewish mourners’ prayer and adapted Rosh Hashanah liturgy . Was Cohen writing and adapting Kaddish for his own impending death? I believe so, although in true Cohen fashion his words also mourn humanity overall, and challenge the divine. Leonard Cohen’s ‘You Want it Darker.’ As I wrote in Prophets of Love , for Leonard as “Cohen” (Hebrew for priest), existential longing and divine connection are inseparably linked at the base of the human condition. So, 10 years later, even if you are already a devotee, have a listen again. Pay special attention to how Cohen challenges, pleads with, chastises and even woos the divine. If you are not yet a fan, buy one of the iconic Canadian’s final albums, when he could feel death waiting at the door . You may find that, just as for many faithful opening the ancient psalms, there’s material in Cohen’s contemporary psalms for every human experience, including yours. Matthew Robert Anderson's research has received funding from the Federation for the Humanities and the Social Sciences (FHSS)

At the end of his life, he boldly exposed the relationship that had been there all along — perhaps most notably in the song “You Want it Darker.” Here, he addressed God as “My lord,” incorporated elements of the Jewish mourners’ prayer and adapted Rosh Hashanah liturgy . Was Cohen writing and adapting Kaddish for his own impending death? I believe so, although in true Cohen fashion his words also mourn humanity overall, and challenge the divine. Leonard Cohen’s ‘You Want it Darker.’ As I wrote in Prophets of Love , for Leonard as “Cohen” (Hebrew for priest), existential longing and divine connection are inseparably linked at the base of the human condition. So, 10 years later, even if you are already a devotee, have a listen again. Pay special attention to how Cohen challenges, pleads with, chastises and even woos the divine. If you are not yet a fan, buy one of the iconic Canadian’s final albums, when he could feel death waiting at the door . You may find that, just as for many faithful opening the ancient psalms, there’s material in Cohen’s contemporary psalms for every human experience, including yours. articles.title: 10 years after Leonard Cohen’s passing, his grappling with the divine lives on

articles.content: Some of the world’s most powerful technology executives are investing heavily in artificial intelligence while simultaneously preparing for the possibility that it could threaten humanity. From underground bunkers to isolated islands , some of the industry’s wealthiest figures appear to be making plans to shield themselves from the very risks associated with the technologies that their industry is helping to develop . The benefits of technological innovation are not necessarily shared by everyone, nor are its risks. Those who profit most from developing new technologies may not be the same people who bear the consequences when things go wrong. Sociologists have long studied this unequal relationship through the concept of “risk positions.” Just as people occupy different positions in society according to wealth and economic power, they also occupy different positions when it comes to risk . At one end of the spectrum are those who reap substantial benefits from producing risks while avoiding most of their consequences. At the other are those who benefit little from these activities but bear a disproportionate share of the costs . Who benefits and who pays? The economic rewards associated with producing risks can be enormous. Industries that generate environmental damage or financial instability , for example, can create substantial private wealth while imposing significant costs on society. Yet few industries have produced fortunes as extraordinary as the technology sector. Some of the fastest-growing companies in history have emerged from the tech sector, while their founders have accumulated astronomical levels of wealth . The prospect of accumulating even greater wealth creates a powerful incentive to keep developing risky technologies . But this is only half the story. To understand why risks may be produced beyond what is socially desirable, we also need to consider who pays for them. When those who produce risks do not bear their full costs, they have an economic incentive to keep producing them, even when the consequences for society are potentially devastating. The more effectively producers of risk can avoid these consequences, the greater the burden placed on everyone else. In this framework, it’s not enough for producers of risk to benefit from said risks; they also need to be able to avoid any potentially catastrophic consequences. They need to occupy the positions of “value skimmers” — those who benefit from upside of risk-taking while avoiding its potentially devastating downside. They are distinct from “value surfers” who gain from risks, but also bear the consequences when those risks materialize . Preparing to escape the consequences The distinction becomes particularly revealing when considering the growing tendency among tech executives to prepare for potential future catastrophes . Several prominent figures in the AI industry have publicly warned that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity . Yet those warnings don’t seem to have slowed the development of AI at all . Locked in a battle for AI supremacy, there doesn’t appear to be an inch to give between competing tech giants . There are also concerns about generative AI that have come from within the industry itself. Employees and researchers working in the field have raised alarms about the scale and ambition of AI development, including comparisons to the Manhattan Project and technologies reminiscent of the fictional Terminators . Yet while some of the industry’s leaders appear to be doing their best to insulate themselves from these risks , their companies’ business models depend on expanding digital infrastructure and collecting as much data as possible. This expansion forces ordinary people to be constantly dependent on digital connection and leaves them fewer opportunities to avoid the risks associated. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into digital networks, those networks also become more vulnerable and risky. To prevent any aspect of our life from being outside internet dependence is to force us to be constantly at the mercy of technology companies. Could the public push back? German sociologist Ulrich Beck argued that modern society is one in which we must constantly face the social, political and economic problems of distributing a “poisoned cake.” His metaphor captured a central problem of what he called the “risk society” — the benefits of modern development are distributed unequally, while the dangers it creates can extend far beyond those who produce them. Yet Beck did not believe citizens would take this lying down. He argued they would come to see the reality of the risks being produced and act collectively to arrest control of this system away from those producing them. The conditions for such a moment may now be emerging. Protests against the expansion of data centres alongside parents’ demands that governments protect children from the harms of social media are just two trends that suggest people are coming to recognize their real risk positions. Perhaps people’s acceptance of bearing the brunt of the risks that they did not create is coming to an end. Whether it’s the people, the politicians or the tech giants who will win this debate is still to be decided. Dean Curran receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC).

articles.content: When a human picks up a coffee cup, we use predictive processing based on our understanding of the world. For a robot, picking up a cup requires extensive training and simulation. (Unsplash) Today’s artificial intelligence technologies have become remarkably good at generating text and ideas that seem profoundly human. Chatbots powered by large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini and Perplexity AI can write poems, brainstorm and find solutions to complex problems. The developers of these products drew heavily on the human brain for inspiration , creating artificial neural networks based on the workings of human neurons. Their systems now produce outputs that often resemble the outputs of human thinking. AI and the human mind, however, do not work the same way. Similar results do not necessarily mean similar processes. “World models” are an emerging technology that could help AI systems move closer to human “thinking” by helping them learn to anticipate what might happen and use that prediction to act. Still, AI will not perceive, learn or understand the world as humanity does. Read more: Cyber attacks? Bioterrorism? To ‘Pace the Frontier’ of AI effectively, we must improve our anticipatory thinking A falling cup, a complex prediction Imagine reaching for a cup at the edge of a counter. The cup may fall and smash if you misjudge the distance, grip it too loosely or move too quickly. For humans, grabbing a cup like this is routine. Yet this simple action relies on the complex ability to anticipate what might happen next. Our minds constantly try to stay one step ahead by understanding events and their causes. We can foresee the mess that would result from moving an overfilled cup or imagine a sofa getting stuck in a doorway even before we buy it. These predictions draw on expectations that form when we interact with the world . What we anticipate can, in turn, impact how we perceive the world and how we act. One influential family of theories, known as predictive processing , proposes that perception works partly in this way. The brain generates expectations, compares them to the information it receives and makes adjustments when the two don’t match. Let’s return to the example of the cup. Imagine reaching for an empty cup that you believe to be full. Your hand, expecting a heavier object, lifts it with more force than necessary. The cup rises abruptly and feels almost weightless. That mismatch provides feedback that helps correct the movement and update your estimate of its weight. What we anticipate shapes our actions, and what happens next updates our expectations. All this happens just to pick up a cup. Does AI predict differently? Even for today’s robots, reliably manipulating cups can require extensive training and simulation . The challenge involves learning how the physical world behaves and predicting the consequences of an action. Chatbots using large language models also make predictions, but of a different kind. They learn to predict the next word or fragment of text . This apparently simple way of predicting can nevertheless produce remarkably capable systems able to solve complex problems. Take the sentence: “A hand bumps a cup near the edge of a table. The cup…” Having learned patterns from enormous amounts of data, a chatbot might continue with “tips over the edge and falls to the floor.” It can do so by predicting patterns from a dataset and without ever physically handling a cup. However, being able to describe plausible outcomes does not necessarily mean a chatbot has learned why they happen . Teaching a robot to anticipate This is where world models kick in — a broad family of AI approaches that aim to predict how situations evolve and, in some cases, how actions may change them. These models can learn from videos, simulations or recordings of what robots see and do. For a domestic robot, this could mean anticipating that gripping too tightly might break the cup, or that a wrong movement could tip it over. By incorporating actions, motion and sensory information , preliminary research shows these systems can help connect predictions with what happens in the physical world. A world model could eventually make the same predictions we do about a cup. And as it learns from actions and sensory feedback, the resemblance to us may become increasingly hard to ignore. Still, arriving at the same prediction does not tell us what knowledge supports it or how that knowledge was acquired. Same prediction, same cognition? To us, a cup is not only a cylinder on a table. It can be graspable, breakable, yours, mine, too hot or almost falling. Our understanding connects the cup’s physical properties to a network of possible actions and consequences. Predicting that the cup will fall reveals only a small part of that understanding. And this understanding develops quite early. Studies suggest that infants just a few months old already have basic expectations about how physical objects behave . Child-development researcher Jean Piaget proposed that children build knowledge through acting on the world. As this knowledge develops, they become able to mentally anticipate consequences without having to carry out each action. For humans, learning involves more than accumulating information about cups. It involves connecting experiences when reaching for one, feeling its weight, seeing it spill and eventually imagining what might happen without even having to try it. Using world models, AI can also learn from actions and sensory feedback, in addition to videos, simulations and other data. Like humans, they can learn to interact with the world. The question is how their experiences contribute to the knowledge they build and use. AI could definitely come closer to anticipating what might happen and using that prediction to act. This alone, however, does not show that AI perceives, learns or understands the world as we do. As AI gets better at replicating the results of human cognition, distinguishing performance from process will only become more important. articles.content: For some, the lesson in needing to look presentable to society began with a reprimand about scuffed shoes. For others, it was a warning about stray hairs, an untidy hairline, trousers that needed pressing or a last-minute stain. A parent was often ready to send you back to the mirror, unwilling to let you leave looking as though nobody at home had taken the time to care for you. Behind these admonitions was an uneasy mixture of affection and discipline. Taking pride in one’s appearance communicated dignity , but it also reflected the demands of respectability in a world where Black people have often worked exceptionally hard for recognition routinely afforded to others. No one needed to grow up attending church to appreciate the ethic of “ Sunday Best .” Rooted in traditions of dressing for worship, the practice reflects a collective belief that appearance can express reverence for an occasion and regard for those with whom we share it. ‘Sunday Best’ exhibition at the AGO At the opening of the Art Gallery of Ontario’s “Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style,” the crowd understood the assignment. Attendees arrived dressed to impress, bringing sartorial flair to the celebration. Conceived and curated by a transnational team, including AGO curator Julie Crooks and fashion historian Jason Cyrus, with Amanda Bock and Clare Sauro , “Sunday Best” brings together garments, photographs and personal effects spanning Black diasporic life from the 1880s to the present. Displays of church fashion recall generations of Black women and the splendour of dress for Sunday worship. Elsewhere, the distinctive uniforms of the Black Panther Party are on display, a nod to the role clothing and fashion play in political organizing. The exhibition also honours Black dandies , alongside those who have challenged conventions of gender through the way they dress. Among them are Toronto-based trans soul singer Jackie Shane and the late fashion icon André Leon Talley, a long-time editor at Vogue magazine , whose styles helped to expand the possibilities of Black self-presentation. The exhibition also contains references to ballroom culture that show how Black traditions of dress and performance have been inherited and reimagined for self-expression and communal recognition. Renewed attention on Black fashion The exhibition traces how Black styles and cultural practices travel through migration. Visitors may recognize traces of traditions from their own families. A hat may evoke an auntie preparing for church, a family photograph the sober pride of relatives posing for a formal portrait . The curators bring these expressions of Black life together, drawing connections between diverse traditions. The exhibition arrives amid renewed public attention to Black fashion. Last year, New York’s Met Gala put Black dandyism on the global stage with its theme, “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style.” “Sunday Best” contributes to this conversation by showcasing the communal rituals that give style meaning. The exhibition calls attention to the pressures under which Black people have fashioned themselves. Respectability and beauty In an iconic 1956 photograph, Gordon Parks depicts Joanne Thornton Wilson and her niece Shirley Anne Kirksey standing beneath a neon “Colored Entrance” sign outside a department store, in Mobile, Alabama . Their elegant and dignified dress contrasts with the indignity of segregation. For generations, dressing well could be understood as a defence against racial scrutiny or a means of improving one’s social standing . But no degree of sartorial excellence could guarantee protection from discrimination. The demands of respectability also placed constraints on those whose expressions of gender or sexuality challenged accepted conventions. Covers of Ebony magazine on display offer another perspective. As a Black-led publication, Ebony helped cultivate images of Black beauty and achievement in the United States that spoke to how Black communities understood themselves, free from the stereotypes and expectations of mainstream audiences. Across these histories, the attention given to one’s appearance carried meanings beyond the judgments of others. Dressing for worship could express reverence, just as a carefully chosen outfit might bring pleasure or communicate regard for others. The Sunday best tradition thus emerges as an ethic of dignity and care, fostered within Black communities even when those qualities went unrecognized by the wider society. Black queerness The exhibition’s treatment of Black queerness unsettles the presumed divide between church traditions and ballroom culture. Black churches have held complicated relationships with queer people , offering spaces for artistic expression alongside experiences of exclusion. Through these church communities, Black queer people have inherited styles and sensibilities they continue to reinvent. Consider drag performer Kennedy Davenport’s viral appearance on The Pit Stop . Reacting to another queen’s outfit, she sang: “Black stockings, white shoes, shouldn’t be allowed in the church.” Her playful critique drew on the rules of Black church fashion, finding humour in a set of esthetic rules passed down through generations. Black queer performers have also helped shape gospel music and traditions of Black religious life , including in spaces where their sexuality was not fully accepted. In “Sunday Best,” the proximity of church fashion to ballroom culture highlights how these traditions inform one another. Through inventive clothing and performance, ballroom turns resourcefulness into glamour, creating spaces where beauty and ambition earn recognition. Read more: Black style and resistance: The Met Gala, dandyism and blackface in Canada A ‘habit of care’ In the exhibition, everyday grooming tools share space with dresses and photographs. Hairbrushes evoke the private rituals behind a public appearance. Many of these belongings have survived for decades. In her book Ordinary Notes , writer and scholar Christina Sharpe describes regard as “a habit of care.” She says: “It is appreciation and esteem. It is the right of repair.” Her words invite us to consider the attention given to these belongings and the lives they represent. The curators extend this ethic of care to bring these histories together. From garments and paintings to archival photographs and moving images, their staging treats Black cultural expression as worthy of preservation and public appreciation. Behind the displays lies the painstaking labour of conservation, ensuring these materials will encountered by new generations. Black artists have long struggled for recognition in Canadian institutions, giving moments like these added weight. In 2019, the AGO hosted “The Feast” , marking 30 years since the groundbreaking exhibition “Black Wimmin: When and Where We Enter.” The gathering brought 100 Black women and gender-nonconforming artists and cultural workers into AGO’s Walker Court. At the opening of “Sunday Best,” the carefully dressed crowd offered another expression of this cultural legacy. Across the gallery, objects once worn with pride had been kept with care, their stories deserving of the same attention. Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style is on view at the Art Gallery of Ontario until Feb. 28, 2027. Cornel Grey does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Is that smoothie boosting your immune system or corporate profit? Research found over 96 per cent of immune-boosting content on Instagram to be from creators that sold or advertised products or services. (Unsplash) We all want a well-functioning immune system to help us fight invasive bacteria and viruses and recover faster from illness. Popular “immune-boosting” ideas, however, might be more of a hindrance than a help. Immune boosting is an online trend. Content producers share immune-boosting recipes — from smoothies to soups to poke bowls and pumpkin loaves . Nutrition books speak of “ super powered immunity ” while naturopathic clinics share immune-boosting “tips.” The “boosting” phrase has become so commonplace that it frequently appears in health content from reputable academic institutions . The COVID-19 pandemic — more so than ever in recent memory — had the public thinking hard about immunity . As interdisciplinary public health researchers studying the influential forces that shape public perceptions, the rise of immune-boosting discourse during this time caught our attention. We researched the trending concept in Google search results and on social media sites like Instagram . We found it to be problematic in two ways: First, content often presents scientific inaccuracies about how the immune system functions; second, it showcases corporations that push ineffective products or services. At a time when trust in evidence-based interventions like vaccines is on shaky ground , this can lead to negative outcomes for our health. Immunity and Society is a new series from The Conversation Canada that presents new vaccine discoveries and immune-based innovations that are changing how we understand and protect human health. Through a partnership with the Bridge Research Consortium , these articles — written by experts in Canada at the forefront of immunology, biomanufacturing, social science and humanities — explore the latest developments and their impacts. Balance, don’t supercharge Not all immunity-boosting content is inaccurate or harmful. Information from research or medical organizations often focuses on healthy eating, exercising , getting proper sleep and avoiding the harms of tobacco and alcohol . The idea of boosting or enhancing one’s immunity, however, remains fundamentally flawed. The immune system needs maintaining, not enhancing. That’s because each person’s immune system is complex, made up of cells, tissues, organs and proteins. This system works innately and non-specifically to keep harmful invader germs out, using, for example, the skin and mucous membranes as a protective barrier. It also works adaptively, deploying a targeted and specific response for harmful invaders. The body’s primary immune response. (Wikimedia Commons/Sciencia58) , CC BY-SA The adaptive immune system uses B-cells that produce antibodies — special proteins that attach to invader germs and either mark them for destruction or neutralize their effects. There are also T-cells, which act as destroyers, hunting and killing cells that have been infected by germs . Amazingly, the adaptive process of the immune system builds memory cells of the pathogens it battles. When the same invader re-enters the body, it can be quickly recognized and targeted more effectively. A well-functioning immune system also correctly differentiates between your own cells versus invader cells . An under-performing immune system increases the possibility and severity of infection . But an over-active immune system can lead to a host of autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis. Maintaining the immune system therefore involves balance — not supercharging its functions and abilities. Corporations boost profits Those who promote the concept of “immune boosting” are often simply trying to generate profit. The very idea of “boosting” can create a sentiment of lacking — that one’s health could (always) be better. This frames health status as a deficit requiring people to continually pursue restorative or optimization efforts — a commonly used health and wellness marketing strategy . The first step is to establish a void, accompanied by anxiety or fear. The second step is to offer purchasable actions that address the void. Our research on Instagram during the pandemic, for example, found that more than 96 per cent of the immune-boosting content we reviewed came from creators that sold or advertised products or services. We found 62 different companies tagged in a sample of 28 posts. We also reflected on how the social media hashtag #immunebooster itself functioned as a rhetorical product used to “generate activity in the online attention economy .” Other companies may promote immunity-enhancing products or services with immunity-enhancing claims, such as hydrotherapy , IV drips, cleanses and detoxes . Cereal companies in the past have also marketed their products as “supporting” immunity . There is no good evidence that any of these activities have immune-function benefit. Stem-cell supplements Dietary supplements in the form of vitamins, minerals or herbs also offer limited benefit to those without diagnosed deficiencies. As noted in an immune-boosting article by a Canadian pharmaceutical chain, “to date, no drug, product or natural remedy has been officially approved by Health Canada to boost the immune system.” Yet corporations market them as either explicitly boosting or generally offering benefit to the immune system . Recent research from our team , for example, assessed the marketing of “stem cell” supplements on the e-commerce marketplace, Amazon. We found more than 40 per cent of the products claimed immunity-related benefits. Supplements are now big business, with a market valuation in the hundreds of billions . It is not surprising to find a broad, all-encompassing marketing approach to products such as “stem cell” supplements that have no clear evidence of efficacy for any health ailment Trust in medicine The commercialization of immunity is a concern for all of us. Commercialized health spaces , can damage trust in health-care systems and confusion around who and what we trust . If our perceptions are shaped by companies and influencers , this might negatively influence vital evidence-based health activities, such as vaccination. Rampant vaccine misinformation during the pandemic dissuaded vaccine uptake and helped promote inaccurate ideas of personal immunity . Vaccine hesitancy is highly complex, with multiple factors at play. Politics and polarization are increasingly influential forces . Inaccurate immunity discourse only further clouds information landscapes and, in turn, vaccination decision-making. Health and wellness marketing is savvy and alluring, carefully crafted to pique our interest and provide solutions. In today’s media environments, we all need to be cautious and critical of companies marketing products and services for our health and well-being. It matters when assessing preparedness for any future pandemic , and how our health-care systems can build and maintain public trust. Accurate understandings of immunity help us maintain well-functioning immune systems and a well-functioning society. Alessandro Marcon is affiliated with The Bridge Research Consortium (BRC) Jia Hu works at the BC Centre for Disease Control where his work is focused on on immunizations and vaccine-preventable diseases.
