articles.content: After decades of relative neglect, menopause is suddenly everywhere — in the news, on social media and in conversations among friends. Some are calling it the “meno-boom,” and booms attract business. The Canadian menopause wellness market — meaning the products, treatments and services designed and sold to help women manage symptoms before, during and after menopause — is projected to reach a revenue of US$784.9 million by 2030 . But alongside the marketing are sensational claims and outright misinformation , including about how the menopausal transition affects mental health. That’s exactly what my research team has been studying for more than a decade. And as a woman now navigating perimenopause myself, I have a personal appreciation for why these conversations matter. I’m far from being in a minority: the Canadian Institutes of Health Research estimates that about 10 million people in Canada are currently navigating some stage of perimenopause, menopause or post-menopause transition . So let’s cut through the noise. Here’s what the evidence actually says about menopause and mental health. Before you know you’re in perimenopause The increased risk of depressive mood arises early in what researchers call the early menopause transition. This stage is marked by menstrual cycles that are consistently seven days shorter or longer relative to a woman’s usual cycle. Someone whose cycle used to average 30 days, for example, might start having 23- or 37-day cycles. So unless you’re tracking your cycle very closely, it can be easy to miss any connection between mid-life mood changes and perimenopause. It also doesn’t help that depressive symptoms have been shown to fluctuate considerably in perimenopause, making it a moving target. Not just about depression and mood swings Though a lot of research on the menopause transition has focused on depressed mood, there’s growing recognition that other psychological symptoms can show up too. For example, a recent study by our team , following perimenopausal women for three months, found that more than half struggled with moderate-to-severe anger and irritability. Weekly changes in sleep quality, hot flash severity, as well as hormones, predicted weekly changes in anger. Estrogen fluctuation in perimenopause has also been associated with greater sensitivity to interpersonal rejection , highlighting that psychological changes in the menopause transition can involve more than just feeling down. This fits with anecdotes from women that say they just “don’t feel like themselves.” Read more: Perimenopause usually begins in your 40s. How do you know if it has started? Hot flashes don’t explain everything Hot flashes are no fun, and they are extremely common in mid-life, with 60 to 80 per cent of women experiencing them in the years leading up to and following their last menstrual period. But as much as hot flashes may negatively impact quality of life, they don’t fully account for the increase in low mood that we see in perimenopause. For one thing, the timing doesn’t line up . Across the population, mood symptoms begin to increase well before hot flashes emerge. And by the time hot flashes reach their peak severity, depressive symptoms are already declining. At an individual level, this translates to many women experiencing depressive mood in the absence of hot flashes and many others experiencing hot flashes in the absence of mood changes. Hormone therapy isn’t a cure-all Menopausal hormone therapy is highly effective in treating hot flashes and night sweats. Vaginal estrogen cream is also a safe and effective treatment for vaginal dryness and sexual difficulties at any age. The benefits for cognitive difficulties (memory and thinking), sleep and low mood are less well-established. Multiple rigorous trials have confirmed that menopausal hormone therapy doesn’t prevent cognitive decline. And though it has been shown to improve sleep difficulties in women experiencing night sweats, evidence for its benefits in women without these symptoms is less conclusive. As for mood, the overall benefits of menopausal hormone therapy have been found to be quite modest, although some women may benefit more than others. Cognitive behavioural therapy and serotonin-based antidepressants remain the first-line treatments for depressive symptoms, including during perimenopause. Future research may help us better pinpoint who stands to benefit most from hormone therapy. In the meantime, it’s worth keeping both its proven benefits and the limits of the current evidence in view. Not everyone struggles with the transition The increased attention paid to menopause and perimenopause is long overdue, and it stands to greatly improve mid-life care. Women should not have to suffer in silence or go untreated. But we should be mindful about how we discuss it. Women have long been dismissed as “hormonal” — meaning less logical, rational and level-headed than men. Careless narratives or conversations about menopause risk reinforcing that stereotype. Our research consistently finds enormous individual differences in how sensitive women are to the hormonal changes occurring in the menopause transition. For some, rapid shifts in hormone levels can trigger a host of negative mood symptoms. For others, the effects are negligible. Women experiencing difficult symptoms deserve recognition and effective treatment. But mid-life can also bring greater confidence, autonomy and opportunities for personal and professional growth. For some, menopause also means welcome freedom from menstruation and concerns about pregnancy. The “meno-boom” has brought perimenopause out of the shadows, and that’s worth celebrating. But attention isn’t the same as understanding. The research reveals that this period is more complicated (and more individual) than pop culture and business marketing can capture. Taking women’s mid-life mental health seriously means resisting easy answers. Jennifer L. Gordon receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR).

articles.content: The appeal of leading man Edward Ferrars, played by George MacKay, is ramped up in this version. (Focus Features) Director Georgia Oakley’s new, unfettered Sense and Sensibility delivers a contemporary take on Jane Austen’s first published novel. At the beginning of the book, Henry Dashwood’s death leaves his grieving wife and three daughters ousted from their home. Norland Park is inherited by the son of a prior marriage, John, while the Dashwood women relocate to a small cottage in another county. The novel focuses on the two eldest daughters, Elinor and Marianne (in Oakley’s adaptation, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles) and their contrasting philosophies of sense and sensibility. Oakley has said she was inspired by Austen’s emphasis on sisterhood, and some reviews have noted the film’s strong depiction of this . The director has spoken to her interpretation of Austen as a writer who “was taking what she knew to be a commercial form … the romance framework,” while including “subversive” content . The film seeks to translate Austen’s 1811 feminism to a modern audience, but, for me as an Austen scholar, some important things are lost. Bold women who revel in nature We expect Austen heroines to take long walks in the English countryside , but this adaptation, more than any before, firmly plants its women in nature. The film is beautiful to watch: In the opening sequence, Marianne reclines on the ground amid tall reeds and contemplates a caterpillar balancing on her fingertip. Later, we see her bathing her feet in a cold brook; Elinor skips stones with her love interest. This is Jane Austen, unbuttoned. Both heroines wave aside social decorum when needed. Oakley’s Elinor even makes the first move. Once Edward Ferrars is a free man, she boldly kisses him on the lips with a windswept landscape as background. In conversation with other adaptations Oakley’s adaptation stands in conversation with previous versions. As literary critic Linda Hutcheon argues, earlier adaptations may “ be just as important as contexts … as any ‘original .’” Oakley draws on Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation in some ways, including in the depiction of leading men. Austen’s Edward Ferrars and Colonel Brandon may be underwhelming romantic interests. But their failure to capture the readers’ imagination is part of the point. While Oakley does highlight the women’s relationships anchoring Austen’s novel, she presents the male suitors more favourably — and this undermines Austen’s subversion of the romance plot. Literary scholar Deborah Kaplan has argued that the 1995 Sense and Sensibility and the 1996 Emma “harlequinize” Austen’s novels. We might say the same is true, to some extent, of Oakley’s version. Trailer for ‘Sense and Sensibility.’ Fulfilment in romance? Lee’s 1995 Sense and Sensibility cast Hugh Grant and Alan Rickman, setting up their respective characters, Edward Ferrars and Colonel Brandon, as romantic leads. Oakley’s men in these roles, George MacKay and Herbert Nordrum, don’t (yet) have the same Hollywood star power. But they follow in Grant and Rickman’s footsteps in romantic appeal. The film suggests both heroines find fulfilment in the courtship plot that Austen interrogates. For example, Oakley’s Edward, like Lee’s, endears himself to the audience by playfully entertaining the 13-year-old Margaret. Such scenes don’t exist in the novel. Oakley further ramps up Edward’s merit. In Austen, it’s not a mark in his favour that he fell in love with Lucy Steele and formed a secret engagement. In Oakley’s film, the alliance was arranged. Once the Steeles lose their fortune, he is expected to dissolve the engagement, but Edward is a man of honour. Treatment of Brandon, Willoughby Oakley’s Colonel Brandon, like Lee’s, is set up as a romantic hero. I initially mistook Oakley’s Brandon for Willoughby because his first appearance — tall, handsome, moody — matches the novel’s description of Willoughby’s horseback arrival. In the new Sense and Sensibility , tension between Brandon and Marianne seems to be there from the beginning. As in Lee’s film, scenes are added to ensure that we trust Marianne has a happy ending. Herbert Nordrum as Colonel Brandon in dialogue with as Daisy Esmé Creed-Miles as Marianne in Sense and Sensibility . Austen leaves us with less certainty. Near the novel’s end, Willoughby, having heard of Marianne’s illness, intrudes upon Elinor to inquire after her sister and offer an account of himself. It’s an explosive scene, and in the 1995 Sense and Sensibility , it was cut. Oakley keeps it — but makes significant changes. In the novel, Elinor is outraged by Willoughby, but she also pities him. As the narrator notes: “She felt that his influence over her mind was heightened by circumstances which ought not in reason to have weight; by that person of uncommon attraction, that open, affectionate, and lively manner … and by that still ardent love for Marianne.” Elinor can’t help but feel “a pang” for him. However, the film depicts Elinor as angry; he is a player, and she tells him as much, which drains the scene of its complexity. It’s curious that the film, at the same time, revises Willoughby’s villainy. In the novel, Willoughby impregnates a 16-year-old girl. In the film, his dalliance is with a widow of mature age. Loss of context around Norland Park The film, like the 1995 adaptation , circumvents an important backstory to the Dashwood women’s economic disenfranchisement. The Dashwood women are forced to leave Norland Park. (Focus Features) The novel’s opening paragraphs establish a complicated family history. Henry Dashwood, Elinor and Marianne’s father, inherited Norland Park from his uncle but on terms that didn’t let him leave it to them. Instead, the uncle’s will designated that Henry Dashwood, upon his own death, must pass the house to his son from a first marriage: John Dashwood, and, in turn John’s son, Harry. The narrator depicts this as unjust. The son already has an ample fortune. Rather than the proprietor uncle rewarding the Dashwood women for their care of him, he is swayed by the young Harry’s “attractions:” “an imperfect articulation, an earnest desire of having his own way, many cunning tricks, and a great deal of noise.” Oakley’s Sense and Sensibility , by contrast, doesn’t give this context and rather portrays the events as a matter of law. In this way, the film alleviates male family members from direct responsibility for the poverty of women. While there is much to enjoy in Oakley’s film, with its stunning cinematography and strong performances, it dilutes some aspects of Austen’s critique. Barbara K Seeber does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

Lee’s 1995 Sense and Sensibility cast Hugh Grant and Alan Rickman, setting up their respective characters, Edward Ferrars and Colonel Brandon, as romantic leads. Oakley’s men in these roles, George MacKay and Herbert Nordrum, don’t (yet) have the same Hollywood star power. But they follow in Grant and Rickman’s footsteps in romantic appeal. The film suggests both heroines find fulfilment in the courtship plot that Austen interrogates. For example, Oakley’s Edward, like Lee’s, endears himself to the audience by playfully entertaining the 13-year-old Margaret. Such scenes don’t exist in the novel. Oakley further ramps up Edward’s merit. In Austen, it’s not a mark in his favour that he fell in love with Lucy Steele and formed a secret engagement. In Oakley’s film, the alliance was arranged. Once the Steeles lose their fortune, he is expected to dissolve the engagement, but Edward is a man of honour. Treatment of Brandon, Willoughby Oakley’s Colonel Brandon, like Lee’s, is set up as a romantic hero. I initially mistook Oakley’s Brandon for Willoughby because his first appearance — tall, handsome, moody — matches the novel’s description of Willoughby’s horseback arrival. In the new Sense and Sensibility , tension between Brandon and Marianne seems to be there from the beginning. As in Lee’s film, scenes are added to ensure that we trust Marianne has a happy ending. Herbert Nordrum as Colonel Brandon in dialogue with as Daisy Esmé Creed-Miles as Marianne in Sense and Sensibility . Austen leaves us with less certainty. Near the novel’s end, Willoughby, having heard of Marianne’s illness, intrudes upon Elinor to inquire after her sister and offer an account of himself. It’s an explosive scene, and in the 1995 Sense and Sensibility , it was cut. Oakley keeps it — but makes significant changes. In the novel, Elinor is outraged by Willoughby, but she also pities him. As the narrator notes: “She felt that his influence over her mind was heightened by circumstances which ought not in reason to have weight; by that person of uncommon attraction, that open, affectionate, and lively manner … and by that still ardent love for Marianne.” Elinor can’t help but feel “a pang” for him. However, the film depicts Elinor as angry; he is a player, and she tells him as much, which drains the scene of its complexity. It’s curious that the film, at the same time, revises Willoughby’s villainy. In the novel, Willoughby impregnates a 16-year-old girl. In the film, his dalliance is with a widow of mature age. Loss of context around Norland Park The film, like the 1995 adaptation , circumvents an important backstory to the Dashwood women’s economic disenfranchisement. The Dashwood women are forced to leave Norland Park. (Focus Features) The novel’s opening paragraphs establish a complicated family history. Henry Dashwood, Elinor and Marianne’s father, inherited Norland Park from his uncle but on terms that didn’t let him leave it to them. Instead, the uncle’s will designated that Henry Dashwood, upon his own death, must pass the house to his son from a first marriage: John Dashwood, and, in turn John’s son, Harry. The narrator depicts this as unjust. The son already has an ample fortune. Rather than the proprietor uncle rewarding the Dashwood women for their care of him, he is swayed by the young Harry’s “attractions:” “an imperfect articulation, an earnest desire of having his own way, many cunning tricks, and a great deal of noise.” Oakley’s Sense and Sensibility , by contrast, doesn’t give this context and rather portrays the events as a matter of law. In this way, the film alleviates male family members from direct responsibility for the poverty of women. While there is much to enjoy in Oakley’s film, with its stunning cinematography and strong performances, it dilutes some aspects of Austen’s critique. articles.content: People who visit emergency departments (EDs) but leave without their care completed are often assumed not to have been ill enough to require that care. However, the high rates of people who leave without completed care is a symptom of the mismatch between the Canadian promise of health care for all and the current capacity of the health-care system. The most profound effects of this mismatch fall on people who are structurally disadvantaged. Our research shows that the people who rely the most on EDs report the poorest care experiences, and often leave without their care completed. This creates a cycle of worsening health and increasing costs. Studying the care experiences of nearly 1,700 patients across three British Columbia EDs, our research team found that people facing the greatest social and economic disadvantages were more likely to report discrimination in the ED, lack access to primary care, depend on EDs for ongoing health problems and rate their care poorly . They were also the most frequent users of EDs. In a different analysis, our research also showed that EDs can significantly interrupt this cycle . Promoting equity Our team at EQUIP Health Care has been researching how to increase effectiveness by supporting health-care organizations to focus on people least well-served by the health-care system. In other words, researching ways to promote equity. Studying primary care clinics that serve people marginalized by poverty, racism and other forms of stigma and discrimination, we identified three key dimensions to doing so: trauma- and violence-informed care , cultural safety/antiracism and substance-use health. We also identified 10 implementation strategies. Our findings showed that patients who received care that promoted equity were more comfortable and confident in their care, leading to increased confidence in preventing and managing their health problems. This, in turn, improved their health outcomes , including depression and trauma symptoms, chronic pain and quality of life. We learned that although education and addressing biases were useful for many providers, inter-professional conversations were needed to develop policy and practices to address racism, stigma and discrimination. We learned that disruption was inevitable and necessary, and that policy change was as important as changes to health-care providers’ practice. More effective care Based on these lessons, we partnered with three B.C. EDs to design an intervention to support leaders and staff to deliver care more effectively. EDs are under immense and increasing pressure, evident in long waits for care and high levels of staff turnover and burnout , fostering a focus on optimizing short-term efficiency. However, the intervention was designed to align with the quintuple aim of health-care improvement , which optimizes effectiveness by enhancing: Patient experiences and outcomes Health-care provider well-being Health equity Service efficiency Health system efficiency Despite significant challenges related to COVID-19 and the worsening epidemic of overdoses and deaths related to the toxic drug supply, staff at two of the EDs mounted intervention strategies. Results showed encouraging trends in patients’ perceptions of the quality of their care and discrimination in the ED, but there were no significant changes in staff sick time. However, most importantly, there was a significant decrease in the percentage of patients who left without their care being completed at the site with the most robust intervention activities. This is crucial because patients who leave the ED before their care is complete often return when their health concerns are more urgent, resulting in significant harms to patients and costs to the health-care system. It’s also demoralizing for staff. We examined how to build on and strengthen these results. Staff and leaders were committed to focusing on those with greatest needs. However, other priorities — such as recruiting and orienting new staff, and responding to escalating crises such as violence against staff, the toxic unregulated drug supply, and COVID-19 — overshadowed their efforts and curtailed the staff and resources needed. Resources and recommendations We identified 10 recommendations for systematically improving care for those who need it most: Initiate interventions within care delivery organizations Conceptualize equity as foundational to health-care quality, not as an “add-on” “Hook” participation by linking equity to the organization’s most pressing “pain points” Seek commitment to effectiveness from leaders across all employment groups Commit sufficient resources to ensure representation from service-users and all employment groups and sufficient leadership and expertise Compose implementation teams of people from all levels and roles, including service-users Assign leadership responsibility to those with leadership roles at executive and clinical levels in alignment with their skills and responsibilities Tailor the intervention to align with the realities of the context Provide some level of education and opportunities for interprofessional dialogue for all Reconsider how time is used to support effectiveness and other elements of the quintuple aim, not efficiency alone To support these recommendations, we created The EQUIP Equity Action Kit , which includes step-by-step directions, assessment and evaluation tools, discussion tools, action tools, videos, animations. We have free on-line courses to support the Action Kit and tools to support the well-being of health-care providers as they face challenging workloads, high stress levels and violence daily. Some resources are available in both English and French. In addition to EDs, many resources have been tailored to other health-care settings such as primary care and cancer care. Colleen Varcoe works for the University of British Columbia, and PreVAIL (Preventing Violence and Inequity Across the Lifespan) a non-profit organization. I have received funding for the research reported in this article from the Canadian Institutes for Health Research and the Public Health Agency of Canada.

articles.content: Police departments across the world use “sniffer dogs” to help in searches — for explosives, for people who are lost, for human remains and for narcotics. These dogs are widely understood as important for police investigations. They are often praised by courts for their accuracy and reliability. In Canada, police officers must have “reasonable and probable grounds” to search a home for evidence of a crime or to search a vehicle for drugs or other evidence during a traffic stop. In a series of cases, including R. v. Kang-Brown and R. v. Chehil , however, the Supreme Court of Canada has applied the lower standard of “reasonable suspicion” to sniffer dog searches. That’s because sniff searches are considered highly accurate and minimally intrusive to the individual searched. My recent research challenges both these assumptions. It suggests that the underlying rationale for the use of the reasonable suspicion standard in sniffer dog searches no longer holds . High rate of false alerts Despite our persistent belief in the “infallible” dog, empirical studies from around the world suggest that even trained and certified detection dogs have an alarmingly high rate of false alerts. In 2023, for example, data from New South Wales police in Australia revealed that nearly 75 per cent of searches following an alert from a sniffer dog yielded no illicit drugs . Similarly, a 2011 Chicago Tribune investigation found only 44 per cent of alerts led to the discovery of drugs or drug paraphernalia. This high rate of false alerts has multiple and overlapping causes. Poor and inconsistent training procedures can have a significant impact on field performance. A dog’s abilities also vary from day to day. In other cases, dogs are detecting minuscule residual traces of drugs on currency or alerting to the smell of drugs and not the drugs themselves. For example, the chemical compound piperonal is found in MDMA, but is also used in vanilla flavouring and mosquito repellent . Another source of error is handler cuing, or the conscious and unconscious cues a dog receives from its human handler. In a 2011 study , for example, dog handlers were told that markers placed in certain search areas indicated where target scents were located, even though no target scents were present. The dogs falsely alerted in 85 per cent of the searches and were more likely to alert at the marked locations, suggesting that handlers’ expectations influenced their dogs’ behaviour. Unconscious racial bias If a police officer harbours unconscious racial biases — even those they would consciously reject — they can transmit them to their dogs through unconscious handler cuing. If these cues cause the dog to falsely alert to the presence of narcotics, this will often give officers reasonable grounds to arrest the individual and, once the arrest is made, to conduct a more thorough search of the person and their immediate surroundings. The use of a reasonable suspicion standard makes it easier for police to conduct the initial sniff search, but the phenomenon of handler cuing operates just the same. This further reduces reliability and can lead to false alerts and unnecessary arrests. Moreover, investigations in the United States have found that police use sniffer dogs in stops involving racialized drivers at a disproportionately higher rate than stops involving white drivers. The 2011 Chicago Tribune investigation similarly found that the dogs’ overall success rate of 44 per cent fell to just 27 per cent when the driver stopped by the police was Latino. Physical and psychological harm Far from being “minimally intrusive,” the use of drug detection dogs can cause both physical and psychological harm . People subjected to a sniffer dog search often report feelings of fear and anxiety stemming from the public humiliation involved. Others describe physical distress, including increased heart rate, sweating and shaking. People who are subjected to a drug dog search also often report feeling uncomfortable in the presence of police and an increased fear of police afterwards. This can damage police-community relations, especially among racialized and marginalized populations where this relationship is often already strained. Reasonable and probable grounds The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not prohibit the use of police sniffer dogs. However, my research suggests that the rationale for applying the reasonable suspicion standard — that sniff searches are highly accurate and minimally intrusive — no longer holds. Instead, the reasonable and probable grounds standard, which has generally been applied to search and seizure powers, should also be applied to sniffer dog searches to ensure that power is used in accordance with the Charter. If this standard creates a legislative gap that makes sniffer dogs a less useful investigative tool for police, that’s a matter for Parliament to address. articles.content: Billions of dollars are being spent on research to find a molecule that will cure Alzheimer’s disease. Yet, as Dr. Louis Bherer explains, adopting certain lifestyle habits could significantly reduce the risk of developing symptoms, in some cases by up to half. Dr. Bherer is a professor in the Department of Medicine at the Université de Montréal and researcher and director at the EPIC Centre, the preventive medicine and physical activity centre at the Institut de Cardiologie de Montréal (Montreal Heart Institute). His work focuses on the impact of lifestyle, physical exercise and cognitive stimulation on the brain health of older adults and patients with cardiovascular disease. At his Montréal laboratory, Bherer and his team develop both physical and cognitive exercise programs. The results of their studies corroborate what other research has found on the importance of lifestyle in the prevention of dementia. This factor has been neglected by public health authorities, explains Dr. Bherer, who is also laboratory director at the l’Institut universitaire de gériatrie de Montréal (Montreal University Institute of Geriatrics). We recently spoke to Dr. Bherer: The Conversation Canada : A new Statistics Canada study indicates a substantial decline in healthy life expectancy in Canada. In 2023, it was 66.9 years, a decrease of 3.5 years from the peak of 70.4 years between 2010 and 2012. Are you surprised? Dr. Louis Bherer: Yes and no. But what we do know is that the healthspan-lifespan gap — the gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy — is widening. For example, nine out of 10 people have at least one risk factor for cardiovascular disease after the age of 65: being overweight, poor sleep, inactivity, high blood pressure, etc. As life expectancy increases, this means more years in poor health. Our lifestyle is not optimal. Stress and anxiety are on the rise. It’s a scourge. What’s more, people are inactive, they have sleep problems, they are neglecting their diet. We eat quickly, and eat fast food or ultra-processed foods. Although the information is there, and available, we don’t always apply it. Nor do we teach our children to. Physical education should be part of the daily school curriculum, and the basics of nutrition should also be taught. This article is part of our ongoing series The Grey Revolution. The Conversation Canada and La Conversation are exploring the impact of the aging boomer generation on Canadian society, including housing, working, culture, nutrition, travelling and health care. The series explores the upheavals already underway and those looming ahead. For that matter, people are quick to turn to pharmaceutical solutions. The popularity of Ozempic is one example. We want to lose weight, but we aren’t addressing the causes of being overweight. We don’t do much to encourage people to change their lifestyle. It is estimated that nearly half of all dementia cases (45 per cent) could be prevented with a healthy lifestyle. Fourteen modifiable risk factors (FRM) have been identified. TCC: Many people tell themselves: I’m 65 or 70, so it’s too late for me to change my habits. I should have started earlier. L.B.: It’s never too late , even though we know that education (a mitigating factor for dementia) is generally acquired at a young age. This is in contrast to hearing loss, which occurs later in life. Many people do not take it seriously or hide it, yet it’s a factor associated with an increased risk of major cognitive impairment or dementia. And, of course, psychological health plays a major role: a person may be inactive because they feel a little depressed or less motivated, but this increases the risks. We don’t realize that overall health factors are all interrelated. Heart and brain health go hand in hand. What’s good for the heart is good for the brain. TCC: Your laboratory, which focuses on cognitive health, is located at the Institut de cardiologie de Montréal. What exactly are you doing there? L.B.: We use stimulation programs to assess the impact of exercise on physical and cognitive health. Our participants range in age from 50 to 95, with an average age of between 68 and 70. We follow them for periods ranging from three months to a year. They may have mild cognitive deficits that people around them have noticed, and sometimes they suffer from anxiety, a condition that can impact memory and be a predictor of dementia. Other participants have no cognitive issues, but they are at risk due to high blood pressure, diabetes, etc. Our programs include memory games on phones, for example, which improve cognitive function, particularly psycho-motor speed, as well as physical exercises: stationary bikes, treadmills, muscle strengthening, etc. The best approach is a combination of both. TCC: What have you observed? L.B.: We are seeing clinically significant improvements. Participants with mild cognitive impairment may see improvements after six months of training, with differences in their attention, alertness and response speed. They are more alert after just a few weeks. We are also seeing an impact on memory, although this takes longer. Using biomarkers, our research attempts to link the parameters that change, both physically and cognitively, to the effects on the brain. With brain imaging, we can measure improvements in blood flow and brain structures, such as the hippocampus, which plays a key role in memory. Physical training, which participants do three times a week, stimulates the production of proteins that promote neuroplasticity. When muscles work, they produce and release myokines and other exerkines . These molecules play an important role in metabolism, inflammation, bone health and even mood. As we often say, exercise is the miracle pill for overall health. TCC: Many people make profound changes in their lifestyle, but good intentions don’t always last. L.B.: Yes, and that’s a shame, because the positive effects of training disappear within a month or a month and a half. And the older we get, the faster it happens . Ideally, you should choose activities that can be easily integrated into your daily routine. I’m thinking of running, for example, which is a very complete exercise, very easy to do, and inexpensive. Brisk walking is also good, but the idea is to work up a bit of a sweat. And supplement that with some exercises to increase muscle strength and others to improve posture and mobility. This is an important factor in maintaining independence as we age. The fear of falling is a concern for many older people. Balance and posture control exercises, such as yoga, can really make a huge difference to the health and lifestyle of older people. Louis Bherer ne travaille pas, ne conseille pas, ne possède pas de parts, ne reçoit pas de fonds d'une organisation qui pourrait tirer profit de cet article, et n'a déclaré aucune autre affiliation que son organisme de recherche.

L.B.: We use stimulation programs to assess the impact of exercise on physical and cognitive health. Our participants range in age from 50 to 95, with an average age of between 68 and 70. We follow them for periods ranging from three months to a year. They may have mild cognitive deficits that people around them have noticed, and sometimes they suffer from anxiety, a condition that can impact memory and be a predictor of dementia. Other participants have no cognitive issues, but they are at risk due to high blood pressure, diabetes, etc. Our programs include memory games on phones, for example, which improve cognitive function, particularly psycho-motor speed, as well as physical exercises: stationary bikes, treadmills, muscle strengthening, etc. The best approach is a combination of both. TCC: What have you observed? L.B.: We are seeing clinically significant improvements. Participants with mild cognitive impairment may see improvements after six months of training, with differences in their attention, alertness and response speed. They are more alert after just a few weeks. We are also seeing an impact on memory, although this takes longer. Using biomarkers, our research attempts to link the parameters that change, both physically and cognitively, to the effects on the brain. With brain imaging, we can measure improvements in blood flow and brain structures, such as the hippocampus, which plays a key role in memory. Physical training, which participants do three times a week, stimulates the production of proteins that promote neuroplasticity. Brisk walking is also good, but the idea is to work up a bit of a sweat. And supplement that with some exercises to increase muscle strength and others to improve posture and mobility. This is an important factor in maintaining independence as we age. The fear of falling is a concern for many older people. Balance and posture control exercises, such as yoga, can really make a huge difference to the health and lifestyle of older people. articles.content: In every culture, humans speak and sing to each other. We have created an astounding array of languages and musical structures across the globe. And yet, within this diversity, some fundamental sequence patterns are repeated. These are often referred to as “universal” patterns in human vocalization. Our new research, published this week in Science , reveals that many of these acoustic patterns in human song and speech are also shared with birdsong . The study compared the songs of 367 bird species with examples of song and speech from 52 human languages. How we gathered the data As researchers in animal behaviour and neuroscience and music, we ( Logan and Jon ) spent 10 years documenting the prevalence of universal human acoustic patterns in the songs of zebra finches . A zebra finch. (Unsplash/Angelo Casto) When Kendra joined our lab during her PhD , she proposed we investigate whether these patterns are shared across other bird species as well. To research this, we needed a large number of birdsong recordings. Luckily, many people around the world are fascinated by the sounds of birds and upload their recordings to public repositories . We collected and manually annotated individual syllables in the songs of over 360 bird species, generating more than 70,000 birdsong syllables for analysis. We then compared these to data sets of human speech and song from a variety of languages and cultures around the world . Fortunately, some of these data sets contain annotated recordings of the same individual producing both speech and song, which was perfect for our comparisons to bird vocalizations. Humans and birds both tend to end their phrases with longer syllable. (Unsplash) Regular and predictable rhythms Overall, we found numerous similarities in the acoustic patterns of bird songs and human vocalizations. For example, humans and birds both tend to end their phrases with longer syllables. Song of a fox sparrow. (Patrik Aberg) , CC BY-NC-SA 35 KB (download) They also organize their syllables in a way that minimizes changes of pitch across adjacent syllables. And they tend to produce their songs with regular and predictable rhythms. In some cases, birdsong appeared more similar to human song than human speech. In other cases, we found birds tended to have songs that were more similar to human speech than human song. Unrelated to vocal learning We designed this study to ask an important question: Does vocal learning ability shape sequence patterning? Humans learn the structure of their vocalizations from others, particularly as they grow up. It turns out many birds also learn their vocalizations as they grow up. We looked at two separate groups of these vocal learning birds: songbirds ( oscines ) and hummingbirds . We compared them to two closely related bird groups that are not vocal learners: suboscines and nightjars . Because humans, songbirds and hummingbirds are all vocal learners, we thought some patterns may be similar within these species and distinct from those within suboscines and nightjars. Surprisingly, we found very little evidence for this. The degree of variation across bird species did not appear to be related to vocal learning. Yellow-rumped warbler, an oscine songbird. (Unsplash) How humans and birds make sound What then might drive the similarities in sequence patterning across so many species? We will need more studies to determine the answer, but we hypothesize that similarities in how humans and birds produce sounds could shape some vocal sequence patterns. For example, the shared need to co-ordinate breathing with vocal musculature could contribute to shared acoustic patterning across birds and humans. Specifically, precise movement of muscles that control the vocal tract are timed with airflow from the lungs across all birds and humans. If this is true, it’s possible these patterns may be found in many other species. Did birds teach us to sing? Did birdsong influence the evolution of human sound? (Unsplash) Songbirds first evolved about 50 million years ago , long before the first lines of humans split from the other great apes. This means that birds have decorated our soundscapes throughout human evolution. The songs of birds have inspired music throughout time and cultures . Might these natural sounds have influenced the earliest humans as they began experimenting with making sounds themselves, discovering the joy of music to their ears? These are some of the big ideas we are excited to explore in future studies. Logan S. James receives funding from FRQNT. He is affiliated with Earth Species Project and Wavelength Science. Jon Sakata receives funding from NSERC, CIHR, and FRQNT. Kendra Oudyk currently receives funding from SSHRC and formerly received funding from FRQNT while working on this project.

articles.content: Cosmologists suggest that fluctuations of the quantum vacuum in the first moments of the universe played a role in the formation of galaxy clusters spanning the cosmos. Pictured here is the spiral galaxy NGC 2090, located in the constellation Columba. (ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, A. Leroy) The word “vacuum” may conjure the image of empty space. Maybe you think of a region far outside the solar system without planets, debris, gas clouds or light. According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty . Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle — which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time — to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still. Instead of an empty space, we can imagine the vacuum as a dynamic object, with regular fluctuations in energy. Physicists at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom recently presented preliminary research showing direct imaging of these fluctuations in a lab-made quantum vacuum . Physicists have “seen” the quantum vacuum many times before, however. And we can all see the effects of the quantum vacuum on atoms in the atmosphere — through the gorgeous light displays of the aurora borealis. The energy fluctuations of the quantum vacuum also create conditions for black holes to shrink. And modern cosmologists believe they played a role in the creation of galaxies, their impact felt in the earliest moments of our universe. Impacts on real objects The idea of a “quantum vacuum” that isn’t truly empty is more than an academic interpretation of equations. The most striking feature of the vacuum is the way it impacts the structure and dynamics of real objects . For instance, there is an ongoing effort geared at observing the quantum vacuum directly in an experiment using high-intensity laser beams . The strong electric fields from the laser pulses interact with the particles fluctuating in and out of the vacuum and, as a result, experience an effect called “birefringence.” The birefringent vacuum treats light of different polarizations differently, similar to how polarizing sunglasses preferentially block light from specific glare-producing sources. This complex and interesting experiment will test the predictions of quantum mechanics on the structure of the vacuum through direct observation. Changing colours of light This will not be the first time scientists have “seen” the quantum vacuum at work. By the mid-20th century, quantum mechanics had been put to test after test and was proving capable of predicting and describing the internal structure of molecules, atoms and nuclei. For theory and experiments to agree, however, scientists had to account for the impact of the quantum vacuum. In many cases, theoretical predictions were tested against the spectra of these objects found through experiments . For example, the electrons in oxygen atoms and nitrogen molecules have specific energy levels. The lowest energy level is the “ground” state, and the rest are “excited” states. Electrons can’t hang out in excited states forever. The quantum vacuum shakes and perturbs them until they fall back to the ground state. Transitions between levels are accompanied by emission of light with specific colours, dubbed the spectra. In the case of oxygen atoms and nitrogen molecules, this spectrum takes the form of dazzling display of greens, reds and violets in the aurora borealis . One of the specific predictions of quantum mechanics for the electron in the hydrogen atom is that the lower energy levels are particularly sensitive to quantum vacuum fluctuations. As the energy levels shift slightly, this changes the colour of the light that can be absorbed or emitted by the atom. This effect in hydrogen was precisely measured in 1947 by Willis Lamb who eventually won the Nobel prize in physics for what is now called the Lamb shift . Modern physics experiments The impact of vacuum fluctuations on the structure of particles and their interaction with the environment has since played an important part in modern physics experiments. The subfield of physics that connects the structure of atoms and molecules to the light they interact with is called atomic, molecular and optical (AMO) physics. I did my PhD in this area of physics, and those of us working in the lab rely on accurate calculation of spectra in order to use lasers to control quantum systems in neutral atom or trapped ion quantum computers and quantum simulators. Quantum computers harness “qubits,” a pair of energy levels analogous to the 0 and 1 making up a classical bit, to perform complex calculations. Quantum simulators, meanwhile, subject quantum particles like ultracold atoms to environments that make them emulate the behaviour of another system, such as a superconductor. Physicists must also take into account the direct impact of vacuum fluctuations on the basic properties of fundamental particles, such as the way in which electron-like particles called “muons” interact with magnetic fields , in order to describe what’s observed in experiments. Shrinking black holes A further interesting prediction of the quantum vacuum is how it behaves near extreme astrophysical objects, such as in the vicinity of a black hole. The first picture of a black hole was captured at the centre of the galaxy M87, using the Event Horizon Telescope. (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration) The strong gravitational acceleration toward the black hole generated by space-time curvature modifies the number and distribution of particles occupying the vacuum. This causes the black hole to “evaporate” into the surrounding empty space . This is the only known mechanism by which black holes shrink and their contents, in some complex manner, escape from behind the event horizon. And this is enabled by the quantum vacuum. Formation of galaxies Modern cosmologists have taken these well-described microscopic effects and worked to glean information about the earliest moments in cosmic history. They suggest that fluctuations of the quantum vacuum in the first moments of the universe “seeded” the small differences in the density of matter that eventually, under the influence of gravitational attraction, formed the cobwebs of interconnected galaxy clusters spanning the cosmos. From the microscopic structure of fundamental particles and atoms to the fate of black holes and the large-scale structure of the universe, the “nothing” of the quantum vacuum takes centre stage. The dynamic quantum vacuum interacts with everything and has important effects, both observed and predicted, offering a fascinating history to reflect on and an exciting range of future experiments to look forward to. Jared Rivera receives funding from The Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC).

articles.content: Cancer is now the leading cause of death in Canada. Two in five Canadians will develop cancer during their lifetime, and one in four will die from it. Every day, nearly 700 people across the country are diagnosed with cancer. According to the Canadian Cancer Society , the most commonly diagnosed cancers are lung, breast, prostate and colorectal cancer. These figures mask a key reality: survival rates vary greatly depending on the type of cancer and, above all, how advanced it is at the time of diagnosis. The statistical data clearly show that survival rates increase when the cancer is detected early. These data highlight the urgent need to improve detection of the disease and, above all, to detect it earlier. A blood test instead of a scalpel This is the context where my research takes place. As a professor of systems engineering at ÉTS Montréal and principal investigator in the cancer research division at the CHUM Research Centre, I am working on liquid biopsy. This approach aims to detect cancer from a simple blood test by analyzing the DNA that tumour cells release into the bloodstream. Unlike conventional biopsies, which require removing a tissue sample from the tumour, liquid biopsy relies on a simple, minimally invasive procedure: a blood test is all that’s needed. The advantages of this approach include reduced pain, lower risks for the patient and less logistical burden associated with hospital procedures. The simplicity of the test also allows for more frequent testing. And finally, unlike many diagnostic procedures, taking a blood sample does not require specialized facilities. Blood can be taken in any health-care setting, whether it’s a local clinic or a community health centre. In medicine, the term “biomarkers” is often used to refer to measurable indicators that provide information about a person’s state of health. The PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test, which has been used for decades to monitor prostate cancer, is a well-known example. Elevated PSA levels in the blood may indicate the presence of cancer, its progression, or a recurrence after treatment. However, the biomarker approach does have limits: PSA is not specific to cancer and test levels can rise for other reasons, which can complicate the interpretation of results. À lire aussi : We designed a new way to build miniature fluidic devices to enable personalized cancer treatment Detecting the invisible Liquid biopsy follows the same logic, but at a different level of precision. Rather than measuring a protein indirectly linked to the disease, it directly detects the genetic traces left by the tumour cells themselves. In this sense, circulating tumour DNA can be seen as a much more specific biomarker, carrying information about the nature of the cancer and its progression. À lire aussi : What adolescents and young adults with cancer want researchers to know The smaller the tumour, the less DNA it releases into the blood. Yet it’s precisely at these very early stages that diagnosis has the greatest impact on survival chances. My aim is to detect these extremely weak signals, sometimes well before the onset of clinical symptoms, or even after treatment, when the cancer appears to have disappeared but may persist in a residual state. Tailoring treatments to each tumour Liquid biopsy also makes it possible to tailor treatments to each patient. By identifying the specific mutations in a tumour, it becomes possible to select targeted therapies that are better suited to the cancer’s genetic profile. This approach paves the way for more precise medicine, which takes into account the biological characteristics specific to each disease. Another major advantage is the ability to monitor the progression of cancer over time. By repeating liquid biopsies before, during and after treatment, it’s possible to observe whether tumour DNA levels are decreasing or increasing. This information can help to quickly determine whether a therapy is effective or needs to be adjusted, thereby avoiding unnecessary treatments and their side effects. When the signal gets lost While liquid biopsy offers promising prospects, it also poses significant technological and methodological challenges. One of the main obstacles is detecting tumour DNA amid a vast background of normal DNA. The mutations we are looking for are sometimes at the very limit of the accuracy of sequencing machines. In my laboratory, we are working to reduce technical errors and develop algorithms capable of distinguishing between a genuine cancer mutation and a false signal generated by sequencing technologies, notably through artificial intelligence approaches. A single blood sample can generate terabytes of data. For each patient, this amounts to billions of DNA fragments to be analyzed, filtered and compared. The management and analysis of this massive data set require robust bioinformatics tools capable of processing the information quickly and accurately. À lire aussi : All for one, not one for all: The promise and challenges of personalized medicine The quality of the analysis also depends on sample preparation. Circulating DNA is often fragmented and degraded. It must be purified, experimental biases must be corrected, and it must be made suitable for sequencing technologies even before the computational analysis stage. A revolution in the making In my view, liquid biopsy represents much more than a technological tool: it is an opportunity to transform the way we detect and monitor cancer. By combining less invasive methods, earlier detection and more personalized medicine, it could improve both patients’ quality of life and their chances of survival. Before becoming standard practice, however, the effectiveness of these approaches will need to be demonstrated in rigorous clinical trials. However, as sequencing technologies advance, what was once the stuff of science fiction is gradually becoming a reality. I am convinced that one day, a simple vial of blood could play a central role in the fight against cancer. Alexandre Pellan Cheng received funding from the École de technologie supérieure, the CHUM Research Centre, the Montreal Cancer Institute, the Mirella and Lino Saputo Foundation, Génome Québec and the Mitacs Foundation for research projects on liquid biopsy. He is a member of the Montreal Cancer Institute and a researcher at the CHUM Research Centre. He is named as an inventor on patents, some of which have been licensed for commercialisation by Eurofins-Viracor.

articles.content: Sleep is fundamental to well-being. Decisions to end bi-annual clock changes and remain on permanent daylight saving time (DST) in British Columbia , the North West Territories , Alberta , Manitoba and northwestern Ontario have consequences for many Canadians due to potential sleep disruption. The health risks of transitioning to DST, including increased heart attacks and fatal car accidents , have led most sleep and chronobiology experts , including the first author of this story , to advocate for ending seasonal clock changes in favour of permanent standard time . Governments justify opting for DST to provide later daylight for a range of reasons, including facilitating evening activites , alignment with other areas and promoting health. While permanent DST provides more daylight in the evening hours — something sometimes appealing for those with flexible schedules and access to outdoor spaces — it comes at the cost of later sunrises. Being aware of the potential effects of permanent DST and how to mitigate these will be important for schools. Read more: B.C.’s switch to permanent DST adds to the ‘perfect storm’ for poorer adolescent sleep and mental health Later dawns Due to the short winter days experienced in Canada, dawn will now occur later than the start times for many schools in many of the regions opting for permanent DST. Communities to the north and west within a time zone will have sunrises later than 8 a.m., or even later than 9 a.m. for a sizeable portion of the school year. Grande Prairie, Alta., will see sunrises in December and January after 10 a.m. In the United States, the the Sunshine Protection Act seeks to make daylight saving time permanent . Because winter days are shorter in Canadian northern areas than the more southern United States, the negative consequences of the move to permanent DST will be more profound for Canadians. Why time matters A major concern around choosing the right clock for society has to do with our body’s internal circadian clock. This circadian clock regulates our daily 24-hour rhythms, including our sleep-wake cycles. This clock naturally follows daylight, so as our days get shifted later with DST, our body rhythms also get shifted later . One challenge that many people will face with permanent DST is social jetlag — a mismatch between what our body clock wants to do (follow the sun) and what our school or work schedules expect us to do (follow our alarm clocks). DST worsens social jetlag in two ways. First, DST moves our social schedule an hour earlier relative to dawn. For people with earlier schedules, such as students and teachers, this means waking earlier than our bodies want with the later dawns during fall and winter. Second, later sunsets delay when our bodies want to fall asleep, leading to less sleep overall . Social jetlag also erodes health in several ways, raising rates of depression, cardiovascular disease and metabolic diseases. How a person will respond to permanent DST depends on both their work or school schedule and their chronotype. Those with flexible schedules can adapt their sleep and activity schedules, but this isn’t a luxury afforded to many. Some people are naturally more morning-types (“larks”), while others are naturally more evening types (“owls”). The people who will struggle the most with permanent DST’s late winter dawns are the owls who have early work and school times. This is especially true for teens: Many of the biological changes occurring during adolescence naturally shift the circadian clock later , so teens are much more likely to fall into the “owl” category. Well-being in education and start times As dawn gets later than school start times, communities and families will likely face many challenges. Research from Russia’s short-lived permanent DST suggests detriments for sleep, social jetlag and mood, especially winter depression. Compared to research on the risks associated with DST transitions, there are relatively few studies on permanent DST . Instead, we can look to research on sleep, school start times and student well-being. Teens are considered chronically sleep-deprived because of the mismatch between their circadian rhythms and most school start times. This poses several public-health concerns related to the consequences of sleep loss for daytime sleepiness, attention and executive functioning. Teens’ sleep deficiency is associated with increased engagement in risky behaviours such as alcohol, drug and tobacco use, caffeine use and increased risk for depression, low grades and car accidents. The greater the circadian misalignment, the more likely adolescents are to experience cognitive and school difficulties . This is especially true for teens with ADHD or other health needs associated with sleep challenges. Decades of research points to later school start times being better aligned with adolescents’ circadian rhythms, with benefits for sleep health, mood , attendance , attention and academic performance . It also points to later start times being associated with decreased rates of illness , headaches and mental-health difficulties, including depression and disordered eating . Researchers have also documented improved sense of well-being , reduced caffeine use and reduced risk of motor vehicle accidents . The extensive benefits associated with better alignment of school times with students’ circadian rhythms have led researchers to suggest that later start times could help reduce educational disparities. And it’s not just students who benefit from later start times. Teachers also experience better daytime functioning and sleep health. Mitigation measures Taken together, as sunrise, school start times and students’ biological rhythms become more out of synch, educators can expect more disruptions to students’ engagement and academics. They could also see increased rates of illness (on top of existing seasonal increases) and absences, especially for middle and high schoolers. This is especially concerning given mounting concerns for under-resourced educational systems and unmet classroom needs that leave teachers ill-equipped. Consequences may be greater in rural and remote communities, where school start times tend to be earlier, as in British Columbia . Likewise, social jetlag and associated health consequences tend to be more pronounced in racialized and economically marginalized communities where many people already have earlier start times, less flexibility in schedules, reliance on public transit and high rates of disability and health problems. This brings up important concerns for equity-deserving groups likely to experience greater academic, social and economic detriments associated with permanent DST. As governments enact permanent DST, evaluation related to well-being and safety will be crucial for informing policy and practice. Risks for negative outcomes may also be reduced through various mitigation measures such as public education on sleep health and seasonal mood changes, later or flexible start times, adapting indoor lighting in schools and traffic and pedestrian safety measures. articles.content: A good and happy life is made in the small connections with others in our communities. (Unsplash) Earlier this year, we convened a meeting of some of the most influential figures in modern happiness research to discuss what they had learned in their 600 combined years of research and professional experience. The group included pioneers like Richard Layard , Sonja Lyubomirsky and Martin Seligman , who turned happiness into a serious science. As a result of their work, 90 per cent of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) member countries are now measuring life satisfaction. Many of these pioneers have remained active into their 80s and 90s, still writing , teaching and mentoring. If any group could identify the ingredients of a good life, this was it. We recently published the outcome of this discussion in the Journal of Happiness Studies . The group identified many central themes to happiness: having basic needs met, relationships, meaningful work and living in ways that align with one’s values and circumstances. Looking ahead, they were concerned about inequalities and declining youth well-being. The single most recurring theme in the discussion, however, was the importance and joy that comes from social relationships. Relationships are the linchpin As an interdisciplinary team of well-being researchers, we expected relationships to be part of the answer. They affect every aspect of life , amplify positive events , mitigate negative events and are considered to be a basic psychological need . This is not only observed in western countries; “having someone to count on” predicts life satisfaction around the world . In short, happy people have strong and satisfying relationships . What we did not expect was how frequently relationships would come up. In nearly every part of the discussion spanning meaning, work, competition, culture, morality, technology and longevity, relationships were the linchpin of happiness. Social engagement is a skill In their personal lives, several of these pioneers deliberately protected time for spouses, relatives, friends or grandchildren. One reorganized a schedule to give their close friendships more room. Another, persuaded by intervention studies , began writing more messages of gratitude , behaving more sociably and trading superficial exchanges for deeper conversations . Social engagement, they suggested, is not a luxury reserved for extroverts or the socially advantaged, but a skill anyone can cultivate . Connection may not always happen on its own, but it often begins with simple acts: taking an interest, reaching out and showing up. These are things we all can do. Their professional lives told the same story. Consistent with the research literature , many pioneers actively built laboratories, departments and collaborations where students and colleagues felt trusted, supported and energized. They saw people do better work when others helped them flourish and they helped others, discovering that others’ success and happiness could add to, rather than subtract from, their own. Relationships help healthier aging Happiness and relationships also offered a plausible link to the unusual longevity represented in the gathering. The scholars did not explicitly agree that their research might have extended their lives, or that any single practice explained their vitality. Still, their own priorities echoed a large body of research connecting close relationships with healthier, happier aging — a finding undeniably witnessed by the Harvard Study of Adult Development . The possibility lingered: Perhaps studying happiness had taught them to invest in the very bonds that helped keep them engaged in life? When the conversation widened from individuals to societies, the relational theme became more urgent. Several participants worried about declining youth well-being , which they attributed to increasingly competitive cultures. Schools rank students against classmates. Universities and workplaces turn peers into rivals. Material comparison makes another person’s gain feel like one’s own loss . Under those conditions, even talented young people can experience education not as discovery or fellowship, but as an effort to survive. Invest in the people around you The group did not deny that competition is part of human life or that it can sometimes spur innovation. But they challenged the assumption that self-interested rivalry is the key to progress. Human beings also survive and thrive through co-operation, social learning and mutual care. They argued that communities organized around a stronger sense of “we” are better positioned to flourish than those trapped in “us versus them.” This is consistent with research on the topic. The moral insight was simple: Your happiness is not my unhappiness. Your well-being can strengthen mine, just as mine can strengthen yours. We flourish by building one another up. The central conclusion was ancient enough to sound obvious but still not always easy to follow in our fast-paced society. A good and happy life is not constructed alone. It is made in the small connections with others in our daily lives, the workplaces we humanize, the rivalries we refuse, the communities we build and the society we all shape. After hundreds of years of combined research, the pioneers’ most compelling insight was simple: Invest in the people around you. The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Officials are meeting this week for the 21st Canada-European Union Leaders’ summit . It comes only a month after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada associate membership . A draft statement from Montréal , where Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, von der Leyen and EU Council President António Costa met for two days to discuss strengthening ties, calls for an “ever closer association” that will result “in a more active foreign and security policy partnership.” The talks follow a series of milestones in the relationship between the transatlantic partners, including the announcement in July that Canada was joining the Eurovision song contest. It’s the first country to do so since Australia entered in 2015. Eurovision is held every year in May, with member countries submitting one original song. Over the years, the event’s format has changed from an exclusive jury vote to a viewer televote and today’s combination of both. Sometimes, voting can become political , with viewers voting according to their geopolitical preferences or diaspora communities casting ballots for their former home countries regardless of the quality of the performance. This may be good news for Canada, which is currently basking in European affection. The current geopolitical romance between Canada and the EU could help a Canadian song win. It wouldn’t be the first Canadian win, though. Céline Dion took home the prize in 1988 , representing Switzerland. Uranium fears in the 1950s The EU and Canada are clearly getting closer. But will historians look back at Eurovision and other developments as the beginning of comprehensive Canada-EU integration? Probably not — and history shows why. A look at the history of Canada-EU relations reveals a shared interest in deeper integration that has rarely materialized into anything concrete. More than half a century ago, a couple of years after the 1957 Treaty of Rome had established the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community , Canada was the first industrialized country to sign an agreement with the latter organization. In October 1959, Canada became a signatory to the Peaceful Uses of Atomic Energy deal. At the time, Canada was worried about losing the United States as a major export market for its uranium. That’s because the U.S. had only agreed to a supply contract until 1962, expecting much lower demand for Canadian uranium after that. Prime Minister John Diefenbaker, who wanted to diversify Canada’s trade relations and revive imperial links with the United Kingdom, looked to Europe for future uranium markets . He added Germany and Italy to the list of countries to buy Canadian uranium. Canada also tried to ensure these new customers would only use the uranium for peaceful purposes. To do so, Canada considered an agreement with the European Atomic Energy Community, of which both West Germany and Italy were member states, as the best option. For its part, the organization believed the agreement with Canada not only provided access to Canadian uranium and civilian nuclear technology but also gave it international visibility. But in retrospect, beyond scientific collaboration, not much else was achieved . Canada had already lost the race to the U.S., whose aggressive export policy led to Western Europe adopting American nuclear technology. Nixon-Trudeau tensions Diversification away from the U.S. was also behind the 1976 framework agreement for commercial and economic co-operation , which Canada signed as the first industrialized country with the European Community , which later became the European Union. Canada was surprised by U.S. President Richard Nixon’s 1971 announcement of a new economic program that abolished the conversion of gold to American dollars and terminated fixed exchange rates. Richard Nixon and Pierre Trudeau talk in Trudeau’s office in Ottawa in this April 1972 photo. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Chuck Mitchell Canada hadn’t been warned about the immediate imposition of a unilateral 10 per cent surcharge on imports, and it wasn’t exempted. In response to these Nixon shocks and fuelled by long-simmering anxieties about Canadian independence, the Liberal government under Pierre Trudeau proposed a third option to reduce dependence on the U.S. and actively seek new partnerships, mostly with Europe. As they did in the late 1950s, the Europeans were receptive to Canadian advances because they wanted access to Canada’s energy resources . This was especially true in the wake of the 1973 oil crisis, which had not only caused Western European countries to desperately search for oil supplies outside the Middle East and the Soviet Union, but also led to their heightened demands for uranium as nuclear power programs ramped up to provide alternative energy. But the framework agreement between Canada and European countries never realized its full potential. Instead, Canada deepened its relations with the U.S. and signed a free-trade agreement in the 1980s . Can momentum be sustained? Today, Canada faces another trade crisis with the U.S. Canadian oil and gas is in high demand, even in a decarbonizing Europe that’s cut off from Russian supplies. In addition, the current nuclear renaissance , the combined result of climate change action and fossil fuel geopolitics, has made Canada’s uranium a highly sought-after resource. No wonder the EU and Canada are seemingly moving closer. But will the rhetoric around middle power solidarity and common values be enough to sustain the momentum? Europeans and Canadians have always seen each other as friends, and Canada’s Eurovision participation will only cement that war relationship. But historically, closer ties have not led to deeper integration in the long run. Petra Dolata receives funding from the Social Sciences and Research Council of Canada, Environment and Climate Change Canada and the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung Kanada.
