articles.content: As Halloween approaches and screen audiences are saturated with the sights and sounds of screaming women in horror films and TV shows, it’s a great time to look at the women whose vocal artistry created genuinely effective screams on screen. Behind every memorable cinematic scream lies a vocal performance that is often reduced to a natural, unreflective outburst. But that assessment obscures the women behind its most powerful manifestations. For example, think of the work of Shelley Duvall in The Shining , Janet Leigh in Psycho or Toni Collette in Hereditary . Certain screen actors have made the scream their calling card to fame and notoriety, under the designation “ scream queen .” These queens are the unsung heroes of the horror industry through their dedication to the vocal performance of the fear and terror in the many guises of horror. Long live the (scream) queen As onscreen horror proliferated in the 1970s, the term “scream queen” became popular, most notably through Calvin Beck’s 1978 book Scream Queens: Heroines of the Horrors . Later, in popular culture, “scream queen” applied to “ any female star who has made a career playing women who survive extreme trauma or peril .” Hollywood actress Jamie Lee Curtis qualifies to bear the mantle of “scream queen,” alongside others like Lin Shaye , Brinke Stevens , Michelle Bauer , and Linnea Quigley . While Curtis is well-known, the other actors may be less familiar even though they collectively have hundreds of film credits to their names , predominantly in low-budget horror productions. Those films occupy a robust and commercially significant segment of the film market. The market has shown remarkable resilience, even during the COVID-19 pandemic that saw a spike in people watching horror films . A trailer for the 2018 film, ‘Hereditary,’ starring Toni Collette. The onscreen scream Screen horror has relied on the scream as a sonic marker since the advent of sound film, and even earlier in the form of the silent scream . Screaming is a non-linguistic vocalization, like laughing and crying, rooted in ancient neural systems associated with survival. Its distinctive acoustic properties can engage subcortical mechanisms of threat detection, triggering heightened vigilance and lending the scream a particular communicative immediacy . Filmmakers exploit the scream’s capacity to evoke terror, but it can also express delight at a surprising revelation (the announcement of the band Donna and the Dynamos in Mamma Mia! ) or amusement over a comedic situation (when cross-dressing Robin Williams’ fake breasts catch fire in Mrs. Doubtfire ). It can likewise signify pain, most notoriously embodied in the male “ Wilhelm scream ” that has found use in more than 400 films, including Star Wars and the Lord of the Rings . Not all screams evoke terror. In this scene from Mamma Mia!, at 00:48:00, a delightful scream takes place. Fay Wray: The original scream queen Cinema of the early 1930s is rife with examples of horror, including Frankenstein (1931), Dracula (1931), The Mummy (1932) and King Kong (1933). It was in King Kong , however, that the prototype of the scream queen emerged through the vocal artistry of Fay Wray . As she later recalled in her autobiography , Wray entered an RKO sound studio before the film was edited to record a repertoire of screams and moans for insertion into the soundtrack — she called it an “aria of agonies.” Her screaming voice was heard in several other horror films of the time, establishing her reputation as the imperilled heroine, a historical precedent to later scream queens. Wray’s screams in King Kong subsequently entered the repertoire of sound effects (re-)deployed by sound engineers , reinforcing her status as a progenitor of the scream queen. Fay Wray in RKO’s 1933 King Kong. (RKO pictures) Empowering modern scream queens As horror cinema exploded into commercial prominence during the 1980s and ‘90s, the scream queen became one of horror’s defining female figures. Jamie Lee Curtis’ performance in Halloween (1978) was decisive not only for her career but for the evolution of the modern horror film and its female protagonist. Alongside Curtis, other scream queens like Linnea Quigley, Michelle Bauer and Brinke Stevens, whose names are less well known, emerged. They helped move the genre from the “final girl” model toward a fusion of horror, camp and sex appeal. The final girl refers to the trope of the last woman standing in a horror film; she’s the one who finally takes on the villain. Still, Curtis’s final girl proved enduring, evolving from a vulnerable survivor in 1978 into a formidable older heroine in the Halloween franchise’s later instalments. The shift toward female strength is exemplified by the career of Lin Shaye , whose work has appeared in more than 100 films over a span of 50 years. Shaye challenged the scream queen’s traditional association with youth and sexualized representations. She was most recently associated with the Insidious franchise, where she has served as the protagonist, psychic medium Elise Rainier. Recognizing that “ people attribute growing older to authority ,” Shaye has redefined the conventions of the scream queen through her portrayal of an older heroine whose experience, knowledge and agency become sources of power. Her body of work reflects an ongoing resistance to constraints that age, gender and genre might impose on her. She believes people want “ to see a person…have strength rather than be a victim .” Although Shaye continues to perform the screams associated with the genre, her portrayal of Rainier privileges authority over vulnerability, transforming the scream queen from a terrorized victim into an empowered agent. A trailer for ‘Insidious: The Last Key’ with Elise Rainer (Sony Pictures). A new era of scream queens As the scream queen transforms from vulnerability to empowerment, another change is in the works. Historically, the scream queen casts were almost entirely white women . This raises the question: What kinds of bodies are privileged to scream on screen? A diverse cast of scream queens may be making their way onto screens. Recent horror movies have introduced a new generation of scream queens to the cultural zeitgeist. Actress Jenna Ortega has been called “Gen-Z’s Scream Queen” , with her high-profile characters in _ Wednesday _, X , and Insidious . Her work has been applauded for her raw emotion, strength and animalistic vocalizations . Jenna Ortega in ‘Scream.’ (Paramount) Ortega’s work, alongside that of British actress Mia Goth , signals a shift in the genre. These women have made greater space for racially diverse and complex representations of women in horror. From victim to agent, the scream queen continues to draw and influence audiences. The scream was never just a simple reflex; it’s always been an artful cry. articles.content: When Canada legalized recreational cannabis in October 2018, one concern was that more legal stores would make cannabis easier for young people to access and encourage adolescent use . But does having more cannabis retailers near high schools actually mean more students use cannabis? Our study suggests the relationship is more complicated. Across more than 419,000 student survey responses collected in four Canadian provinces, we found little consistent evidence that greater access to nearby cannabis retailers was associated with whether adolescents used cannabis. However, accessibility was associated with more frequent use among existing users during the first year of legalization. Our research team examined this question in a study published in the Drug and Alcohol Dependence journal . Our findings offer new insight into how cannabis retail accessibility relates to adolescent use as Canada’s legal market matures. Retail accessibility and cannabis use We examined student survey data collected between 2018–19 and 2023–24 through the COMPASS study in Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario and Québec. We measured accessibility using the distance to the nearest retailer, the number of nearby stores and a measure that gives greater weight to closer retailers. Overall, greater retail accessibility was not consistently associated with ever using cannabis, past-year or past-month use, or daily and almost-daily use. Cannabis use also declined in our study sample. Past-year use fell from 22.2 per cent in 2018 to 10.0 per cent in 2023. Past-month use declined from 13.0 per cent to 6.4 per cent, while almost-daily use fell from 4.2 per cent to 2.4 per cent. These figures describe students in participating schools, not a nationally representative sample. For national context, Health Canada’s Canadian Student Alcohol and Drugs Survey reported that 18.3 per cent of students in Grades 7 to 12 used cannabis in 2023–24. This estimate comes from a separate survey and should not be directly equated with our findings. One important exception emerged among students who had already used cannabis. In 2018, greater retail accessibility was associated with more frequent use. This association weakened and was no longer statistically significant in subsequent years. Proximity may have mattered for frequency of use early after legalization, but it did not remain a consistent predictor. Store proximity may not tell the whole story Adolescents do not necessarily obtain cannabis directly from legal retailers. They may access it through friends, family members or other social connections, so the distance between a school and a store may not reflect how easily young people can obtain cannabis. Research on American high school students has identified friends as an important source of cannabis, whether through sharing or purchasing it. This research helps explain why the distance between a student’s school and the nearest cannabis retailer may not reflect how easily they can obtain cannabis. However, our study did not examine where students obtained cannabis, so access through friends is one possible explanation for our findings, not something we directly tested. Other factors, including peer influences and perceptions of risk, may also affect use. Our study cannot establish which factors explain the findings. What does this mean for cannabis policy? Our findings do not mean adolescent cannabis use is harmless or that governments should abandon safeguards. Research has linked adolescent cannabis use with health and educational concerns. A meta-analysis found associations with depression and suicidal ideation, while other research examined associations between cannabis use and poorer academic outcomes. A 2024 systematic review also examined cannabis retail availability and health outcomes, underscoring the need to consider different populations and outcomes rather than assume store proximity affects everyone in the same way. Restrictions on how close cannabis stores can operate to schools may still serve important purposes. However, our findings suggest that store proximity alone may be insufficient to understand or prevent adolescent use. Prevention efforts may also need to address social access, peer influences and factors associated with frequent consumption. Our study has limitations. Cannabis use was self-reported, and we surveyed students across successive years rather than following the same people over time. We measured retail access around schools, which may not reflect where students live or spend their time. The COVID-19 pandemic also disrupted school and social environments during the study period. The number of cannabis stores near a school is easy to measure, but it is only one part of a larger picture. Understanding adolescent cannabis use requires looking beyond store locations to consider how young people obtain cannabis, why they use it and how to prevent harmful patterns of consumption. Jamie Seabrook has received funding from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Children's Health Research Institute, and the Children's Health Foundation for his ongoing research on the health and wellbeing of children and youth. Adam Cole has received funding from the Canadian Cancer Society and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research. Jason Gilliland has received funding from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada, the Public Health Agency of Canada, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Heart & Stroke Foundation of Canada, the Lawson Foundation, the Children's Health Foundation and the Children's Health Research Institute for his ongoing research on the health and wellbeing of children and youth. Shiran Zhong does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Halloween, the fall holiday and $13.5 billion industry , lurks around the corner. But what’s behind the more than 11,000 acres of pumpkin patches across Canada and $3.9 billion in consumer spending on candy alone? Halloween has ancient origins in the pre-Christian religion and practices of the Celts . It was custom to honour the transitions between the seasons and harvest, acknowledge the thin veil between different planes of existence and also to commemorate the dead. Modern-day commercialization has shifted how people experience Halloween, but the spirits of the dead continue to play a significant role in the occasion and the time of year. The day’s appeal and its marketability extends beyond a one-day “holiday.” Many people are drawn to carefully curated encounters, seeking thrilling yet sanitized experiences that allow them to engage with the macabre and mortality from a safe distance. Consequently, Halloween’s commercial success in commodifying dread and the monstrous can be analyzed alongside broader “dark tourism” — an umbrella term that explores tourism involvement with sites of death, disaster and a difficult heritage. Anthropologist Philip Stone notes that a range of motivations exist for promoting engagement with death, disaster and the macabre : for example, political reasons or remembrance, education, entertainment or economic gain. So how should we think about worldwide Halloween-related attractions that not only seek to entertain but also promote interpretation and engagement with sites marketed as scary, which often have genuinely dark pasts? Prisons, forts For example, a tourism attraction at Eastern State Penitentiary — a former prison in Philadelphia — markets itself as a Halloween festival of epic proportions . The onetime prison was an 11-acre institution that was the first jail in the United States to introduce the practice of solitary confinement in the late 1800s. In the late ‘90s, the property switched gears, launched “terror behind the walls” as an annual haunted house and then rebranded as “ Halloween Nights .” The facility notes that proceeds from Halloween Nights benefit a mission to preserve the site and advance “public understanding of the criminal justice system and its impact on the lives of those affected by it [and] to inspire a more just future,” including through public education and exhibits . Another example is Fort Henry in Kingston, Ont. Although Fort Henry was never a battlefield site, it was the site of an 1838 execution . It was also used as a prison for combatants captured during the 1837-38 Rebellions in Upper and Lower Canada and again during the First and Second World Wars for “civilian enemy aliens.” Today, coffin rides and a monster shooting range are part of the Heritage Sites tourist attraction called Fort Fright , which simulates a haunted attraction and experience throughout the month of October leading up to Halloween. Historical educational programming exists through the year. These types of attractions are examples of fright tourism , when people seek scares and thrills for pleasure at a destination that may have a sinister history or is promoted as having one. Other forts have also offered similar experiences timed to Halloween . Urban ghost stories Urban ghost stories also continue to spark interest, both at Halloween and at other times. The Lost Souls of Gastown Tour , a performance-theatre experience in Vancouver, is one example. Visitors participating in the tour immerse themselves in the city’s stories of crime, disaster, historical figures and hidden urban spaces. Victoria Ghost Walking Tours offers a tour touching on “horrible deeds” and other eerie experiences for folks on Vancouver Island, as do other cities. Important questions raised Why do people seek fear if it’s associated with danger? Why do tourists travel for entertainment or fun to places with tragic or apparently haunted pasts, sometimes associated with horrible, disturbing or traumatic events? Although fear is fundamentally a warning mechanism that alerts us to potential danger, it also generates the release of adrenaline. In settings where people perceive themselves to be safe, this tension between threat and security can become an appealing experience . Stone analyzes dark tourism along a spectrum. The “darkest” end of the spectrum is characterized by experiences pertaining to education and authentic sites where death and suffering happened. The “lighter” end is “heritage-centric,” with an entertainment orientation perceived as inauthentic and more associated with tourism. Many Halloween-themed sites and experiences are arguably situated on the lighter end of the dark tourism spectrum and marketed as entertainment. As mentioned, some are linked to real experiences or engage with stories or sites associated with death, social control, crime and disaster. Ethical boundaries? Researchers studying dark tourism in prison museums have noted that people’s interactions in these spaces demonstrate that “not all dark experiences are equally 'dark’ to all visitors.” This means that sites cannot dictate how their curated experiences will be received. This suggests it’s important to pay close attention to the ethical boundaries between interpretation and entertainment. When these boundaries are blurred, the dignity of victims can be compromised while the educational and commemorative value of historic sites may be diminished. This raises important questions about the responsibilities of tourism providers when presenting difficult and often painful histories, and, as Stone also examines, their relationship to political ideology. Read more: A prison is no place for a party Some argue the boundary between a tourism attraction and the site of a traumatic past can become nuanced — for example, when former prisons, as attraction sites, provide educational resources for visitors . All attractions situated along the dark tourism spectrum, whether they lean toward the “lighter” or “darker” end, must carefully navigate the line between respectful engagement and exploitation. This is particularly relevant for Halloween tourism experiences that draw upon stories or sites that intersect with crime, death or tragedy. When attractions encourage visitors to engage with local history, they should not glorify perpetrators , sensationalize violence or trivialize suffering. In these cases, exhibit operators should prioritize historically grounded narratives that provide context, acknowledge victims and encourage reflection. This may be a daunting challenge. articles.content: Every summer, Québec rivers increasingly reach water temperature levels that threaten Atlantic salmon ( Salmo salar ). Just a few extra degrees can make the difference between a favourable and hostile habitat for this iconic species. Because of climate change, the issue is no longer simply predicting how much rivers will warm, but determining where to take action to protect them. One possible solution is the reforestation of riparian zones , the edges of streams and rivers. Trees lining waterways provide shade, which limits sun exposure and keeps temperatures cooler. But how can we determine what areas will actually benefit from reforestation? Our study , conducted on the Dartmouth River in the Gaspé Peninsula — a major waterway in the region known for its Atlantic salmon population and recreational fishing — provides a new tool to answer this question. When water temperature is a problem A river’s water temperature depends on several factors including air temperature, flow rate and groundwater inflow. However, solar radiation remains one of the main sources of energy responsible for rivers warming during the summer. More sunlight reaches the water’s surface in areas where riparian vegetation has been degraded by human activities. The consequences of this are particularly significant for Atlantic salmon, a species adapted to cold waters. Atlantic salmon growth and performance are generally optimal at temperatures below 20°C, and signs of physiological stress appear when the water temperature exceeds 20–23°C. Beyond these critical thresholds, this stress can affect the growth, feeding, and reproduction of the species . Protecting thermal refuges has therefore become a major conservation topic. Mapping shaded areas To better understand the effect of riparian vegetation on water warming in the Dartmouth River, our research team at the INRS’ Eau Terre Environnement Research Centre launched a project funded by The Foundation for Conservation of Atlantic Salmon . The goal of this study was to assess the role of riparian vegetation in providing shade and controlling solar exposure — two key factors that determine the quality of salmon habitat. We used a remote sensing technology called LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging), which produces a highly detailed three-dimensional representation of the terrain and surrounding vegetation. The analysis was conducted at a resolution of just one metre, allowing us to identify the most exposed sections of the watercourse with high precision. By combining LiDAR data with spatial modelling tools, we were able to simulate the amount of solar radiation reaching the surface of the Dartmouth River. We then compared these results with water temperature data. Shading varies The results showed that wide, sparsely shaded sections receive more solar energy, while areas that are steep-sided or bordered by dense vegetation are naturally protected. To take this further, we calculated an indicator called “unitary radiation,” which represents the amount of solar energy received within a given volume of water. This measure helps identify the areas most vulnerable to warming. We observed that certain narrow, shallow and sparsely shaded sections received up to 25 times more energy than other parts of the river. These areas appear to be particularly sensitive to summer heat waves. Reforesting riverbanks We then simulated a restoration scenario in which a 30-metre-wide riparian strip would be re-established with a tree canopy at least 12 metres high. This simulation was applied only to degraded sections of the river, where the loss of riparian vegetation limited natural shading. It therefore represents a realistic reforestation scenario that could be implemented as part of salmon habitat restoration projects. The results are encouraging. Reforestation leads to a widespread reduction in the amount of solar radiation absorbed by the water. In some areas, the reductions reach nearly 40 per cent. This reduction helps maintain cooler water temperatures, which is particularly beneficial for Atlantic salmon. Our study has identified certain river sections with a much higher potential for reducing solar radiation. It’s precisely these locations that should be prioritized during restoration efforts. Targeting investments more effectively The economic resources allocated to reforestation are limited. In a river system that spans hundreds of kilometres, it’s not possible to take action everywhere. Our study proposes a spatial prioritization method to identify the areas where every dollar invested in restoration could yield the greatest reductions in water temperature. On the Dartmouth River, these priority areas are concentrated mainly in the upstream sections as well as in certain tributaries, where the river connects to another watercourse that is particularly exposed. This approach could be applied to other watersheds in Québec to support conservation organizations, river managers and public decision-makers in their efforts to adapt to climate change. In Scotland , similar tools are already being used to identify river sections where tree planting offers the greatest potential for cooling the water and protecting Atlantic salmon in the face of global warming. A promising adaptation strategy Riparian reforestation is one of the concrete solutions that can be implemented locally as an adaptation measure starting today. By restoring the trees that line rivers, it’s possible to create more shade, protect thermal refuges and increase the resilience of Atlantic salmon habitat in the face of increasingly hot summers. At a time when every degree counts, trees could well become essential allies for the future of Québec’s salmon rivers. We would like to acknowledge the contribution of Mathias Cabal, a master’s student, as well as Professors Normand Bergeron and André St-Hilaire of the INRS’ Centre Eau Terre Environnement Research Centre, and Carole-Anne Gillis of the Gespe’gewa’gi Institute of Natural Understanding (GINU). Their expertise, collaboration, and commitment were essential to the completion of this research project. Eva Enders is a member of the Interuniversity Research Group in Limnology (GRIL), Résources Aquatiques Québec (RAQ), the Centre interuniversitaire de recherche sur le saumon atlantique (CIRSA), and the Atlantic Salmon Research Joint Venture (ASRJV). This research was supported by the Foundation for Conservation of Atlantic Salmon (FCAS) and the Alliance Advantage Program of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC). Nour El Houda Bejaoui is a member of the Interuniversity Research Group in Limnology (GRIL). She has received funding from the Foundation for Conservation of Atlantic Salmon.

articles.content: A Victorian-era séance. (Pearson's Magazine, 1910) In November 1857, during a séance in Jersey City, the medium Leah Brown claimed her body produced luminous particles . So intense was the luminosity emanating from her, she recalled in her memoir , that it almost burned her hands. She rinsed her hands under a tap and then pushed them into the damp earth outside. The following evening, luminous particles were discovered in the soil where she’d pressed her hands. They were later identified as phosphorous. In her memoir, Brown admitted to the presence of phosphorous but insisted her body had produced it. She further claimed that the manifestation of spirits in the body naturally produced “phosphoric lights” and the particles came naturally from her body. She added that mediums’ bodies could produce phosphorous and implied that they were part of what was then known as ectoplasmic remains — the viscous, gauze-like substance historically claimed by 19th- and 20th-century spiritualist mediums to exude from their bodies during trances. In truth? She’d probably secretly brought phosphorus with her and had used it in the séance. But her account shows how phosphorus was used in séances decades ago — and provides a glimpse of the chemistry behind making the dead seem visible as Halloween approaches. The dangers of phosphorous White phosphorus, also called yellow phosphorus, gives off a faint light as it slowly reacts with oxygen in the air. The effect is chemiluminescence, light from a chemical reaction — it’s not evidence of supernatural energy. In a dark room, the glow could indeed be rather uncanny and convincing of a phantom presence. Phosphorus is not a safe chemical. It’s toxic if swallowed and inhaling the fumes too can be harmful. It’s unclear whether those living in the Victorian era knew about these dangers or if they had any knowledge of the dangers of phosphorous. White phosphorous was used in “strike anywhere” matches , and many people — mostly women — working in factories where it was used developed a disease called phossy jaw . It affected teeth and jawbone. Certainly, long-term factory exposure is not comparable to séances, and we don’t have any definitive evidence of mediums suffering from this disease, but what’s relevant here is that white phosphorus was a known industrial poison and yet it was used regularly for seances. Nonetheless, a glowing ghost was not always a toxic ghost. In 1910, the magician William Marriott demonstrated how spirit hands could appear with some props and luminous paint. In 1877, William Henry Bailman’s luminous paint used calcium-sulphide and became a major commercial success. This compound could absorb light and glow in darkness . Ties between sciences and spiritualism Historian Richard Noakes’ work has shown physical sciences had a difficult yet symbiotic relation with spiritualism. Bailman’s paint is an example that ghost-making was part of a broader culture of chemical experimentation. In 1874, William Crookes, a renowned chemist, investigated self-luminous objects at séances. He specifically tested phosphorised oil and phosphorous lamps to see if he could understand the process better. Yet Crookes did not dismiss spiritualism as complete hoax. His writings suggest sciences and spiritualism were not completely separate worlds, and their methods sometimes overlapped. It’s important to examine the role literature played in understanding the link between phosphorus and ghosts. The most famous literary example of the use of phosphorus for ethereal spectacle comes from Arthur Conan Doyle’s The Hound of the Baskervilles , where the dog is treated with phosphorous to create the ghostly effect. Doyle’s work had profound impact on the development of forensics . The fictional use of phosphorous to create a spectral hound very likely brought more attention to the use of phosphorous within the spiritualist community. Ironically, the Scottish author had a keen interest in the paranormal and wanted to believe that ghosts existed. It’s strange how the creator of world’s most popular rational detective — Sherlock Holmes — was so deeply invested in the supernatural. Disposable bodies More recently, British author Laura Purcell’s Gothic novel, The Shape of Darkness , deals specifically with mediums and their use of phosphorus. Purcell’s novel is about a poor child medium who is unaware that the glow in her body is because of phosphorous and imagines that the burn she feels is because of the spirits. Her father is suffering from phossy jaw from his work at a match factory, and the book focuses on the inescapable nature of poverty and how the child is now the family’s only source of income. In both Purcell’s novel and The Hound of the Baskervilles , toxic phosphorous is used on subjects without any agency. The victims, a dog and a child, suffer health hazards just to create a supernatural phenomenon. Both these works of fiction give voice to a very real issue — some bodies have always been considered more disposable than others. Our Halloween decors today are filled with spooky things that glow. But once upon a time, a mysterious glow held the promise of extraordinary proof that the dead had returned for those gathered in darkness. Séances claimed to dissolve the boundaries between the dead and the living. And while we may continue debating whether ghosts are real, that spooky light in the dark decades ago was certainly not supernatural. Aditi Sen does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: A new study with unprecedented access to Atlantic salmon farms in British Columbia raises urgent questions about the federal government’s approach to regulating salmon farms and highlights disease risk to wild salmon populations. The Broughton Aquaculture Transition Initiative — a multi-government agreement with the province and the Mamalilikulla , ’Na̱mǥis and Kwikwasut’inux̱w Haxwa’mis First Nations — enabled this rare access to salmon farms for scientists unaffiliated with the aquaculture industry. Read more: Learning from Indigenous knowledge holders on the state and future of wild Pacific salmon Scientists from the Pacific Salmon Foundation, Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the University of British Columbia repeatedly examined the open-net pen salmon farms over more than a year, finding outbreaks of the viral disease heart and skeletal muscle inflammation (HSMI) on most farms sampled. Three independent pathologists confirmed the diagnosis, and the First Nations subsequently removed the farms from their territories. As a viral ecologist at the University of British Columbia and as elected Chief Councillor of the ’Na̱mǥis First Nation, we participated in this research and are co-authors of the publication. Our findings suggest HSMI outbreaks are much more common on farms in B.C. than Fisheries and Oceans Canada reports. They raise questions about the federal government’s policy not to regulate piscine orthoreovirus (PRV) — the virus that causes HSMI — as a “disease agent” or cause of the disease. These findings also echo longstanding warnings about the government’s approach to salmon farming in B.C. , which prioritizes industry needs over risks to wild salmon. A history of government denial Heart and skeletal muscle inflammation gained notoriety in B.C. after researchers first documented the disease in farmed Atlantic salmon , and the virus that causes the disease was shown to spill over to wild salmon . Fisheries and Oceans Canada has repeatedly downplayed the significance of these findings , emphasizing uncertainty over whether the disease occurs in the region due to the application of diagnostic criteria more stringent than those applied in other salmon-farming regions. These criteria were developed by Fisheries and Oceans Canada alongside the aquaculture industry itself . The Broughton Aquaculture Transition Initiative program studies the presence of infectious agents in and around open-net fish farms. (Pacific Salmon Foundation) Fish farms heavily infected with pathogens Prior research has documented the consequences of fish farm diseases on wild fish. Farms are frequently infected with pathogens such as piscine orthoreovirus . These pathogens flow freely into the water and are transmitted to wild salmon . They have been associated with decreased survival and population declines in wild salmon . Fisheries and Oceans Canada’s assessment of diseases associated with fish farms deserves renewed scrutiny in light of these findings. The evidence that PRV should be regulated as a disease agent has become overwhelming, yet the department has not updated its policy since 2019, when it concluded that PRV is not an infectious disease agent . ‘Namgis First Nation initiated a judicial review of this policy in 2019, and then put the action on hold in 2021 as it appeared the federal government would follow up on its mandate to remove fish farms from British Columbia. In 2024, the First Nation reactivated the judicial review after losing faith in the government’s commitment to remove the farms. Independent scrutiny is crucial First Nations, independent scientists, non-governmental organizations and even Fisheries and Oceans Canada’s own scientists have repeatedly raised concerns about whether the department’s science advice is sufficiently independent from its policy mandate to promote and regulate aquaculture. Author Gideon Mordecai explains the risks of PRV from B.C. salmon farms to wild salmon. (UBC Faculty of Science) The way PRV is regulated exemplifies these issues and illustrates why independent scrutiny is crucial. Our study, combining Indigenous-led research and independent scientific assessment, has provided an important check on institutional assumptions. It will hopefully ensure that future decisions affecting wild salmon are grounded in transparent, evidence-based assessment of the risks. The federal government is currently stalling on its commitment to remove salmon farms from B.C. Whichever policy option the government ultimately chooses must be weighed against its potential risks and benefits — and that requires accurate information about the risks salmon farms pose to wild salmon. The contrast between the peer-reviewed literature and Fisheries and Oceans Canada’s own science advice demonstrates that the government is currently failing to provide decision-makers with an accurate assessment of those risks. Gideon Mordecai receives funding from the Sitka Foundation and Raincoast Research Society. He serves on the Board of Directors of Evidence for Democracy. Don Svanvik is the elected Chief councillor of the Namgis first Nation, which actively opposes open-net pen fish farms.

articles.content: AI adoption in medicine is accelerating: more than 12,000 primary care clinicians have enrolled in Canada Health Infoway’s national AI scribe program , about 5,000 Ontario physicians use AI scribes and roughly one in five Canadian physicians now use AI tools. Almost 60 per cent report a cut in administrative time. AI scribes are tools that, with the patient’s consent, listen to a clinical visit and automatically draft the physician’s notes. We’re writing as an emergency physician who has led digital transformation in emergency departments for six years and advises on AI readiness (Ali Abdalvand), and an organizational psychologist studying burnout and responsible AI adoption (Ehsan Etezad). Our observation is that AI keeps its narrow promise of saving time. But without proper frameworks, it quietly adds new burdens that absorb those savings. We believe the fix is organizational. Burnout stems from mismatches in workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values; not from any single task such as paperwork. One study found electronic health record design and use accounted for just 6.8 per cent of the differences in burnout between clinicians. When work conditions such as a chaotic atmosphere and lack of control over workload were also considered, that number rose to 36.2 per cent. In emergency medicine , physicians are interrupted 7.9 times an hour, and prescribing error rates nearly triple with interruptions. No scribe changes that. How AI quietly adds to physicians’ work I think we can all relate to the idea that when you complete one task efficiently and save some time, new demands fill the space, making it seem as though nothing was saved in the first place. But as AI introduces new ways of reducing the time physicians spend on documentation, it comes with novel ways of adding work, too. The time dividend gets spent. Saved time rarely comes back to clinicians. In Canada’s national AI scribe program , half of clinicians put the time they saved into other administrative work, and one in five used it to add appointments. Studies from the United States show the same pattern: AI scribe adopters across five health systems saved 13.4 minutes of daily EHR time and delivered 0.49 more visits per week. Errors do happen and patient safety is at stake. In two simulated tests , Ontario’s auditor general reported that most of the 20 government-approved AI scribes made errors. Twelve recorded the wrong drug, nine invented treatment steps and 17 missed key mental-health details in at least one test. The province says there are no known reports of patient harm. OntarioMD, a subsidiary of the Ontario Medical Association that helps physicians adopt digital health tools with funding from the Ontario Ministry of Health, responded that physicians “know they must review every clinical note generated by their AI scribe.” That safeguard is essential — and it is also work. Used to be authors and now editors. Automation often leaves humans the hardest job, which is watching for rare but serious errors. When physicians at one U.S. health system got AI-drafted replies to patient messages, replying time did not decline as physicians still have to edit the text to make sure it was accurate. More tools, more switching. In our experience, many AI tools sit outside core clinical systems. As an example, in one of our emergency departments, starting a night shift means logging into the work station, the health record, the dictation system, the imaging viewer, the EKG viewer and, most recently, an AI scribe; six systems before seeing the first patient, and a copy-and-paste at the end of every interaction because the scribe lives outside the chart. Thirty-nine per cent of Canadian physicians named better-connected, interoperable systems as a priority. Always learning because it’s always changing. Keeping up with constant learning is a job demand in its own right and it can wear people down. This is also known as AI fatigue , defined as the overwhelming pressure of keeping up with AI tools for people’s jobs. Change fatigue is a predictable response to how change is managed by the health-care system and health-care leaders and it is not a reflection of someone’s failing to learn or to adapt. A better way We propose a practical framework that can be used by health-care organizations to improve the adoption of AI. This framework, GRACE, was co-developed by one of the authors, Ehsan Etezad, and it sets out five principles for moving toward responsible adoption. GRACE framework for responsible adoption of AI. (Ehsan Etezad) , CC BY Govern adoption . Include front-line clinicians on AI committees. Give every pilot a stop-rule written in advance. If the pilot doesn’t return measurable time, or audits find errors above an agreed threshold, it ends or is redesigned. Respect autonomy . Keep use voluntary and let clinicians choose among vetted tools. Respecting autonomy is an essential component of responsible AI adoption. Advance access. Build tools into the core clinical record so no one has to copy and paste. Fund access fairly. Cultivate competence. Offer protected, paid learning time and peer “AI champions.” Evaluate effectiveness. Track burnout, after-hours work, note accuracy and whether time actually comes back. Another practical tool, the AI Adoption Matrix, maps organizations on two dimensions. Enablement is how broadly people can access, use and build skills with AI. Governance is how well policies, oversight and accountability work. We encourage health-care organizations to map themselves on this quadrant and work toward being “Responsible Pioneers” with GRACE. We encourage health-care organizations to map themselves on this quadrant. (Ehsan Etezad) , CC BY The real test There is increasing pressure to move fast with AI adoption in health-care systems and it will likely continue. We would like to clarify that we’re not arguing against adoption of AI in health care. We actually encourage it and are excited about the future it will bring to all of us. That said, we encourage health-care organizations to adopt AI responsibly because stakes are high in medicine and patient safety could be at risk. We believe success should be measured by how happy a physician can feel at their job and about their job, not just how many patients they can see in one shift. None of us wants our loved ones to be treated by an exhausted and overwhelmed physician, so let’s ask ourselves how can we reimagine a health-care system that won’t burn out our physicians. Ali Abdalvand is the chief medical officer for Elewana Advisory, a consulting firm specialized in health-care digital transformation. He is also a founding director of Western MedTech, a non-for-profit society focused on supporting health-care innovators. Ehsan Etezad provides private consulting at MEUS Science with a focus on Leadership & Culture, Responsible Adoption of AI, and Psychological Health & Safety.
articles.description: AI adoption in medicine is accelerating: more than 12,000 primary care clinicians have enrolled in Canada Health Infoway’s national AI scribe program , about 5,000 Ontario physicians use AI scribes and roughly one in five Canadian physicians now use AI tools. We’re writing as an emergency physician who has led digital transformation in emergency departments for six years and advises on AI readiness (Ali Abdalvand), and an organizational psychologist studying burnout and responsible AI adoption (Ehsan Etezad). articles.title: Why using AI saves doctors time but won’t fix physician burnout

articles.content: For older adults with dementia or Parkinson’s disease, staying hydrated can be more complicated than simply drinking more water. Dehydration can occur when fluid intake is insufficient, the body loses too much fluid or both occur together. This problem is widespread. A review of studies found that about one in four older adults outside of hospital settings experience dehydration due to insufficient fluid intake. In Canada, a study of more than 96,000 Ontario long-term care residents aged 65 and older found that approximately one in six experienced dehydration during the study period. When an older person becomes dehydrated, the advice seems straightforward: drink more water. But people with brain disorders, including dementia and Parkinson’s disease, may need help putting that advice into action . Drinking is partly a brain-regulated behaviour : the brain detects changes in the body’s fluid balance, generates thirst and helps translate that signal into the behaviour needed to seek and drink water. Research involving people with Alzheimer’s dementia suggests that cognitive impairment may weaken their protective thirst response, reducing their ability to recognize and respond adequately to the body’s need for water. People with dementia may also forget to drink. Similarly, older adults with Parkinson’s disease may struggle to drink enough because of swallowing difficulties , even when they recognize thirst. Dehydration can, in turn, worsen confusion and impair thinking . Why bladder health matters Canadians are becoming increasingly aware of the importance of keeping their brains healthy and resilient to age well, not simply to live longer. A growing body of research shows that lifestyles that include a rich social life, frequent physical activity, eating a healthy MIND (Mediterranean-DASH Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay) diet and doing new and challenging things like cooking new recipes are important in keeping our brains healthy. Yet, one aspect of protecting our cognitive functioning that is often neglected is maintaining our bladder and urinary tract health . Preventing urinary tract infections (UTIs) is a key part of keeping our brains healthy as we age. How the risks of UTIs relate to brain health While we typically think of UTIs as relatively minor infections, the health risks are not the same for all populations. UTIs are common, with more than 150 million people affected globally every year. While these infections are common in young sexually active women, seniors over the age of 65 also experience higher risk. The incidence rate then increases further after age 85. UTIs present differently with age. UTIs are more common among the elderly, yet are often missed due to atypical symptoms . In younger populations, the classic UTI symptom is a burning and/or painful sensation when urinating. Older adults may not show classic UTI signs . Sudden behavioural changes or changes in personality are important reasons to seek assessment. These can be indicators of UTIs in older adults, and can include mental fog, confusion, mood changes, extreme fatigue, balance problems and/or falls, loss of appetite, and new or increasing incontinence. UTIs can cause inflammation. If unrecognized and untreated, this inflammation can impact the brain and cause cognitive decline. The risk is particularly high for those already suffering from brain disorders such as Alzheimer’s dementia and Parkinson’s disease. People with dementia are more likely to be dehydrated, and dehydration increases the risk of urinary tract infections . Risk of dehydration is high for those in long-term care. It’s important to know that in older patients, UTIs can trigger delirium — a sudden change in attention, thinking and awareness. This delirium is often interpreted as part of dementia rather than as a symptom of a possible UTI, which can lead to delays in seeking treatment. And even more concerning, a growing body of research suggests that the impact of infection-induced delirium is not necessarily temporary. Research published in Alzheimer’s and Dementia discusses how UTI-related delirium “ accelerates cognitive and functional decline .” The study’s senior author, Dr. Shouri Lahiri, describes a “vicious cycle” in which dementia patients are at greater risk of infectious, while the delirium that accompanies infection contributes to cognitive decline. Preventing dehydration and UTIs in seniors Practical ways to prevent dehydration and UTIs in seniors include: • Offering water and other drinks throughout the day , rather than waiting for them to ask. • Paying attention to whether they’re actually drinking. • Helping them use the toilet regularly and making it easier for them to find and reach the bathroom. Respond patiently to accidents and assist with personal care while respecting their dignity. • Seeking prompt medical assessment for sudden, unexplained confusion or changes in alertness or behaviour. These changes can have several causes in which UTI could be one. Caregivers play an important role in noticing sudden changes in behaviour, alertness or thinking. These changes should prompt medical assessment rather than being dismissed as aging or dementia. Nurses and doctors should investigate the cause and decide whether urine testing is needed. articles.title: Dehydration, UTIs and cognitive health: Getting enough to drink is complicated for people with brain disorders

articles.content: A computer-generated image of objects in Earth orbit that are already being tracked, before any massive new satellite megaconstellations. Approximately 95 per cent of the objects are space debris in the form of non-functional satellites. (NASA) SpaceX has started a trend. More American companies are betting that they can beat the laws of physics by launching thousands of enormous satellites to create orbital “AI data centres” with names like Cowboy Space’s Stampede. Space commercialization has progressed to a point where numerous aerospace and technology experts view these ambitious corporate orbital agendas as entirely detached from practical reality . How satellites could be distributed around Earth in megaconstellations. (ESA) This technology is untested. Some of the proposed satellites are twice as large as the International Space Station . Extrapolations for re-entry into our atmosphere suggest that if these satellites were launched, hundreds of them would drop large pieces on Earth every year. There are also many other serious safety , atmospheric pollution and light pollution problems with these proposals. A licensing assembly line First, SpaceX filed a proposal for one million satellites , invoking the hypothetical Kardashev scale (originally proposed to measure an alien civilization’s level of technological advancement) and other language that looked more like teenage fan fiction than a serious government document. The United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC) parroted this language back when filing acceptance documents, stating: This satellite system will represent the “first step towards becoming a Kardashev II-level civilization – one that can harness the Sun’s full power.” Four other companies then filed copycat orbital data centre plans within weeks of SpaceX: Blue Origin (involving 51,600 satellites), Starcloud (88,000 satellites), Cowboy Space (20,000 satellites) and Orbital Compute (100,000 satellites). They all plan to launch from the U.S., which means they only need approval from the FCC — an agency that is increasingly mandated to approve anything and everything American in what it describes as a “ licensing assembly line .” This graph shows how congested it would be if five orbital data centre megaconstellations used their proposed rings of orbits. Data from Jonathan McDowell at https://planet4589.org. (Samantha Lawler) , CC BY-NC-ND For example, the FCC recently approved Reflect Orbital for launch of a test orbital mirror. This despite thousands of comments in opposition from the general public, research papers by scientists demonstrating harm to ecosystems and human health and even a direct admission of possible permanent eye damage by Reflect Orbital in its own documents. Large satellites landing on Earth The FCC licensing process is opaque. The unprecedented scale of the SpaceX million satellite request in particular at least made the FCC ask more public follow-up questions than they usually do for satellite licensing. The most recent round of questions forced the companies to reveal the mass and cross-sectional area of their satellites, previously undisclosed. The answers, and their implications for re-entries and orbital safety, are truly alarming. SpaceX gives the mass of each of their one million proposed satellites as four tonnes, with other companies giving similar masses. SpaceX’s Starlink is the most numerous mega-constellation thus far, with more than 11,000 satellites in orbit as of October 2026. These satellites have five-year operating lifetimes and on average one or two car-sized satellites re-enter every day, depositing their mass in the upper atmosphere as metal vapour . If they don’t burn up completely, pieces may hit the ground . One piece of a Starlink satellite has been discovered on the ground — by a Saskatchewan farmer in 2024 . Thanks to geography, land use and Starlink’s chosen orbital distribution, Saskatchewan is the easiest place in the world to find space debris. A chunk of a SpaceX rocket also landed in a farmer’s field there in the same year. Conservatively, assuming the Starlink debris is the only piece that made it to Earth, that would give Starlink a 0.05 per cent re-entry survival rate. If SpaceX’s million satellite orbital data centre mega-constellation has the same re-entry survival rate, then 500 satellites would drop pieces on the ground every five years. SpaceX also recently stated in a New York Times article that up to five per cent of the mass of some of their satellites could survive re-entry. That implies 500 satellites could each drop 400 pounds of debris over the five-year operating lifetime of the million-satellite orbital data centre. The casualty risk of each re-entry is low. But SpaceX plans to roll the dice a million times, and the consequences may land on our heads. Larger satellites, higher risks All the companies want to use the exact same narrow band of “sun-synchronous terminator orbits.” Theoretically, these orbits allow constant access to sunlight. But due to Earth’s axial tilt, that’s only true for orbits above 1,400 kilometres altitude . This means that you can either have continuous sunlight or low-latency communications (without much time lag), but not both. Notably, all of the filed orbital data centre proposals include much lower altitude orbits than 1,400 kilometres. Image of the proposed satellites with solar wing dimensions, presented to the U.S. FCC by Cowboy Space in a letter dated June 23, 2026. (Cowboy Space) The cross-sectional areas listed for several companies’ individual satellites are ludicrous. Cowboy released sketches that imply each of their 20,000 satellites will have a cross-sectional area more than twice as large as the International Space Station. This is the largest structure ever in orbit — larger than a six-bedroom house, featuring six sleeping quarters, two bathrooms and a gym — and was built from separately launched modular pieces. Much larger satellites mean much higher collision risks, and the risks are already high with today’s satellites and debris. Artist’s digital image of International Space Station (ISS) passing over Florida. (NASA) A sky filled with satellites The proliferation of commercial satellites has already changed the night sky for everyone in the world. Sometimes when I first glance up at the stars, I have a moment of dizziness as my brain scrambles to determine which points are moving and which are stationary. I was part of a team that predicted one in 15 visible points in the night sky would soon be a moving satellite , not a star. Back in 2022, when that paper was published , many thought we were being sensationalist or exaggerating. Now, I’m convinced we were too conservative. The same team recently authored a paper showing what the proposed orbital data centres would look like as they move across the sky in rings in the morning and evening. The future of low-Earth orbit and our shared night sky is straight out of a science-fiction novel. And it looks like the U.S. Federal Communications Commission will get the deciding vote on whether it’s a dystopian one. Samantha Lawler receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. She is a fellow of the Outer Space Institute and a member of the Center for Space Environmentalism.

articles.content: In early September, Conservative Party MP Dean Allison held a four-day independent, unsanctioned “inquiry” for “Canadians to share their personal experiences of injuries…from the COVID-19 vaccine(s).” The event heard testimony that alleged the response to COVID-19 was “a miserable failure,” not least due to the “assaults on freedom and other malign actions.” An opinion piece in the Toronto Sun subsequently claimed that COVID-19 vaccine programs “killed thousands of Canadians,” repeating a call for an immediate stop of COVID-19 mRNA vaccinations, as well as “resignations, arrests and a full public inquiry…by the prime minister.” It further claimed that Canada’s COVID-19 vaccination efforts represent, at best, the “biggest health policy mistake in Canadian history.” But testimony heard at this inquiry — and responses to that testimony — conflate factual claims with ethical claims. As a consequence, it fails to recognize the ethical factors critical to understanding and justifying COVID-19 vaccination efforts. As public health ethicists, we’re interested in clarifying the factors necessary to substantiate claims about “policy mistakes” and informing expectations for future vaccination policy decisions. The conflation of facts and ethics Some of the claims made in the Allison inquiry and related reporting pertained to facts, both stated and omitted. Other claims were ethical in nature. The difference is critical to understanding and justifying COVID-19 vaccination efforts. For example, questions of facts are: How many people were injured or died as a result of COVID-19 vaccination How were vaccine candidates tested and regulated How many people were saved by vaccines . Immunity and Society is a new series from The Conversation Canada that presents new vaccine discoveries and immune-based innovations that are changing how we understand and protect human health. Through a partnership with the Bridge Research Consortium , these articles — written by experts in Canada at the forefront of immunology, biomanufacturing, social science and humanities — explore the latest developments and their impacts. Getting on the same page about these facts and dispelling mis- and disinformation remains crucial. For example, the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) records 455 reports of deaths following COVID-19 vaccination, noting these deaths weren’t necessarily attributable to the vaccine. After assessing causality, PHAC reports a total of four deaths consistent with causal association to immunization. To put this in context, more than 100 million COVID-19 vaccine doses have been administered in Canada. But getting on the same page about facts is not enough. That’s because claims about whether the government is justified in imposing certain obligations or burdens on the public — for example, requirements that citizens get vaccinated — are not answerable by facts alone. These are questions of ethics. These claims are about what one should do or what governments have legitimate authority to do, morally speaking: in other words, what is considered good or right or just. Values and policy decisions Such ethical claims are a matter of values, which people or groups may prioritize differently. For example, in deciding on health policy options, some may prefer the option that preserves personal autonomy above all else. Others may prioritize fairness and the policy option that minimizes deaths or health disparities. And some may locate the preservation of autonomy in policy options that are fair for all and that saves lives. Critically, no policy decision is ever free of values and value judgments. All policy decisions, including those related to vaccination, involve trade-offs of competing values. That necessarily means there will be trade-offs in the distribution of benefits, risks and burdens experienced across individuals and groups in society. While evidence can tell us what those benefits, risks and burdens might be, it cannot by itself tell us what the right trade-off is. That is, whether it is ethically justifiable to limit autonomy in some ways in order to preserve autonomy in others or to protect certain segments of the population from severe illness or death. In other words, facts alone will not determine how those competing values should be balanced, what outcomes matter the most and whose interests should be prioritized, among other things. Discussions about the legitimacy of Canada’s COVID-19 vaccination efforts or determining whether it was the “biggest health policy mistake in Canadian history” requires not only solid scientific facts, but also explicit ethical reasoning. This entails careful analysis of the values at stake, how trade-offs may reasonably be made between those values and ultimately what governments are ethically justified in doing in the name of public health. The ethics of imposing risk Fundamentally, the nature of the ethical claims made throughout the Allison inquiry and relevant reporting relate to one’s freedom to choose whether to be placed at risk by taking the COVID-19 vaccine. Yet, as our research argues, such claims about vaccine risks often fail to acknowledge or attend to the reciprocal nature of those risks and the reciprocal nature of freedom . At the same time that we may be exposed to risk when getting vaccinated (since no medical intervention is entirely risk-free), we also impose risk on others by choosing to forgo vaccination or choosing policy options that fail to effectively address vaccine-preventable diseases. Just as having the freedom to engage in an activity necessarily entails accepting some of the risks that are created in doing that activity, imposing risks on others can correspondingly justify limits being placed on one’s freedoms. A useful example is driving a car: Choosing to drive means accepting risks to one’s own safety, and it also imposes risks on other road users. Those risks to others can justify restricting the freedom to drive at high speeds by imposing and enforcing speed limits. The existence of risk alone doesn’t preclude governments from implementing policy or health interventions. Every choice carries risk, including the choice not to act. While vaccines themselves do entail some small risks, they are used to reduce a much greater risk of disease that people may not be able to avoid or mitigate on their own. Vaccination policies are not implemented against a backdrop of zero risk, and so doing nothing — such as choosing not to introduce vaccination policies — also creates risk. In certain situations, such as pandemics, it can create more risk, and governments should be accountable for these risks as well. Some of the statements made at the Allison inquiry and in corresponding media coverage appear to hold that governments cannot impose risk on the public. From an ethical standpoint, this is not a given, especially when action and inaction both involve risk. Such claims need further ethical analysis and reasoning that examines the nature of the risks and benefits, how they are distributed and the strength of the justifications used to defend policy action or inaction. Greater attention to ethics in policymaking and evaluation is critical to help identify the values at the heart of policy prescriptions, including related to freedom and risk, and to separate factual uncertainty from disagreement about those values. Only then will we be able to have constructive discussion about vaccination and vaccine policy in Canada. Maxwell J. Silva and Kari Pahlman do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: The fire that swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright over the weekend in Alberta killed four soldiers and injured 39 people, including 19 reported in critical condition. The thoughts of Canadians are with the families, the military community, the people of Wainwright and the responders who answered the call. But what happened after the fire deserves attention too. Wainwright’s hospital became a triage hub for what the town’s mayor described as the largest mass casualty event the community has ever seen. Patients were also transferred to hospitals in Edmonton, Calgary and Red Deer. The response mobilized 22 ground ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters . The Canadian Armed Forces relies on civilian systems for specialized services and mass casualty events . Civilian health readiness is therefore part of national defence. Thirteen months before Wainwright, Canada rehearsed the challenge of a casualty surge . Its findings deserve action. A system with little slack The response to a mass-casualty event does not play out in an otherwise empty health-care system. It competes with everyday care for staff, beds, transport and supplies. The Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) reports that hospital beds increased by only four per cent between 2014–15 and 2023–24 as Canada’s population grew by 13 per cent. Beds per capita fell by seven per cent. These national figures don’t establish Alberta’s capacity on the day of the fire, but they show why having enough infrastructure, staff and expertise is so important. Alberta has two burn centres, in Edmonton and Calgary . That specialist capacity is an asset. But rural hospitals need staff, supplies and transportation to stabilize severely injured patients and move them safely to burn centres while continuing to serve their own communities. Canada’s health-care system sits at the centre of what’s known as a polycrisis : several systems are under strain, each situation compounding the other. Read more: ‘Polycrisis’ may be a buzzword, but it could help us tackle the world’s woes Climate change is prolonging wildfire seasons. Inflation is squeezing budgets and supply chains. Workforce shortages are persisting after the COVID-19 pandemic . The flu season is surging. The consequences of these crises affect health system response and care. Wainwright is experiencing its mass casualty event amid this ongoing polycrisis. The question is whether any system can absorb the next shock while still dealing with the last. What Canada already learned In September 2025, 79 people from health-care systems across the country, federal agencies and the Canadian Armed Forces gathered in Toronto for Exercise Canada Paratus . Paratus assessed overseas casualties, but the lessons apply to all hazards. Led by key disaster management teams and leaders, the exercise simulated about 100 casualties a week arriving in provincial and territorial health-care systems in Canada from a war in Europe. The post-exercise report is blunt. Three findings are relevant to planning after Wainwright: • Capacity: The report identified workforce challenges and the need to expand infrastructure, staffing and expertise for sustained casualty surges. • Patient tracking: Canada has no integrated system to follow casualties as they move between military and civilian care. At Wainwright, the injured were dispersed across several hospitals within hours. • Governance: The report called for a federal–provincial–territorial health emergency and security authority with clear leadership, roles and decision rights. At the moment, there’s no organization co-ordinating health-care system capacity across federal, provincial and territorial governments. Health care is defence infrastructure NATO already recognizes the link between healthcare and defence. One of its seven baseline requirements for national resilience is the ability to manage mass casualties and disruptive health crises, including functioning civilian health systems and secure medical supplies . Canada’s allies already treat health-care systems as strategic infrastructure, alongside energy grids and supply chains. At the 2025 Hague NATO summit , allies agreed that up to 1.5 per cent of GDP within their new five per cent defence spending target could support resilience, including civil preparedness. Finland’s comprehensive security model treats health security as a vital societal function , while Sweden’s total defence approach recognizes healthcare as essential to defence . Canada should seize this opportunity to make a clear case for health investments that strengthen defence readiness. 5 steps Canada must take Canada already has the diagnosis. As the polycrisis deepens, sudden events like Wainwright will keep exposing the cost of failing to fill gaps. Here’s how Canada should respond: First, implement the Paratus recommendations with a public timeline. Second, create the permanent federal–provincial–territorial health emergency body the report calls for. Third, build patient tracking that works across civilian and military care, so every casualty can be followed from the scene to recovery. Fourth, treat surge capacity, including rural hospitals near bases and critical infrastructure, as a defence-relevant investment. Finally, make the next national exercise a domestic, sudden scenario that applies a sudden mass-casualty event onto a system already under strain. New tools, including AI-enabled polycrisis simulation, allow authorities to rehearse these compounding scenarios before they happen; they’re already being developed . The clinicians and paramedics who responded at Wainwright were part of Canada’s defence capacity, regardless of whether we call them that. Paratus asked whether our health system could survive intact if war came to us from overseas. Wainwright answered a harder question: what happens when the emergency is already here. This article was co-authored by Stacey Litvinchuk, RN, MN, CHE, founder and CEO of Axiora Governance and former senior program officer for provincial surgery operations at Alberta Health Services. Marcia Clark is affiliated with - President of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada Bhavini Gohel does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Conversations about sex after illness, disease or the onset of disability tend to stall on the same question: How far does the sex you’re having now fall short of the sex you used to have? That comparison can make it difficult to imagine what satisfying sex might look like when pain, fatigue, reduced mobility, changes in sensation or difficulty holding certain positions make familiar sex harder to sustain. Some people keep trying to reproduce the sex they used to have. Others withdraw from sex altogether. Sexual scripts are cultural and interpersonal routines that guide who initiates sex, what activities follow and how it should end. Traditional ones tend to centre penile-vaginal intercourse as “real sex,” and everything else is treated as tangential — a warm-up or an afterthought. Adapting to these changes tends to require sexual flexibility — a willingness to explore new and different ways of experiencing sexual satisfaction , pleasure and intimacy. Sex toys can help facilitate that shift. Used as accessibility tools, they can deliver controlled stimulation, reduce the physical effort sex requires and broaden what satisfying sex can involve and look like. From taboo to useful toolkit For many years, sex toys were associated with films like Secretary and Fifty Shades of Grey , or with alternative sexual lifestyles. Now, the tide is turning. Media and public discourse increasingly present sex toys as positive, adaptive tools. Netflix’s How to Build a Sex Room , for example, and the popularity of affordable products such as the viral “rose toy” , point to growing normalization. Accessibility begins with choice: for one person, adapting might mean trying out a clitoral vibrator with air-pulse technology. For another, it might mean adding a pillow to make certain positions more comfortable. Making the decision to purchase a sex toy can be daunting, and choosing the right one isn’t always easy. Many tools are expensive, come in conspicuous packaging or are simply too loud. And some may not be safe , like those containing chemicals that can disrupt hormones. Tools that do the heavy lifting Sex toys have real potential to function as sexual health aids that support satisfaction and pleasure at every stage of life. Vibrators are among the most familiar sexual aids. A recent nationally representative study of 1,170 women found that 50.6 per cent of Canadian women have used one before. But the category is broader than the word suggests . Vibrators range in function, design and where they offer stimulation, from wands and rabbits to discreet clitoral and bullet vibrators. There are many options for different preferences, and design can really matter for accessibility. Models with ergonomic handles may be easier for someone with limited grip, while hands-free toys can remove the need to hold a device in place, which can be quite useful when disability or fatigue makes repetitive movement tiring. Vibrators can also provide stimulation when sensation is reduced, help close the orgasm gap and create opportunities for self-exploration . Read more: The orgasm gap and why women climax less than men Of course, vibration is not necessarily for everyone. For some, it may help to start at a low intensity or to use a toy over clothing. Other tools redistribute sexual effort in different ways. Sex swings, wedges, adaptive seating and even ordinary pillows can support body weight, which may benefit people with limited hip movement, paralysis or joint pain. Sensory play — sex involving blindfolds, whips, paddles or restraints — can also help expand intimacy beyond genital stimulation. And if vaginal dryness is an issue, lubricants can help make sexual exploration more comfortable. By and large, supportive-care oncology research shows that combining sex toys with adaptive practices, such as mindfulness and expanding one’s definition of sex , can improve sexual satisfaction, desire and relationship quality. Likewise, studies have shown that clitoral vibrators benefit women with multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injuries and can improve pelvic-floor and sexual functioning more generally. Where access breaks down For those with disabilities, there are additional barriers that increase the challenge of cultivating a satisfying sex life. Alongside stigma and assumptions that disabled people have little or no interest in sex comes limited provision of sexual health information about pleasure and adaptation. Privacy is also limited for those living with family or receiving support at home, which constrains masturbation and the practical business of acquiring and storing a sex toy. However, there are resources that can help. Platforms such as OMGYes illustrate the range of ways tools can be used to adapt sex. Sex therapy is also a beneficial way to learn about how to adapt sex and improve sexual relationships. Sexual satisfaction should not depend on following one dominant sexual script. With ongoing communication, attention to consent and safer-sex practices , sex toys can help cultivate forms of intimacy that respond to changing bodies across the lifespan. Maha Khawaja receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC) Canadian Graduate Research Scholarship – Doctoral (CGRS-D).

articles.content: Rats are on the ballot in Canadian municipal elections this fall, with several political parties promising to tackle city rat problems . While rats may seem like a niche election issue, they can point to broader societal concerns about housing, public services and civic engagement. Rats are ubiquitous urban residents that cities have attempted to evict for centuries . Often portrayed as dirty pests and bringers of plague, they can harbour pathogens that cause illnesses to people and pets , like rat bite fever and leptospirosis . So why have cities had so little success in reducing rat numbers? Well, rats are synanthropes , species that benefit from living alongside humans, and have adapted remarkably well to our paved, cacophonic and bustling streets. Cities provide abundant resources for rats to thrive : food scraps are meals; standing water on sidewalks supplies drinking water; and cracks in buildings offer access to shelter. Municipal policies and bylaws shape how these environments are built and maintained, influencing living conditions for both people and rats. Thinking about rats through municipal elections can offer a more tangible way to understand how complex it is to manage rats without addressing broader issues. We reviewed studies from high-income country cities. Using synthesis and complex systems mapping methods, we examined the social and environmental conditions linked to urban rats, how they influence where people encounter rats across different neighbourhoods and how they impact residents’ ability to respond. Here are a few of our findings and how they connect to municipal issues, using examples from Vancouver’s upcoming election. Habitability, affordability and security Our homes are the most intimate spaces where we can encounter rats. Adequate housing is a human right enshrined under many nations’ laws, including Canada’s . Housing habitability, affordability and security — components of adequate housing — can impact encounters between residents and rats. Cracks and gaps in older, poorly maintained dwellings allow rats into places where people eat and sleep .
