When housing costs leave little money for other essentials due to people “ paying more than they can afford ,” residents may be unable to pay for measures to prevent or remediate rat infestations, adding financial strain to households already facing competing needs. Housing insecurity is also central to why some residents might be more impacted by rats than others. For example, renters may be more likely to experience sustained rat infestations. Fear of eviction or landlord-tenant conflicts can discourage renters from seeking help. Landlord inaction can leave tenants living with persistent infestations and little power to act. Commitments to strengthen tenant protections could reduce barriers in resolving these problems by holding landlords to the city’s maintenance standards . This bylaw requires owners to eliminate pest infestations and maintain their properties to prevent pest harbourage. Unhoused populations may be at higher risk of rat contact. In Vancouver, the number of unhoused people increased 12 per cent between 2023 and 2025, a general trend mirrored across Canada Prolonged periods outdoors, alongside limited sanitation access , can also increase contact with rats. This speaks to candidate concerns that “ in a wealthy city like Vancouver, people are sleeping rough .” Yet city councils have some power over housing supply . Municipalities play an important role in land use policy and regulations, which matter for reducing rodent exposures through availability of safe, stable housing. Waste, sanitation, neighbourhood conditions Cities are hubs for consumption and waste like trash, food scraps, and sewage. Missed garbage pickups and dirty streets are more than a nuisance, they’re also culprits of ratty conditions. Previous studies have linked rat problems with dog waste and human waste . These findings connect to candidate criticisms like “ city streets and parks are covered with animal and human poop .” In fact, open defecation is an ongoing urban issue related to housing insecurity and limited public washrooms. But, when it comes to waste and rats, not all neighbourhoods are the same . Conditions and resources that support rats and residents’ ability to address them vary across neighbourhoods, with infestations often occurring in neighbourhoods experiencing long-term disinvestment and structural marginalization . Civic engagement So how do municipalities know where to target interventions? Many cities use municipal 311 services to understand how rats are distributed across neighbourhoods. They also capture resident concerns to draw municipal attention to problems affecting everyday life. When it comes to rat management, 311 aligns with pledges for “ a City Hall that listens ” and seeks “ involvement of local residents .” However, rat studies acknowledge the limitations of these data in their current form: residents differ in access, ability, knowledge and trust to report to 311 systems . So, while 311 services can be channels for civic participation and a pragmatic way to monitor and manage rats, they can also reflect broader social inequities . Beyond the elections The real work is done after voting day comes and goes. Luckily, Vancouver, like numerous other cities, already has a Healthy City Strategy that aligns with proactive and equitable rat management. This approach prioritizes determinants of health — including housing, sanitation and access to protective resources — by addressing root causes and directing resources to where barriers are greater. For rat management, this means identifying where infestations and conditions that sustain them coincide with limited resident resources to respond. So, the next time you see a rat scurrying along, perhaps you’ll think about what rats symbolize — not just dirt and disease, but our everyday urban living. articles.description: Rats are on the ballot in Canadian municipal elections this fall, with several political parties promising to tackle city rat problems . articles.content: As the days darken, making more room for arts-based practices and experiences is one way to bring useful, interesting or sustaining activities into the seasons ahead. For families and people working in schools, this may be particularly relevant as the school year settles into its routines and demands. Making more room for the arts can expand the resources available to students , families and educators, including opportunities for curiosity, connection and enjoyment in daily life. Even positive or eagerly anticipated changes require us to adapt , which can take attention, time and emotional energy. What requires little thought once it becomes habitual can require considerable attention when new. Our capacity to navigate these changes is shaped by the resources available to us and the relationships and systems we are part of. A student who was excited to be back at school may stumble with figuring out new friendships, expectations or responsibilities, while another may feel the dread that can emerge after difficult experiences or alongside boredom and uncertainty. Parents and caregivers support these day-to-day challenges alongside everything else they carry and manage, while teachers lead classrooms within school systems where time, staffing and other resources are often stretched thin . Art to expand our resources As an art therapist, my work generally begins when someone is already struggling. This has led me to consider what happens further upstream: what experiences, relationships and resources might become part of everyday life before difficulties become overwhelming? Everyday art-making is not art therapy, nor is it a substitute for professional support when needed. But a growing body of research suggests that arts engagement can contribute to health and well-being , including social and personal dimensions of well-being in educational settings . Making room for creative activities in schools can give students additional opportunities to explore their interests and express themselves. (Unsplash) Making and experiencing art can expand the resources people have available and help them discover capacities they may draw on in other parts of their lives. While creative practices can help expand the ways we express or comfort ourselves in difficult moments, they can also bring curiosity, imagination, connection and enjoyment into ordinary days. Read more: For both artists and scientists, slow looking allows surprising connections to surface Something interesting and pleasurable Sometimes, the value of making art simply lies in being absorbed in something interesting or pleasurable. Like exercise, reading or other activities that sustain us, engaging with the arts does not have to begin with a problem that needs solving. I am focusing here on visual art, though music, theatre, dance, writing and other creative practices may be more inviting depending on people’s interests and affinities. One common obstacle is the expectation of being “good” at art right away. Artistic skills and visual languages can be learned and explored , with people bringing different strengths, ways of learning and interests to them . Making art will not appeal to everyone, but deciding it is “not for you” because it does not come easily at first can mean giving up something you might enjoy. Most people who enjoy cycling will never compete in the Tour de France, nor would they want to; the pleasure and value of cycling do not depend on reaching that level of ability. Getting lost in doodling can take the imagination somewhere else. Knitting or beading can offer repetition and rhythm that feel welcome after a day filled with too many unknowns. Clay, collaging and painting engage the senses differently and offer room to experiment, play or express what is difficult to put into words. Photography can invite closer attention to our surroundings. None of these need to become a project, accomplishment or regular practice to have value. Creative resources can be kept within easy reach: a student might keep a container of putty among their school supplies, something tactile to turn to in a stressful moment. These resources need not disappear with childhood. A tired parent might appreciate their own ball of modelling clay during yet another Zoom meeting. Keeping creative corners accessible Experiencing the arts can spark curiosity, introduce experiences beyond our own, or let us encounter something of our own experience in another person’s work. Access to the arts can be built into places people already spend time. A creative corner in a school staff room could offer materials to explore and opportunities for colleagues to connect differently during a break. Libraries, museums, galleries and community centres offer inexpensive or free ways to engage with the arts . Making these experiences accessible is important, particularly when time, money, space or access to materials can limit people’s options. Building capacity also means looking beyond what individuals can do for themselves to what resources families, schools and communities can make available. What we make available to one another is also part of how we build care and support into our environments. Making more room for the arts is one way to do this. Through all seasons, we can think beyond what needs to be accomplished and build in more of what can help people stay connected, engaged and resourced. Heather McLaughlin does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: When you seek medical care, you hope that your doctor will present you with treatment options that are proven to be effective for your condition, that harms do not outweigh benefits and that recommended treatments are affordable and account for your personal situation. But if your doctor has been influenced by messages, payments or gifts from drug companies, that is unlikely to be the case, as our team from Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States found. Pharmaceutical industry promotion is a global phenomenon. In the mid 2010s, companies in the U.S. spent just under US$30 billion annually to convince doctors to prescribe their products. Figures in other countries are harder to come by but in the mid 2010s, close to CA$500 million was being spent in Canada on advertising in medical journals and on sales representatives who visit doctors’ offices. Between 2015 to 2024, 17,519 Australian doctors received AU$148.7 million from pharmaceutical companies for conferences, travel costs or consultancy fees. In 2020, seven of the top 10 largest pharmaceutical companies globally spent more on marketing than on developing new drugs . Our research examines the relationship between pharmaceutical promotion and doctors’ prescribing. Evidence shows the effects of promotion Our Cochrane systematic review looked at the results of 93 studies involving millions of doctors and published largely over the past two decades. Due to their rigour, Cochrane reviews are considered the gold standard for evidence synthesis. We examined what happens to the appropriateness, quantity and cost of prescriptions when doctors accept payments or meals from the pharmaceutical industry or rely on pharmaceutical representatives for their education or prescribing information. We looked at the effects of a range of types of promotion: advertising and industry-sponsored education, gifts such as free meals and payments for consulting or advisory board membership and free drug samples. The result is not good news for patients. Doctors who receive gifts or payments prescribe less appropriately and issue more prescriptions — and those prescriptions tend to be more costly. Exposure to pharmaceutical advertising or education probably increases how many prescriptions a doctor issues and may increase costs and decrease appropriateness. The evidence on the effects of free samples is less clear, as there were fewer studies. We also looked at whether conflict-of-interest policies make a difference. Some medical schools and hospitals have policies limiting interactions among students, trainees or doctors and the industry, such as banning sales visits or specific types of gifts. The result is more appropriate prescribing and possibly fewer prescriptions. The longer the exposure and the stricter the policies, the greater the effect. Greater exposure to promotion has greater effects The more company-sponsored meals that doctors ate and the more gifts or payments they received, the more their prescribing deteriorated. The more expensive the gift or the higher the value of the payment, the worse the outcome on prescribing. A meal worth as little as US$20 led to more prescriptions for the drug made by the company providing the meal. With each additional meal, doctors issued more prescriptions. Disturbingly, given the legacy of opioid addiction and deaths from overdose, the more meals from opioid manufacturers doctors received, the more opioids they prescribed . ‘I can’t be bought for the price of a sandwich’ Doctors recognize the commercial motivation behind industry’s interactions with them, but do not believe they are affected . Comments to the effect of “I can’t be bought for the price of a sandwich” are a common refrain. Our results convincingly demonstrate those denials cannot be justified. Most doctors who interact with drug companies are not being bribed; companies do not require prescriptions in exchange for gifts. Clinicians are affected through the “ gift relationship .” Receiving a gift of any kind or size, whether wanted or unwanted, creates an obligation — often unconscious — for individuals to repay what they have received. Michael Oldani, a former sales representative who is now a medical anthropologist who researches pharmaceutical marketing tactics, describes the central role played by the gift relationship in an ethnographic analysis of the influence of sales representatives on prescribing. Promotion also provides a reminder that focuses clinicians’ attention on promoted products so they’re more likely to think of these products when making a prescribing decision. From transparency data to public health action The extent of our review is possible because of a recent large expansion in research on pharmaceutical promotion due to the implementation of the 2013 Physician Payments Sunshine Act in the U.S., and other similar national transparency databases that record payments from drug companies to doctors. The Sunshine Act alone includes payments to more than a million doctors. Another database records the several million prescriptions written by these doctors. Combining these databases offers significantly more data, allowing for the identification of more precise associations between payments and prescribing. That includes showing that the greater the exposure, the greater the effect. Our findings reinforce why pharmaceutical promotion must be addressed as a commercial determinant of health — a key pathway through which corporations negatively impact public health. Commercial determinants of health have been defined as “the systems, practices, and pathways through which commercial actors drive health and equity.” Commercial determinants play a key role in the obesity epidemic, the rapid global growth in noncommunicable diseases and the climate emergency. Our review convincingly settles the debate about the effects of promotion on the way that doctors prescribe and shows that promotion is likely to be a major commercial determinant of (ill)-health. The medical community and governments can no longer ignore the consequences of the promotion of medicines on prescribing. It is time for strong concrete action to be taken to put an end to the way that companies are allowed to influence doctors. This article was also co-authored by Geoffrey Spurling, Associate Professor at the University of Queensland, Riaz Qureshi, Assistant Professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, and Lisa Bero, Professor of Medicine and Public Health at the Center for Bioethics and Humanities, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. Between 2023-2026, Joel Lexchin received payments for writing a brief for a legal firm on the role of promotion in generating prescriptions for opioids and for co-writing an article for a peer-reviewed medical journal on semaglutide. He is a member of the Board of the Canadian Health Coalition. He receives royalties from University of Toronto Press and James Lorimer & Co. Ltd. for books he has written. He has received funding from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research in the past. Alice Fabbri is currently working as a public health physician at the Hygiene and Public Health Unit in Ravenna, Department of Public Health, Azienda Sanitaria Locale (AUSL) Romagna, Italy. Barbara Mintzes receives funding from the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC). She is an expert witness for Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration, and has acted as an expert witness for Health Canada. Dr Mintzes is a member of Association Mieux Prescrire and Health Action International and is General Secretary of the International Society of Drug Bulletins (ISDB). Quinn Grundy served as consultant for the Government of Canada Competition Bureau in 2025. Dr. Grundy has received research funding from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Social Science and Humanities Research Council, the World Health Organization, and the Greenwall Foundation, a not-for-profit bioethics research foundation. Dr. Grundy serves as Director of the World Health Organization Collaborating Centre for Governance, Transparency, and Accountability in the Pharmaceutical Sector.

articles.content: When the Swedish Academy announced Anne Carson as the recipient of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature , in Stockholm, I was participating in a panel discussion in the same city at Stockholm University about possible laureates — and the literary traditions they represent. Before the announcement, I had spoken about two Canadian writers, Margaret Atwood and Carson , whose international recognition reflects different trajectories within contemporary literature. Carson’s work challenges the very categories through which we usually classify literary achievement. It moves between poetry, translation, philosophical reflection and the reconfiguration of ancient myths. The Swedish Academy justified its decision by praising Carson’s “bold and inventive oeuvre” and its “playful dialogue with the classical tradition” that have allowed her to create new forms for contemporary literature. This formulation captures a fundamental paradox of her writing: Carson’s literary modernity emerges from a persistent return to antiquity , not as a stable cultural inheritance to be preserved, but as an unfinished reservoir of images, voices and fragments capable of unsettling contemporary experience. Meaning of fragments Fragments of ancient text occupy a privileged position in Carson’s literary universe. These establish a connection between the material survival of ancient texts and the discontinuous forms associated with modern and postmodern writing. ‘If not, Winter: Fragments of Sappho’ translation by Anne Carson. (Penguin Random House) Carson’s translation of Sappho’s surviving poetry in If Not, Winter (2002) exemplifies this approach. Carson preserves the gaps and interruptions of the original fragments, rather than attempting to disguise them through speculative reconstruction. The resulting poems make absence visible, allowing silence and discontinuity to participate in the production of meaning. This attention to what remains incomplete establishes an unexpected affinity between archaic poetry and modern literary experimentation. Fragmentation is frequently associated with the crisis of representation in 20th-century literature. Carson reveals that the ancient textual tradition already contains discontinuities that resist the modern desire for completeness. ‘Eros the Bittersweet’ This relationship between ancient thought and contemporary experimentation is central to Carson’s long essay Eros the Bittersweet (1986) . This work combines classical scholarship, philosophical inquiry and poetic reflection. Carson begins with the Greek understanding of eros as an experience that combines pleasure and suffering. She draws particular attention to Sappho’s description of desire as glukupikron , or bittersweet. Vase image depicting Sappho, from c. 470 BCE. (Wikimedia) , CC BY-SA The apparent contradiction contained within this expression becomes the starting point for an investigation into the structure of desire, which depends upon distance, incompleteness and the impossibility of fully possessing its object. Carson explores the fundamentally relational character of desire: Desire emerges in the interval separating the lover from the beloved. It is precisely this distance that generates both the intensity of attraction and the suffering associated with absence. Her reading of ancient Greek literature connects this paradox to the emergence of self-consciousness , since the experience of desiring another person also reveals the limits of the self. The beloved remains irreducibly other. The attempt to overcome this separation exposes the impossibility of complete identification. Carson’s treatment of eros also reveals what might be called an archaic drive within her postmodern writing, provided that the term is understood as the persistence of fundamental human experiences that resist closure, not as nostalgia for an idealized past. Desire, vulnerability and the confrontation with absence return through ancient metaphors, while their literary expression is continually renewed by contemporary forms. In this sense, Carson is a philosopher who works through metaphors, allowing poetic language to produce concepts rather than merely illustrate ideas established elsewhere. ‘Autobiography of Red’ The philosophical reflections developed in Eros the Bittersweet acquire a remarkable narrative form in Autobiography of Red (1998) . This novel in verse reconfigures the ancient myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster defeated by Herakles. Carson draws upon the surviving fragments of the Greek poet Stesichorus , whose account of Geryon belongs to a mythological tradition organized around the heroic exploits of Herakles. Yet Carson shifts the narrative perspective towards Geryon himself, rather than reproducing the familiar opposition between the victorious hero and the monstrous adversary. This shift transforms a figure traditionally defined through his defeat into the protagonist of an intimate exploration of identity, desire and emotional vulnerability. This reversal is significant because it changes the moral and narrative structure of the ancient myth. The monster becomes a subject capable of remembering , suffering, loving and reflecting upon his own difference. He is no longer simply the embodiment of an external threat against which heroic identity can be established. The relationship between Geryon and Herakles also reconfigures the ancient narrative through the language of contemporary sexuality and emotional experience. Their intimacy is marked by attraction, separation and the unequal experience of desire. This recalls the philosophical paradox examined in Eros the Bittersweet : love is sustained by an irreducible distance between individuals, even when they seek closeness. What emerges is not simply a modernized version of Greek mythology, but a transformation of the relationship between heroism and monstrosity. By granting Geryon an autobiographical voice, Carson questions the authority of inherited narratives and the distribution of visibility within the classical tradition. The novel’s poetic form reinforces this instability through the co-existence of lyric intensity, narrative development, visual imagery and reflections on the act of representation. Ancient sources, postmodern insight? To describe Carson’s work as postmodern may initially seem paradoxical, given the centrality of ancient Greek literature to her intellectual formation. Yet this apparent contradiction is precisely what makes her writing distinctive. She uses some of the most recognizable techniques of postmodern literature — intertextuality, hybrid genres, disrupted chronology and unstable narrative authority — to reactivate experiences and symbolic structures inherited from antiquity. In this way, Carson examines anew forms of experience that continue to inhabit contemporary culture: desire, loss, violence, otherness and the limits of language. Reinvention of literary forms The Swedish Academy’s recognition of Carson invites us to reconsider the relationship between literary tradition and innovation. As a Canadian writer deeply connected to ancient Greek literature, Carson resists what could be understood as conventional classifications of national literary identity — though Carson, also a member of the Order of Canada and an awarded poet in the country , has also inspired questions about Canadian literature and culture . Carson’s Nobel Prize recognizes not simply the survival of classical literature within contemporary writing, but the capacity of ancient fragments to generate new literary possibilities. articles.content: Canadian poet and author Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize for literature . The honour comes in the midst of Canada’s literary prize season and provides some clues into how Canadian talent finds an international audience. Carson , born in Toronto, moves between poetry, essay, translation, classics and drama, often challenging the boundaries separating these forms. Read more: Anne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature – how she discovered new possibilities within language Anne Carson at the 2024 National Book Awards finalist reading in the NYU Skirball Center in New York. (Jay Dixit/Wikimedia) , CC BY-SA Her reputation has developed through institutions associated particularly with poetry and experimental literature, including the Griffin Poetry Prize , the T.S. Eliot Prize, a MacArthur Fellowship and Spain’s Princess of Asturias Award for Literature . Carson shows how experimental writing can circulate through poetry, translation and academic as well as literary networks. The Giller Prize, meantime, has announced its 2026 shortlist . The proximity of these two major literary awards announcements invites us to consider Canadian literature at two different scales. The Giller identifies and celebrates literature in Canada, while the Nobel operates within an international literary field where writers, languages and literary traditions acquire very different degrees of visibility. Prizes part of longer process As a researcher in cultural studies , I am interested in literary prizes in the francophone world and, more broadly, the literary systems and strategies through which writers gain recognition . From this perspective, prizes are not simply rewards for individual achievement. They are part of a longer process involving publishers, critics, juries, translations and other cultural institutions that contribute to establishing literary reputations . The Nobel Prize offers a particularly visible example of this process at the international level . Carson and fellow Canadian Margaret Atwood regularly appear in public and in media speculation about possible Nobel laureates. Read more: Meet the Canadian writers and researchers who deserve to win the Nobel Prize Nonetheless, the Swedish Academy’s confidential selection process is shrouded in secrecy even after the fact. According to statutes structuring the process, information about nominations must remain confidential for 50 years after the nomination year . Canada’s relationship with Nobel Prize Canada’s relationship with the Nobel Prize in Literature illustrates how the idea of a “Canadian writer” can be complicated. Saul Bellow , who received the Nobel prize in 1976 , was born in Lachine, Québec, in 1915. But Bellow moved with his family to Chicago as a child and built his literary career in the United States. The Nobel Prize’s presentation situates him within the history of the American novel. His trajectory reminds us that birthplace, citizenship and literary belonging do not necessarily coincide. Alice Munro , the only Canadian to have been awarded the Nobel prize in literature, represents a different case. She remained closely associated with Canada, and particularly southwestern Ontario, throughout her literary career. Read more: Re-reading Alice Munro in the light of the secrets she kept and pain she caused When the Swedish Academy awarded her the Nobel in 2013 , it crowned a process of literary recognition that had developed over several decades, including the Man Booker International Prize In Canada, prior to this, Munro won three Governor General’s Literary Awards and two Giller Prizes. She was also a member of the Giller Prize’s inaugural jury in 1994, alongside Mordecai Richler and David Staines . She returned as a juror in 2006. Being recognized, recognizing other writers Margaret Atwood has similarly occupied both sides of the Giller Prize, winning it for Alias Grace in 1996 and serving as a juror in 1998, 2000, 2008 and 2013. This circulation between being recognized and recognizing others is important. Established writers also become jurors, critics, mentors and institutional figures who participate in recognizing other writers and, in doing so, help define literary value. Atwood and Munro’s histories with the Giller show how literary recognition becomes a collective and institutional process. Canadian literary infrastructure The Canadian literary field has developed a substantial infrastructure for producing this recognition. The Governor General’s Literary Awards , created in 1936 and administered by the Canada Council for the Arts since 1959, recognize literature in both English and French across several genres. The Giller Prize , founded in 1994, created another influential institution devoted to Canadian fiction. Its emergence coincided with a period in which writers including Atwood, Munro, Michael Ondaatje and Mordecai Richler acquired substantial recognition in Canada and internationally. This demonstrates how prizes also organize visibility. Shortlists generate critical and media attention. Winning can introduce authors to new readers and publishers, and sometimes strengthen their profiles in those markets. Positioning for international readerships Souvankham Thammavongsa’s Pick a Colour was already published and reviewed in the United Kingdom before it won the 2025 Giller Prize . Following the award, however, international publishers incorporated the distinction prominently into the book’s presentation . Cultural reference points Atwood’s career combines Canadian literary recognition with exceptional international circulation: Governor General’s Literary Awards, the Giller Prize and two Booker Prizes accompany a body of work translated and published internationally. Some of her novels have acquired cultural lives far beyond literature. The Handmaid’s Tale , first published in 1985, has travelled through television , visual culture and political protest. Read more: The Handmaid’s Tale reflects Margaret Atwood’s eerie talent for reading the palm of power Her Giller Prize-winning Alias Grace was adapted into a six-part CBC/Netflix miniseries written by Sarah Polley and distributed internationally by Netflix. These adaptations and appropriations give Atwood’s work new audiences and cultural meanings across different media, making her an international cultural reference as well as a novelist. Multiple trajectories, traditions These contrasting trajectories also remind us that Canadian literature cannot be reduced to a single tradition. Canada contains Indigenous literary and storytelling traditions, and English- and French-language literary traditions informed by transnational cultural hybridity — including Canadian writers whose careers cross languages, territories and national boundaries. This linguistic dimension matters internationally because literary circulation is unequal: writers working in globally dominant languages have more direct access to publishers, reviewers and readers, while others depend more heavily on translation and international publishing networks. Read more: Indigenous-authored novels: 5 great contemporary reads for young adults From Canada to Stockholm The Nobel can be understood as a mechanism of literary consecration situated within a much larger system. Before a writer reaches Stockholm, publishers have invested in the work, critics have discussed it, juries have rewarded it, translators may have carried it into other languages and universities, and festivals and readers have contributed to establishing its place in literary culture. There is no single route from Canada to the international stage, including, potentially, the Nobel. What matters is the accumulation of recognition and the capacity of a body of work to circulate beyond its original literary environment. The more interesting question may be how writers move to a position where their work can be recognized as part of world literature — and what recognition makes that movement possible. articles.content: The September 2026 removal of a sculpture from the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., has prompted criticism. The move is understood by arts activists as reflecting United States President Donald Trump’s wider efforts to appropriate and rebrand the Center and curtail modern styles at federal facilities. The Associated Press reports that a “Trump-aligned board” at the Center is fighting in court for the right to put Trump’s name on the historic institution . Read more: Trump has gotten rid of many of the checks and balances that could stop him from demolishing the Kennedy Center Trump took aim at “modernist” architecture and promoted “traditional” and “classical” structures in two executive orders issued in 2020 and 2025 . The group Hands Off the Arts , described the decision to remove artist Joel Shapiro’s sculpture Blue as “ authoritarian ” and as an act of “ vandalism .” The large blue geometric sculpture playfully evoked the human form in motion. Born in 1941, the late Shapiro was known for bridging modernism and postmodernism with sculptures that combined minimalist abstraction with figuration and movement. The abstract sculpture was removed from the Kennedy Center and follows executive orders from U.S. President Donald Trump to promote ‘traditional’ and ‘classical’ structures. (Jeff Vincent/Flickr) , CC BY In addition to the Kennedy Center, Trump has sought to transform Washington D.C. in other ways. His demolition of the East Wing of the White House, repainting of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and plans to build a new triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery have all raised questions about legal and regulatory limits on presidential actions impacting cultural heritage. Read more: Trump wants an ‘Independence Arch’ — How famous arches warn about dangers to republics Outside of Washington D.C., work on the border wall between the U.S. and Mexico has damaged and continues to threaten Indigenous archaeological and sacred sites . Trump’s attempts to dismantle , politicize and take over public institutions for arts and learning have been well documented. Such attacks on cultural heritage in the U.S. are not unique. In recent years, several governments have placed at risk the very heritage they are charged to protect. Cultural policy and state control International law places primary responsibility for protecting cultural heritage on states. The U.S. proposed the World Heritage Convention to the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) in 1972 and was the first state to ratify it . According to the convention , each state party to it “recognizes that the duty of ensuring the identification, protection, conservation, presentation and transmission to future generations of the cultural and natural heritage … belongs primarily to that State.” But recent research suggests attacks on cultural heritage and institutions are sometimes part of democratic backsliding and broader strategies to normalize political corruption and institute authoritarian policies. Trump and his administration have repeatedly criticized UNESCO, accusing the UN agency that seeks to safeguard heritage of supporting “woke, divisive cultural and social causes.” Trump withdrew the U.S. from UNESCO in 2019. The U.S. rejoined UNESCO in 2023 under the administration of former president Joe Biden . But the U.S. is slated to withdraw from the UN agency once again at the end of 2026 . Russia: Trinity icon Contested state decisions impacting culture and heritage can be seen elsewhere. In 2023, curators warned that Russian president Vladimir Putin’s plans to transfer a masterpiece of 15th-century Russian religious art from the State Tretyakov Gallery to the Russian Orthodox Church would put it at risk. Experts cautioned that removing Andrei Rublev’s Trinity icon from its climate-controlled museum case would likely damage it, a scenario that has now unfolded, according to a report from RBC media outlet publicized in the Moscow Times and the Art Newspaper in September 2026. Painted in the 1420s, Rublev’s icon is widely regarded as a treasure of Russian cultural heritage and one of the greatest examples of Orthodox icon painting. Putin’s transfer of the icon to the church in 2023 has been interpreted as politically motivated : a recognition of the loyalty of Patriarch Kirill, leader of the Russian Orthodox Church, who has steadfastly supported Russia’s war against Ukraine. Turkish case: Hagia Sophia In Turkey, five years ago, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan removed the museum status of Istanbul’s Hagia Sophia and converted it back into a mosque. Built in the sixth century on a site occupied by earlier churches since the fourth century CE, Hagia Sophia was the largest and most important church of the Greek-speaking Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire for nearly a millennium. It was converted into a mosque following the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453. In 1934 it was a made a museum by the founder of the Turkish Republic Mustafa Kemal Atatürk who sought to establish Turkey as a modern secular state. Hagia Sophia remains a singular masterpiece of Byzantine architecture and preserves unique mosaics of Roman rulers and Christian saints. It became part of the UNESCO World Heritage Historic Areas of Istanbul in 1985. In 2022, reports emerged that heavy machinery used for cleaning had cracked marble floor slabs inside Hagia Sophia. Hagia Sophia is one of several former Byzantine-era churches in Turkey that Erdoğan has converted into mosques in recent years. These acts have been seen as attempts by Erdoğan, amid wider strategies, to shore up support from his conservative Muslim base and represss political opposition . The conversion of Hagia Sophia has been opposed by scholars , museum workers and world leaders . UNESCO stressed the universal value of Hagia Sophia’s heritage and said it “deeply regrets” Turkey’s decision to strip Hagia Sophia of its museum status without prior consultation. Interior of Hagia Sophia following its conversion back to a mosque. (Sourabh.biswas003/Wikimedia) , CC BY-SA State-centred frameworks Over the course of the 20th century, NGOs, Indigenous Peoples, religious groups and local communities have played a growing role in the conservation and protection of cultural heritage. Their participation has gained increasing recognition in international cultural heritage law. UNESCO acknowledges that the protection of cultural heritage “cannot rest on State Parties alone” and that representatives of civil society can “strengthen conservation, foster awareness and education, empower local communities and offer independent monitoring when challenges arise.” In addition to established understandings of intrinsic esthetic and historic values of heritage, new emphasis on development reconceptualizes heritage as a resource that can generate economic development, tourism, employment and social cohesion. But legal frameworks remain largely state-centred, often limiting what civilian groups can accomplish without state co-operation. These developments raise the question: How can cultural heritage be protected when the state threatens rather than safeguards it? Read more: Trump has gotten rid of many of the checks and balances that could stop him from demolishing the Kennedy Center Trump took aim at “modernist” architecture and promoted “traditional” and “classical” structures in two executive orders issued in 2020 and 2025 . The group Hands Off the Arts , described the decision to remove artist Joel Shapiro’s sculpture Blue as “ authoritarian ” and as an act of “ vandalism .” The large blue geometric sculpture playfully evoked the human form in motion. Born in 1941, the late Shapiro was known for bridging modernism and postmodernism with sculptures that combined minimalist abstraction with figuration and movement. The abstract sculpture was removed from the Kennedy Center and follows executive orders from U.S. President Donald Trump to promote ‘traditional’ and ‘classical’ structures. (Jeff Vincent/Flickr) , CC BY In addition to the Kennedy Center, Trump has sought to transform Washington D.C. in other ways. His demolition of the East Wing of the White House, repainting of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and plans to build a new triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery have all raised questions about legal and regulatory limits on presidential actions impacting cultural heritage. Read more: Trump wants an ‘Independence Arch’ — How famous arches warn about dangers to republics Outside of Washington D.C., work on the border wall between the U.S. and Mexico has damaged and continues to threaten Indigenous archaeological and sacred sites . Trump’s attempts to dismantle , politicize and take over public institutions for arts and learning have been well documented. Such attacks on cultural heritage in the U.S. are not unique. In recent years, several governments have placed at risk the very heritage they are charged to protect. Cultural policy and state control International law places primary responsibility for protecting cultural heritage on states. The U.S. proposed the World Heritage Convention to the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) in 1972 and was the first state to ratify it . According to the convention , each state party to it “recognizes that the duty of ensuring the identification, protection, conservation, presentation and transmission to future generations of the cultural and natural heritage … belongs primarily to that State.” But recent research suggests attacks on cultural heritage and institutions are sometimes part of democratic backsliding and broader strategies to normalize political corruption and institute authoritarian policies. Trump and his administration have repeatedly criticized UNESCO, accusing the UN agency that seeks to safeguard heritage of supporting “woke, divisive cultural and social causes.” Trump withdrew the U.S. from UNESCO in 2019. The U.S. rejoined UNESCO in 2023 under the administration of former president Joe Biden . But the U.S. is slated to withdraw from the UN agency once again at the end of 2026 . Russia: Trinity icon Contested state decisions impacting culture and heritage can be seen elsewhere. In 2023, curators warned that Russian president Vladimir Putin’s plans to transfer a masterpiece of 15th-century Russian religious art from the State Tretyakov Gallery to the Russian Orthodox Church would put it at risk. Experts cautioned that removing Andrei Rublev’s Trinity icon from its climate-controlled museum case would likely damage it, a scenario that has now unfolded, according to a report from RBC media outlet publicized in the Moscow Times and the Art Newspaper in September 2026. Painted in the 1420s, Rublev’s icon is widely regarded as a treasure of Russian cultural heritage and one of the greatest examples of Orthodox icon painting. Putin’s transfer of the icon to the church in 2023 has been interpreted as politically motivated : a recognition of the loyalty of Patriarch Kirill, leader of the Russian Orthodox Church, who has steadfastly supported Russia’s war against Ukraine. Turkish case: Hagia Sophia In Turkey, five years ago, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan removed the museum status of Istanbul’s Hagia Sophia and converted it back into a mosque. Built in the sixth century on a site occupied by earlier churches since the fourth century CE, Hagia Sophia was the largest and most important church of the Greek-speaking Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire for nearly a millennium. It was converted into a mosque following the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453. In 1934 it was a made a museum by the founder of the Turkish Republic Mustafa Kemal Atatürk who sought to establish Turkey as a modern secular state. Hagia Sophia remains a singular masterpiece of Byzantine architecture and preserves unique mosaics of Roman rulers and Christian saints. It became part of the UNESCO World Heritage Historic Areas of Istanbul in 1985. In 2022, reports emerged that heavy machinery used for cleaning had cracked marble floor slabs inside Hagia Sophia. Hagia Sophia is one of several former Byzantine-era churches in Turkey that Erdoğan has converted into mosques in recent years. These acts have been seen as attempts by Erdoğan, amid wider strategies, to shore up support from his conservative Muslim base and represss political opposition . The conversion of Hagia Sophia has been opposed by scholars , museum workers and world leaders . UNESCO stressed the universal value of Hagia Sophia’s heritage and said it “deeply regrets” Turkey’s decision to strip Hagia Sophia of its museum status without prior consultation. Interior of Hagia Sophia following its conversion back to a mosque. (Sourabh.biswas003/Wikimedia) , CC BY-SA State-centred frameworks Over the course of the 20th century, NGOs, Indigenous Peoples, religious groups and local communities have played a growing role in the conservation and protection of cultural heritage. Their participation has gained increasing recognition in international cultural heritage law. UNESCO acknowledges that the protection of cultural heritage “cannot rest on State Parties alone” and that representatives of civil society can “strengthen conservation, foster awareness and education, empower local communities and offer independent monitoring when challenges arise.” In addition to established understandings of intrinsic esthetic and historic values of heritage, new emphasis on development reconceptualizes heritage as a resource that can generate economic development, tourism, employment and social cohesion. But legal frameworks remain largely state-centred, often limiting what civilian groups can accomplish without state co-operation. These developments raise the question: How can cultural heritage be protected when the state threatens rather than safeguards it? articles.title: Attacks on cultural heritage are unfolding with authoritarian politics in the U.S. and beyond

articles.content: The recently published thriller The Most Dangerous Games is a collaboration between James Stephen “Jimmy” Donaldson, better known as MrBeast, and popular author James Patterson. It tells the story of 100 contestants competing for US$1 billion while enduring an escalation of increasingly brutal challenges. The publisher explicitly markets the book as an extension of his Prime Original program Beast Games : “the games are more dangerous than ever.” Each book purchase gets the buyer a chance to enter an online game and potentially compete for US$1 million. The book is the latest extension of a format MrBeast developed on YouTube years before Beast Games reached television. Beginning with challenges such as “ Last To Leave Circle Wins $10,000 ” in 2018, his videos increasingly centred on contestants competing for large cash prizes. The promotional language for Beast Games puts it bluntly: What wouldn’t you do for $5 million? When money becomes the spectacle The idea of making people confront their fears for money is not new to reality television. Joe Rogan hosted Fear Factor from 2001 to 2006, putting groups of contestants through three stunts for a chance to win US$50,000. The program opens with the words: “ imagine a world where your greatest fears become reality .” But contestants were not forced to confront common fears such as public speaking or cold-calling strangers. Instead, the program traded in shock, disgust and spectacle. Despite being revived twice after its initial cancellation, Fear Factor did not acquire the longevity of other reality formats in which contestants compete for cash. Survivor , for example, has just celebrated its 50th season, while The Amazing Race has produced nearly 40. Unlike these programs, Fear Factor was gimmicky and vulnerable to a shrinking audience once the novelty wore off. There was no real way for the show to evolve beyond its basic format. Even Joe Rogan admitted he expected it to be cancelled quickly and mainly took the job to gather material for his stand-up comedy career. The reality competition series ‘Fear Factor’ made fear, disgust and spectacle central to its format. In one challenge, contestants were strapped down and covered with dozens of snakes for three minutes. Long-running reality competition programs like Survivor and Big Brother clearly demonstrate that viewers are fascinated by watching people compete for financial gain. The reason for this is obvious. We like money; it facilitates survival and we all wish we had more of it. But not all competitions are equal, and neither are the reasons people watch them . While Fear Factor is now mainly a footnote in reality TV history (it did get rebooted again in January 2026 ), it was notable in part for making money itself the spectacle. For contemporary viewers, no one does this more obviously than MrBeast. Competition or ordeal? The level of spectacle in Beast Games is very different from competition shows where the money is structurally important but narratively sidelined. While the ostensible objective in Survivor is to win US$1 million, the format converts that goal into something more complicated for the audience. Viewers become invested in strategy, social relationships, general competence, travel, personality and questions of deservingness. The pleasure of watching goes far beyond “look what this person will do for this money.” James Patterson and MrBeast’s ‘The Most Dangerous Games’ extends the MrBeast competition format into fiction. (William Morrow and Company) Beast Games does not provoke debates about who can or should win and how. Rather, it stages a demonstration of what money can make people agree to. This helps explain to what extent Beast Games is inspired by the Korean drama Squid Game , which depicts desperate people submitting themselves to degrading and dangerous conditions to win money. The willingness of the Squid Game contestants to return to the games, even once they realize that the outcome could be deadly, is an indictment of the pervasive economic precarity that is sadly familiar to many viewers. This functions as a profound, and at times even moving, critique. Beast Games , however, exploits this precarity and turns it back into mere entertainment. While traditional reality competition shows ask, “Can you out-game the other players and win the money?”, Beast Games explores how much you will endure – or subject someone else to – for a transformative financial sum. This distinction between competition and ordeal can be deepened when we consider the roles played by precarity, humiliation and spectatorship . Humiliation as entertainment The spectacle of humiliation is hardly new. In entertainment it is an ancient practice, tracing as far back as slaves in the Roman Colosseum engaging in deadly competition while spectators placed bets on the outcome . Early reality programs were frequently accused of being exploitative. American Idol showcased terrible auditions and mocking judges, while Big Brother confined and surveilled contestants. Survivor continues to foreground deprivation as part of the journey to becoming sole survivor. In its early years, it featured its own share of Fear Factor -style food challenges . Yet over time, the pleasure of watching many of these legacy programs has shifted from schadenfreude to inspiration. MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, has built his online career around elaborate challenges and cash prizes. (Amazon MGM Studios) The key to this transformation is in the different ways these experiences are organized and made productively legible to viewers. Big Brother turns confinement into social observation. Survivor builds a mythology of adventure and strategic gameplay on top of deprivation and personality conflicts. The popular social deduction game, The Traitors , is a relative newcomer to the world of reality competition shows, but it has quickly established itself as an international favourite. Traitors stages a theatrical parlour game in which everyone is actively “pretending.” Building the prize pot is secondary to the often conflicting goals of finding traitors and getting to the end. The MrBeast approach strips away much of this genre’s camouflage and positions the enormous pile of money as central to the mise-en-scène . The business of desperation This is where Squid Game offers an uncomfortable comparison. The drama was supposed to make us uneasy with watching desperate people endure unsavoury ordeals for transformative wealth. Yet it has helped establish the aesthetic vocabulary for unironic real competitions like Beast Games . Read more: ‘Squid Game’ highlights plight of South Korean workers sacrificed for nation’s economic gain The class distinction is particularly apparent when the money on offer is framed as coming directly from MrBeast himself, as an altruistic gesture for which he is celebrated. In reality, this money comes primarily from sponsors . Even if we take the premise at face value, it remains uncomfortably reminiscent of a familiar scenario in which people in financial need become fodder for the entertainment of the wealthy. Not unlike the infamous Bumfights series, it asks: What can someone with relative wealth induce needy people to do by dangling enough money in front of them? The more difficult question, however, might be: Why are humiliation, fear and economic need seen as entertainment? Tiara Sukhan does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: “Math rock” band Angine de Poitrine seems to be everywhere now: the Saguenay, Québec duo won two prestigious Polaris prizes on Sept. 22, and recently appeared on the United States-based Tonight Show and other international venues . The Polaris Prize honours important Canadian music and is adjudicated by over 200 critics and curators. Angine de Poitrine won both the album and song prizes. The latter is jointly awarded by Polaris and the Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada . The band became a viral sensation in early 2026 and has been performing sold-out shows around the globe . A significant part of the attention they have garnered is due to their outlandish stage presence and self-described status as an “anonymous art project” — guitarist “Khn” and drummer “Klek” wear polka-dotted outfits and giant papier mâché heads in the guise of being alien rock stars . Read more: Dada: how 1916 art movement reacting to world war is inspiring improvisation artists today But the band’s music, which features microtonal melodies, dense, elaborately constructed textures and wonky, complex rhythms, has also captured the attention of a legion of music fans. Just as the duo has dominated social media and the summer concert circuit, iconic Canadian progressive rock power trio Rush has been on a much-hyped, epic global reunion tour , marking almost 50 years in the music industry. Does their popularity suggest, improbably, that we are witnessing a progressive rock renaissance? Emergence of ‘prog rock’ In the late 1960s, shaped by developments in psychedelic rock especially, progressive rock (or “prog”) emerged as a rejection of commercial pop and blues-based rock music, borrowing from other musical traditions — art music, jazz, non-western music — and focusing on technical virtuosity, long-format songs, experimentation, quasi-symphonic textures and classical forms. Prog’s popularity declined precipitously in the mid ‘70s, and the genre — with its legendary excesses, including self-indulgent soloing, abstruse lyrics and pompous conceits — was eclipsed by the advent of punk. Rush played a key role in the development of prog. Forming in Toronto in 1968 and releasing its first album in 1974 , Rush blended heavy blues-based rock in the vein of Led Zeppelin, The Who and Cream with the richer palette offered by seminal British prog groups. The progressive aspects of Rush’s music have included atmospheric guitar textures, virtuosic melodic bass lines, technically demanding drum parts and the use of irregular meter (which instead of the usual multiples of four, sees the music grouped into “irregular” units of five or seven, for example). In the 1980s, this gave way to a more radio-friendly approach, leading to a succession of very successful, chart-topping Rush songs throughout the decade. Angine on the prog rock spectrum While Rush emerged from this “classic” prog era, Angine de Poitrine occupies a different part of the prog rock spectrum. The band’s music is typically described as math rock , a sub-genre of prog that originated in the early 1990s. Writer Jeff Gomez has traced its history in his recent monograph Math Rock , going back through free jazz, progressive rock and thrash metal. While there is no universal agreement on the meaning or value of the label “math rock,” it’s safe to say that it consists primarily of instrumental rock music that features virtuosic, highly precise playing and significant rhythmic and metrical complexity . The music not only makes use of irregular meter and phrases of irregular length — common in classic prog — but can also be polymetric, with simultaneous musical lines being counted in different time groupings. Angine de Poitrine perform at the Polaris Prize on Sept. 22, 2026. Layered, looped music parts In the case of Angine de Poitrine, the band’s guitarist plays a double-necked instrument that includes a bass guitar. Guitar and bass parts are performed in real time and looped . That is, the parts are recorded digitally as Khn plays them, and then they repeat in continuous circuits. Loop is layered on top of loop; the loops are different lengths, and are counted in different time groupings. The math of this music has to do with how the loops progress cyclically and eventually line up. The effect is kaleidoscopic, in that multiple melodic lines complete for the ear’s attention, and shift in and out of phase with each other, creating a succession of new relationships. It requires some elaborate choreography. The loop station and a cluster of volume pedals, which bring loops in and out of the mix, sit on the floor and are controlled by the guitarist’s feet. The drummer plays steadily against the polymetric guitar and bass parts, at times in tension with the guitar parts and then locked in when the parts align, creating some decidedly funky grooves. The new Rush? Is Angine de Poitrine really “the new Rush,” as some fans have claimed on social media? Can we compare these two bands and, if so, what can we say about the state of “progressive” music? While on tour, the members of Rush sang the praises of Angine de Poitrine , sensing some affinities between the duo and their own esthetic tradition. And the complexity of both Rush and Angine appeals directly to other musicians, who respect the challenges of composing this kind of music, and co-ordinating parts in live performance. But Rush’s prog rock pedigree is now also overwritten by a strong nostalgia element and by a legacy of radio-friendly songs that have become unchallenged fixtures in the classic rock firmament. Angine de Poitrine is undeniably impressive, and they are certainly exciting to hear and see live , but the costumes, “alien rock star” conceit and absence of singing could suggest a short shelf life. Building complex musical textures is no longer novel, with looping technology entering its third decade, and with math rock bands — like the San Francisco post-rock duo Giraffes? Giraffes! — making similar quirky, loop-driven music since the early 2000s. Ongoing boom of less commercial music Perhaps, then, we didn’t exactly see a prog rock renaissance in 2026. But in some ways, prog never really went away. Not only have bands like Rush carried on (for almost 50 years, alongside other still-active prog dinosaurs like Styx and Yes), but the prog rock impulse towards music that is less commercial, with more elaborate, long-format songwriting, has evolved. It can still be heard in the music of recent prog groups like Dream Theatre , Porcupine Tree , Big Big Train and Wobbler , but also in the music of more mainstream acts like Radiohead , Tool and Primus. Thanks to social media and streaming, commercial radio no longer dictates the forms of music production. The success of bands like Angine de Poitrine at least show that rock music can challenge our ears and doesn’t need to be dumbed down or Tik Tok-ified to find a huge and appreciative audience. Alexander Carpenter does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Shane Hollander (played by Hudson Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (played by Connor Storrie) face-off in a scene from 'Heated Rivlary.' (Sabrina Lantos/HBO Max) Hockey has made it big on the small screen. TV’s buzziest show, Heated Rivalry , debuted in late 2025, with Off Campus following in 2026. They join beloved Canadian show Shoresy , which has a sixth season going into production this fall . These shows all challenge traditional hockey culture in their own ways. Shoresy promotes an inclusive vision of hockey that includes women and Indigenous people in leadership positions. Heated Rivalry ‘s queer romance challenges the sport’s longstanding assumptions of heteronormativity . Off Campus highlights the issue of sexual assault within hockey . But as the NHL season begins, a series of controversies suggests that many of the sport’s longstanding cultural issues appear to remain unresolved. Hockey’s culture problem Hockey has long been associated with traditional ideas about masculinity, toughness and heterosexuality. The culture surrounding hockey has historically marginalized women and LGBTQ+ people. Sexist phrases like “puck bunny” are used to diminish female fans , while Hockey Canada’s 2022 discrimination report found that negative comments about sexual orientation and gender identity accounted for 61 per cent of incidents witnessed by officials. Players’ self-reported allegations were most commonly related to race, sexual orientation and gender identity. It is also one of the most expensive sports , with participation typically limited to families who can afford to spend thousands of dollars on equipment, league fees and travel costs. Players and managers in the NHL are predominantly white , with the league having the lowest level of player diversity among the four major North American professional sports leagues. We Breed Lions: Confronting Canada’s Troubled Hockey Culture by Rick Westhead. (Penguin Random House) These issues have become increasingly visible in recent years as hockey organizations have faced pressure to address questions about safety, inclusion and accountability . The publication of TSN reporter Rick Westhead’s book We Breed Lions further intensified national conversations about hockey culture. In it, Westhead documents sexual abuse and hazing in junior hockey and examines the sport’s impact on its players’ physical and mental health and its growing exclusivity. The book demonstrates that these issues are systemic, not isolated incidents. We need to address the culture that encourages such behaviour and the way teammates, coaches and other personnel are complicit. Recent controversies The 2025 NHL season and 2026 summer off-season saw a number of controversies that reflected broader debates about accountability, institutional responsibility and inclusion in hockey. The Vegas Golden Knights’ signing of Carter Hart in 2025 drew criticism from some fans and media figures . Hart was one of the five former Hockey Canada players charged in an alleged 2018 sexual assault; all five were found not guilty in July 2025 . During the Stanley Cup Final, some fans chanted “no means no” when Hart was on the ice. The Edmonton Oilers’ later signing of another former Hockey Canada player who had been charged in the same case and was also found not guilty prompted longtime Oilers fan Mama Stanley to announce she would no longer support the team . The teams’ recent off-season hiring of Mike Babcock, who has been accused of abusive coaching tactics , was similarly controversial. Meanwhile, fans pushed back against the Dallas Stars’ announcement that it would not hold a Pride Night during the team’s 2026-27 season at a time when discussions about queerness and hockey were receiving increased attention. Challenging hockey culture The fact that these recent decisions are controversial suggests that a new generation of hockey fans have entered the arena. I am in the early phases of a research project about online hockey “counterpublics” with my colleague, creator culture expert Jess Rauchberg. A counterpublic is a group that has been excluded from the dominant discourse and challenges normative ideas . Some early findings show that hockey content creators are using online spaces to criticize aspects of hockey culture and challenge the behaviours and traditions documented by Westhead. Our preliminary analysis of comments on NHL teams’ Pride Night social media posts suggests that many old school fans are guarding the sport from these incursions. While many fans embrace Pride Nights as forms of inclusivity, others respond with slurs or argue Pride has no place in hockey. Sports are imbued with social and political values, often leading to what political scientist Jules Boykoff calls “sportwashing,” or using sports to deflect from political crises and normalize nationalism and human rights abuses. Given that hockey is so tied to Canadian national identity , challenges to hockey culture can be seen by some fans as challenges to their own identities. Can stories change hockey? The hockey shows of the 2020s imagine a world in which hockey can be better. In Heated Rivalry , the two best hockey players in the league are queer men — a challenge to masculine ideals about who belongs in elite sport. In Off Campus , main protagonist Hannah receives support from an NHL prospect when she discloses her rape by a hockey player. Shoresy presents a version of hockey where women not only have a place in a hockey team’s front office, but can be respected leaders, and Indigenous players and management personnel are equal to their white counterparts. Sudbury Blueberry Bulldogs team manager Sanguinet (played by Harlan Blayne Kytwayhat) stands behind bench during hockey game in Shoresy . (Bell Media) Rachel Reid, the author of the romance series from which Heated Rivalry was adapted, has said she set out to challenge the culture of the sport she loved . In the wake of the show’s massive success, some NHL players have said they would support a gay teammate . But recent developments show hockey culture is difficult to challenge. While popular media seems to be confronting some of the norms embedded in hockey culture, hockey itself appears resistant to change. My research into online hockey counterpublics and fan responses to Pride Night suggests that supporters and critics are both actively shaping the future meaning of the sport. Popular media is challenging some of hockey’s traditional norms, but whether those challenges lead to broader changes within hockey itself remains to be seen. Clementine Oberst does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: The Métis are one of the most misunderstood Indigenous groups in Canada . The Canadian Constitution recognizes that “Aboriginal peoples of Canada includes the Indian, Inuit and Métis Peoples of Canada,” yet in practical terms the Métis have continually fought, and continue to fight, to have their inherent rights as Indigenous people fully recognized. Our peoplehood comes from a shared history, political will, cultural traditions and kinship networks that predate colonial boundaries . Our homeland spans the Prairie provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba as well as parts of British Columbia, Ontario, the Northwest Territories and North Dakota. Yet we are often and erroneously mistaken as simply half European and half First Nation. As a post-contact people who were seen as different from our First Nations relatives by those who encountered us, we don’t fit easily into racial categories. Our positioning between worlds presents a conundrum for those from outside the Métis community as we proudly embrace our complexities, ambiguities and contradictions . Still, this complexity has caused confusion and left us vulnerable to those who knowingly exploit Canadians’ widespread lack of knowing. Read more: Becoming Indigenous: The rise of Eastern Métis in Canada Knowing this, there is a great need for ongoing authentic Métis voice and representation, and expression of our unique cultural identity. Seldom-heard Métis truths In these times of “Truths Before Reconciliation,” one of the lesser-known facts in Canadian history is that Métis people have routinely asserted their Indigeneity and rights through legal means . As respected Métis author and retired lawyer Jean Teillet details in The North-West Is Our Mother The Story of Louis Riel’s People, the Métis Nation (2021), the Métis have gathered and organized ever since the birth of our nation. These meetings included legal discussions and plans. Métis historian Lawrence Barkwell details some of the numerous petitions sent to the Dominion of Canada starting in the mid-1840s as the Métis made extensive use of their right to petition the government for recognition of their rights, including land rights. Very few, if any, of these petitions proved successful. Hopeful moments unrealized The inclusion of the Métis into the Canadian Constitution in 1982 as one of three “Aboriginal” groups was a promising moment led by Métis leader Harry Daniels and others. In the years that followed, another hopeful moment arrived with the Supreme Court of Canada’s Powley decision that asserted Indigenous harvesting rights for Métis people. But this court-imposed definition of the Métis, with its geographical and cultural limitations set out in “the 10-point Powley Test,” raised more questions than solutions . Years passed, and another moment of hope was sparked in 2016 with the Daniels decision from the Supreme Court of Canada that ruled Métis and non-status peoples fall under the category “Indians” under section 91(24) of the Constitution Act, 1867. However, the legal ruling’s “mixed ancestry” wording was problematic. Ultimately, myriad confusing legal decisions have stalled progress in Métis rights recognition — for example, in land rights, education and health. Métis scholar and writer Chelsea Vowel has termed the provincial-federal passing of Métis rights recognition a jurisdictional “hot potato.” A stunning example of stalling is found in the flawed scrip system that purportedly extinguished Métis land rights in the late 1800s, but is more accurately described as “Canada’s greatest land swindle” by lawyer Jason Madden . Inequities in Indigenous rights Marking the 10th anniversary of the Daniels decision , the Métis National Council had this to say: “Ten years later, Métis citizens continue to experience disparities in access to essential services. In many cases, Métis governments are stepping in to fill gaps without corresponding and sustained federal support.” In all of this uncertainty, government officials and policymakers continue making decisions without any real understanding of how our nation of people came to be or who the Métis are today . Gathering and organizing as Métis Outside of the courts, Métis people have routinely organized and held gatherings to talk about the pressing issues of the day. While many are familiar with Louis Riel’s 1885 execution for high treason , a lesser-known reality is that the Métis endured years of violence during the Reign of Terror imposed by incoming colonial powers. For generations after, Métis gathered to address the poor living conditions and ongoing injustices that Métis people faced, in community gatherings held across the homeland. One example of this is depicted in PowWow at Duck Lake , the powerful 1967 short National Film Board film. Along with Cree activist Harold Cardinal , the film features the first Métis person in Canada to earn a PhD, Howard Adams , who inspired a new generation of Métis to stand up for their Indigenous rights through his compelling speeches and insights. As Teillet reminds us, the Métis have always gathered to discuss important matters. After the 1885 Resistance, those who knew the importance of preserving our side of the story, the Old Wolves as they were called, took part in “ meetings — that’s how they did it. They met repeatedly. They talked and talked again .” Their actions ensured that the Métis side of the story was not going to be lost. Métis continue to gather together across the homeland at significant historic sites, including Batoche , to celebrate culture, language and our rich history. Other formal gatherings of Métis people continue today, arranged by our representative organizations: the Métis Nation of British Columbia , the Otipemisiwak Métis Government (Alberta), the Métis Nation of Saskatchewan , the Manitoba Métis Federation and the Métis Nation of Ontario . Restoring Métis stories Respected Elder and educator-author Maria Campbell set out what was lost through ongoing acts of colonial injustice in her classic 1973 book Halfbreed . Her candid words of truth took an artistic route to educating, and punctured a hole in the fabric of the western literary canon. Today, these breakthrough efforts are gaining momentum through a collective of academics and knowledge-holders who are determined to ensure the Métis side of the Canadian story is heard. In contributing scholarly momentum to the project of mobilizing and revitalizing Métis-specific knowledge traditions , we educate others about the Métis . By deliberately creating gathering spaces for Métis thinkers of all kinds, from academics to community members, in diverse settings, we are making important strides towards self-determination . The hosting of a third annual conference in Calgary this Sept. 20-24 provides further evidence that the Métis are creating intentional space to have their dreams, stories and lived experiences heard. The conference is called the Mawachihitotaak Métis Studies Conference , and Elder Verna DeMontigny, from the Prairie to Woodlands Indigenous Language Revitalization Circle , gifted the gathering with this name, which means “let’s get together” in southern Michif. At this event, Métis thinkers and creators from a range of disciplines and professions will together share ways of understanding the world while celebrating and sustaining our culture. Dr. Yvonne Poitras Pratt has received funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and, more recently, from the Canada Council for the Arts for her digital storywork. Dr. Poitras Pratt is a citizen of the Otipemisewak Metis Government. Madelaine McCracken, PhD Candidate, received the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council's Doctoral Graduate Award for her doctoral research on Métis contributions to Truth Before Reconciliation through podcasting. Madelaine is a citizen of the Manitoba Métis Federation and a former citizen of the Otipemisiwak Métis Government. She contributed to this article in recognition of her passion for supporting Métis-specific conversations and education across Canada within her capacity as a graduate student. Melanie Griffith Brice has received funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council to support her research on Métis/Michif epistemology. She is the President of the Canadian Association for the Study of Indigenous Education (CASIE), an constituent association of the Canadian Society for the Study of Education (CSSE), as well as a member of the Board of Directors of the Federation for the Humanities and Social Sciences. Dr. Griffith Brice is a citizen of the Métis Nation - Saskatchewan.
