articles.content: A Canadian non-profit performance rights organization is suing Suno, an American genAI music creation platform, over streaming AI outputs that allegedly replicate songs without consent or compensation. The Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada (SOCAN) lawsuit cites 150 Suno songs that it says are identical or nearly identical to the works of Canadian artists including Joni Mitchell, The Weeknd, The Tragically Hip and others. SOCAN wants the AI company to comply with copyright law and for artists to have a say in how their works are used (or not). The statement of claim , which seeks $20,000 per work and $10,000,000 for infringement, joins a series of recent lawsuits against Suno. These include a US$500-million joint copyright lawsuit originally launched by major labels of Warner, Sony and Universal ( Warner has since signed a licensing deal with Suno ) and a class-action lawsuit from Jason Isbell and other musicians . There are also music publisher and record label lawsuits. SOCAN’s lawsuit raises questions about the place of Canadian artists in a music industry increasingly shaped by American tech companies. SOCAN’s complaint says in response to a prompt consisting of lyrics to ‘Both Sides Now’ by Joni Mitchell, Suno generated an output that is virtually identical including in melody, harmony and lyrics. (SUNO) Musician livelihoods at risk A wide range of issues pertaining to AI technology and musicmaking are putting musician livelihoods at risk. “It definitely feels like an existential struggle for artists today against AI,” rapper Cadence Weapon told The Canadian Press . The artist says 129 of his songs have been found in datasets to train AI music generators. We conducted a survey this past summer with 267 working musicians in Canada . The survey was sent to 1,025 musicians ( Polaris-longlisted artists between 2006-25 who have appeared on the Earshot charts seven or more times with Gold records; some were added for geographic representation). We asked 26 questions about their music-making and relationships to aspects of the music industry, including companies like Spotify, Live Nation and Suno. Read more: Artists’ Spotify criticisms point to larger ways musicians lose with streaming — here’s 3 changes to help in Canada Musician responses We found that 87 per cent of respondents view AI technology in music creation negatively. One respondent said they are “personally and professionally offended by the existence and use of genAI tools for artistic practices” and that the AI tech tools encourage the theft of copyrighted works. Another said AI tools are compromising musicians’ ability to make money from music. One artist said they avoid AI “like the plague.” The majority of survey responses indicate a clear line between creativity and the type of music production encouraged by a platform like Suno. These artist responses challenge the way Suno is marketed to users. A recent post by the company said that Suno is “ grateful to build tools that let everyone experience the joy of making music .” The survey also found many Canadian musicians feel forced into using particular tools or platforms, or forced to work with large companies that dominate within a particular sector of the music industry. In one survey response to a question asking about an artist’s relationship to ticketing company Ticketmaster and concert promoter Live Nation, the respondent said they are in “a relationship, but forced into it.” Proliferating AI-generated content AI music is becoming a battleground over the future of tech, culture and community. In January 2026, Billboard magazine reported on a media consumption survey that found the vast majority of music consumers in the United States are uninterested in engaging with AI-generated songs as well. Another U.S.-based survey documented increased discomfort with GenAI in music , especially among younger listeners. Part of this growing distaste for AI music comes from increased exposure. A recent example of this unwelcome intrusion happened when one of the authors of this story was listening to YouTube Music and was algorithmically recommended an AI song , which had a similar sound to the country-folk artist that was originally selected. The YouTuber whose profile is listed as posting this song is Lee Vybrony, who uses AI avatars of sexualized women to generate videos for a range of AI-generated songs and whose profile has more than 32,000 subscribers. One of Vybrony’s songs, “Both Sides of Us,” seems to rip off Joni Mitchell’s “Both Sides Now.” AI avatars front AI-generated songs, including one that appears to rip off Joni Mitchell’s ‘Both Sides Now.’ (YouTube) Trade, sovereignty concerns For Canadian musicians, artists and other creators the stakes are raised by the current trade war with the U.S. During the latest skirmish over tariffs, U.S. negotiators demanded Canada drop requirements for streamers like Netflix to promote Canadian content. But Canadian cultural production should not be sacrificed. If anything, the hostility toward our sovereignty and protecting our culture should be a call to strengthen these laws and support Canadian artists. Read more: Caught between culture and commerce: Canada’s high-stakes trade clash with the United States Artist input into copyright In addition to efforts by SOCAN and others to stop the exploitation and mining of artistic works, a broader range of solutions are needed if we are to ensure artist livelihoods are protected and celebrated. It’s important that artists influence policymaking, particularly copyright law . Read more: Should global media giants shape our cultural and media policy? Lessons from satellite radio AI-generated music needs to be labelled on streaming platforms . Listeners should be empowered to filter it out if they choose. Ideally, users should have to opt-in to AI-generated music. The Online Streaming Act should be expanded to require a certain percentage of Canadian content be heard, viewed and promoted across online and streaming platforms, just as Canadian content regulations have done for broadcast radio. Tighter regulation, more competition We also need to advocate for digital tools and platforms that are built and regulated in Canada , as well as more competition in the music industries. In the U.S., a jury recently decided Live Nation and Ticketmaster have operated as a monopoly and overcharged fans . Recently, the Consumers Council of Canada filed an application to sue Live Nation in Canada around similar concerns . And as we’ve documented , consolidation in the Canadian music industry by non-Canadian companies has only tightened: Universal, Warner and Sony have a triopoly in the recording and publishing market; SiriusXM has a monopoly in satellite radio and Google/YouTube, Spotify, Apple and Amazon have an oligopoly of the streaming music market. “Now old friends are acting strange,” Mitchell wrote back in 1967 , after she had relocated to the U.S. from Canada a couple of years prior . “Well something’s lost,” Mitchell laments, “but something’s gained.” Through strategic opposition to tech platforms and music monopolies, we could gain a music industry that allows Canadian music to flourish. articles.description: A Canadian non-profit performance rights organization is suing Suno, an American genAI music creation platform, over streaming AI outputs that allegedly replicate songs without consent or compensation. The Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada (SOCAN) lawsuit cites 150 Suno songs that it says are identical or nearly identical to the works of Canadian artists including Joni Mitchell, The Weeknd, The Tragically Hip and others. SOCAN wants the AI company to comply with copyright law and for artists to have a say in how their works are used (or not). The statement of claim , which seeks $20,000 per work and $10,000,000 for infringement, joins a series of recent lawsuits against Suno. These include a US$500-million joint copyright lawsuit originally launched by major labels of Warner, Sony and Universal ( Warner has since signed a licensing deal with Suno ) and a class-action lawsuit from Jason Isbell and other musicians . There are also music publisher and record label lawsuits. SOCAN’s lawsuit raises questions about the place of Canadian artists in a music industry increasingly shaped by American tech companies. SOCAN’s complaint says in response to a prompt consisting of lyrics to ‘Both Sides Now’ by Joni Mitchell, Suno generated an output that is virtually identical including in melody, harmony and lyrics. (SUNO) Musician livelihoods at risk A wide range of issues pertaining to AI technology and musicmaking are putting musician livelihoods at risk. “It definitely feels like an existential struggle for artists today against AI,” rapper Cadence Weapon told The Canadian Press . The artist says 129 of his songs have been found in datasets to train AI music generators. We conducted a survey this past summer with 267 working musicians in Canada . The survey was sent to 1,025 musicians ( Polaris-longlisted artists between 2006-25 who have appeared on the Earshot charts seven or more times with Gold records; some were added for geographic representation). We asked 26 questions about their music-making and relationships to aspects of the music industry, including companies like Spotify, Live Nation and Suno. Read more: Artists’ Spotify criticisms point to larger ways musicians lose with streaming — here’s 3 changes to help in Canada Musician responses We found that 87 per cent of respondents view AI technology in music creation negatively. One respondent said they are “personally and professionally offended by the existence and use of genAI tools for artistic practices” and that the AI tech tools encourage the theft of copyrighted works. Another said AI tools are compromising musicians’ ability to make money from music. One artist said they avoid AI “like the plague.” The majority of survey responses indicate a clear line between creativity and the type of music production encouraged by a platform like Suno. These artist responses challenge the way Suno is marketed to users. A recent post by the company said that Suno is “ grateful to build tools that let everyone experience the joy of making music .” The survey also found many Canadian musicians feel forced into using particular tools or platforms, or forced to work with large companies that dominate within a particular sector of the music industry. In one survey response to a question asking about an artist’s relationship to ticketing company Ticketmaster and concert promoter Live Nation, the respondent said they are in “a relationship, but forced into it.” Proliferating AI-generated content AI music is becoming a battleground over the future of tech, culture and community. In January 2026, Billboard magazine reported on a media consumption survey that found the vast majority of music consumers in the United States are uninterested in engaging with AI-generated songs as well. Another U.S.-based survey documented increased discomfort with GenAI in music , especially among younger listeners. Part of this growing distaste for AI music comes from increased exposure. A recent example of this unwelcome intrusion happened when one of the authors of this story was listening to YouTube Music and was algorithmically recommended an AI song , which had a similar sound to the country-folk artist that was originally selected. The YouTuber whose profile is listed as posting this song is Lee Vybrony, who uses AI avatars of sexualized women to generate videos for a range of AI-generated songs and whose profile has more than 32,000 subscribers. One of Vybrony’s songs, “Both Sides of Us,” seems to rip off Joni Mitchell’s “Both Sides Now.” AI avatars front AI-generated songs, including one that appears to rip off Joni Mitchell’s ‘Both Sides Now.’ (YouTube) Trade, sovereignty concerns For Canadian musicians, artists and other creators the stakes are raised by the current trade war with the U.S. During the latest skirmish over tariffs, U.S. negotiators demanded Canada drop requirements for streamers like Netflix to promote Canadian content. But Canadian cultural production should not be sacrificed. If anything, the hostility toward our sovereignty and protecting our culture should be a call to strengthen these laws and support Canadian artists. Read more: Caught between culture and commerce: Canada’s high-stakes trade clash with the United States Artist input into copyright In addition to efforts by SOCAN and others to stop the exploitation and mining of artistic works, a broader range of solutions are needed if we are to ensure artist livelihoods are protected and celebrated. It’s important that artists influence policymaking, particularly copyright law . Read more: Should global media giants shape our cultural and media policy? Lessons from satellite radio AI-generated music needs to be labelled on streaming platforms . Listeners should be empowered to filter it out if they choose. Ideally, users should have to opt-in to AI-generated music. The Online Streaming Act should be expanded to require a certain percentage of Canadian content be heard, viewed and promoted across online and streaming platforms, just as Canadian content regulations have done for broadcast radio. Tighter regulation, more competition We also need to advocate for digital tools and platforms that are built and regulated in Canada , as well as more competition in the music industries. In the U.S., a jury recently decided Live Nation and Ticketmaster have operated as a monopoly and overcharged fans . Recently, the Consumers Council of Canada filed an application to sue Live Nation in Canada around similar concerns . And as we’ve documented , consolidation in the Canadian music industry by non-Canadian companies has only tightened: Universal, Warner and Sony have a triopoly in the recording and publishing market; SiriusXM has a monopoly in satellite radio and Google/YouTube, Spotify, Apple and Amazon have an oligopoly of the streaming music market. “Now old friends are acting strange,” Mitchell wrote back in 1967 , after she had relocated to the U.S. from Canada a couple of years prior . “Well something’s lost,” Mitchell laments, “but something’s gained.” Through strategic opposition to tech platforms and music monopolies, we could gain a music industry that allows Canadian music to flourish. articles.content: A still from Saffron Kingdom (Daffodil Studios) Saffron Kingdom is a rare and special film about Kashmir, created by a Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh. Although the film was released in 2024 (Daffodil Studios), there was only one Canadian screening, in October 2025 , meaning it was a hard film to see. That’s changed with its recent release on the streaming service Watermelon Plus, making the drama available to a larger audience. The film offers a rare glimpse into how everyday life in Kashmir is impacted under militarization and surveillance. The Indian state prefers to tell a different version of the story. The film is centred on Masrat, a woman from Indian-administered Kashmir who, after her husband’s enforced disappearance in 2014, escapes the valley with her son. The movie follows her family’s displacement over three generations from their life in Kashmir to their current life in Atlanta, Ga. The film uses memory and family stories to guide viewers through Kashmir’s political history. It emphasizes silence, rituals and inherited grief. It portrays displacement not as a clear timeline of dates and policies but as a complex loss transmitted across generations, often explained imperfectly. Read more: Borders and orders: How settler-government occupations violate Kashmiri sovereignty The filmmaker’s father, well-known Kashmiri singer Ghulam Nabi Sheikh , disappeared in 2003 while travelling by train. His family describe it as an enforced disappearance by the Indian army. Though the film is not autobiographical, it’s inspired by true events as it deals with the collective issue of disappearance, including extrajudicial killings, and political repression in Kashmir . Sheikh says the film grew out of his years spent travelling throughout Kashmir and hearing stories of loss and violence. The trailer for Saffron Kingdom (Daffodil Studios). Reclaiming the story of Kashmir The film opens in Jammu and Kashmir’s summer capital of Srinagar in 1989. Young Masrat lives a simple life. Her father is teaching her to nurture their land. But her childhood is disrupted when the Indian military suddenly barges in and the child, threatened, runs into the arms of her aunt. The army attacks her father, a revolutionary poet. The film portrays the Gowkadal massacre of January 1991 through the story of Masrat’s family. On the day of her paternal aunt’s wedding, the aunt’s fiancé is killed in the massacre and the Indian army kills Masrat’s father at the wedding. For most of its cinematic history, India has largely controlled Kashmir’s story, spending years turning the area into a national fantasy and using it as a setting for romance, honeymoon songs and beautiful landscapes. It’s a narrative that has helped sustain Kashmir’s image as a tourist destination. In her book Territory of Desire: Representing the Valley of Kashmir , Prof. Ananya Jahanara Kabir of King’s College London explains how Bollywood has leaned heavily on propaganda. More recently, Kashmir has been serving as a backdrop for stories about the Indian military. In both portrayals, Kashmiris are generally in the background, either as props or villains. For many years, external voices have predominantly shaped the global and Indian narratives of Kashmir’s history. In contrast, Saffron Kingdom focuses not on Kashmir as the Indian state views it, but on the local perspective. It’s about a Kashmiri family and an honest portrayal of the very real impact the conflict has had on their lives. Why the film couldn’t be made in Kashmir A viewer may note the absence of genuine Kashmiri locations and actors. In fact, some critics note that the film’s English-accented dialogue and largely non-Kashmiri cast creates distance from the subject. However, this is not due to artistic choices or financial limits. Sheikh explained in interviews why Saffron Kingdom could not be filmed in Kashmir and why none of the Kashmiri characters are played by people living there. He said it would be impossible to make the film under current circumstances and warned that families of local actors likely would have faced retaliation from Indian security forces. Press freedom has declined sharply since 2019. In the years following the abrogation of Article 370 , an article of the Indian Constitution that granted some autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir — including the right to have their own constitution and some legal and land rights — press freedom has declined. Read more: In India, Modi’s nationalism quashes dissent with help from the media Journalists are faced with increased surveillance , harassment, travel restrictions and legal action under anti-terror laws because of their reporting. By streaming Arfat Sheikh’s Saffron Kingdom , Watermelon Plus is providing a rare platform for Kashmiri stories told by Kashmiris. The film may help to bring international attention to Kashmir’s overlooked suffering. The film ends with an interview with the last survivor of the Gowkadal massacre. Saffron Kingdom is available to view on Watermelon Plus. Shambhavi Siddhi does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Behavioural scientist Louis Busch weaves Indigenous teachings from Knowledge Keepers across Turtle Island with western psychological practice. Busch, a Bear Clan member of Nisichawayasihk Cree Nation, offers a framework for moving through pain rather than around it. In this Q&A, the psychotherapist talks about his book, Carry Your Heart: Indigenous Helping Wisdom and the Science of Psychological Flexibility , that integrates these two ways of knowing. The Conversation Canada: What does it mean to “carry your heart” in life? Louis Busch: That teaching came from a relative of mine. The Cree word is kita-pimōtātamān kitēb . It loosely translates to “walking while carrying your heart.” In a practical sense, it means noticing the urge to flee from our difficult experiences, whether a worry, a bad memory, grief, a difficult experience or an intrusive thought. Often, we are very motivated to find a distraction, a positive affirmation, medication — whatever we can get relief from. And that’s normal, but I think to “carry your heart” means to pause, look at [the difficult experiences], and then hold them in a gentle way and make a bit of space for them. [While working on this book], I really loved seeing the synergies of some of these First Nations teachings and the things that I had learned in acceptance and commitment therapy . We’ve been trained from Day One [that] the pursuit of happiness is the ultimate goal of being alive. And if you’re not doing that, there’s something wrong with you, right? You are broken. You’re pathological. You have some kind of dysfunction, and it’s inside you. It’s this thing that you have. So to ask somebody to do something different, it’s like flipping the idea of healing on its head. TCC: You organize the book around belonging through kinship, presence and purposeful action. Can you talk about structure? LB: At first I thought I was going to write a clinical manual, a “how to work with First Nations Peoples in a culturally safe way.” That was my goal initially. I thought it was important to have a strong first section on positionality — who am I and why am I writing this. Then I started getting into typical textbook on culturally adapted therapies. I started to lose motivation a bit, and I shared it with a friend of mine. She said, “I was hooked, then when I got to the second chapter, I thought, ‘Where did you go?’” I thought a lot about [that]: if [I wrote that kind of] book, I would probably talk about the people I learned from and the people who I think have really guided me on this journey. So the book’s structure [turned into] a bit of a road trip of healing and learning — visiting with [Elders], and then pausing to reflect on my own experience with whatever they were sharing. I was able to [include] some important messages about how we do healing in the colonial system that exists around us. I decided to break the book down to three core teachings. It shouldn’t be viewed as “here is the wisdom of the Indigenous Peoples of Canada or North America,” instead it should be looked at as “here is the wisdom of these particular Knowledge Keepers, and their context Nations, in dialogue with me.” And hopefully that’ll be useful for you. But it certainly does not reflect an Indigenous philosophy on wellness or an Indigenous therapy. We’re 600-plus nations in Canada, 80-plus language families, all different experiences and languages and spirituality and protocols. I talked to lots of different people because I feel like there are just such rich experiences, but I hope people walk away knowing that the book is limited to those relationships and contexts. TCC: Indigenous knowledge has a long history of being extracted and repackaged by non-Indigenous institutions for profit. How did you think about this tension when writing for a mainstream publisher? LB: It was a very hard book to write because that thought was always in my mind: how do I protect our communities, how do I protect this knowledge and how do I share it in a way that is respectful but also may benefit people? Though I primarily wrote it for Indigenous Peoples, when we say all our relations, we mean everybody in the world. We’re all relatives. I say this is for you if you are struggling with your experiences. Just please, treat it respectfully as you would treat your own grandmother’s teachings. There are different forms or levels of knowledge. There is sacred knowledge, and there is community knowledge, and some of those things are not meant to be shared in the pages of a book. Like a description of a ceremony in great detail or specific stories that we only share at specific times and with specific people. So [certain elements] fit within the realm of sacred knowledge, and maybe should be protected or at least communicated in a way that the Knowledge Keepers are comfortable with. What I [would tell] the reader is that if you are interested in this particular thing that I’m not going to talk about, take some tobacco, find a Knowledge Keeper and ask the question — do it in a respectful way. I had quite a bit of discomfort with the idea of taking the teachings of Elders and Knowledge Keepers and putting them out in a market. Books sell. So one of the ways that I have approached that is that the author royalties that come after the publication of the book will go to the Thunderbird Partnership Foundation and the Legacy of Hope Foundation . Anything that comes from this book, at least financially, goes right back into community. And that makes me feel a bit better about it. The Elders were happy with that also. This interview has been condensed for length and edited for clarity. Join us on Sept. 14 at Toronto’s Another Story Bookshop for the launch of Louis Busch’s Carry Your Heart , including a discussion moderated by Jesse Wente. This event, co-sponsored by The Conversation Canada, is free. To reserve a spot, click here . articles.content: Rocky Horror fans everywhere have been celebrating the life and work of actor and cult cinema icon Tim Curry, who passed away at the age of 80 at his home in Los Angeles . Curry brought distinctive charisma, energy and dramatic flair to countless films, including Annie (1982), Clue (1985), Legend (1985) and Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (1992). Children of the 1990s may remember him as the murderous, wisecracking clown Pennywise in the TV adaptation of Stephen King’s It (1990) . Curry was also a familiar face on Broadway and London’s West End, where he starred in many productions, including Amadeus (1979) and Spamalot (2005). An illustrious, nearly six-decade career notwithstanding, Curry remained best known for his 1975 screen debut as The Rocky Horror Picture Show ’s Dr. Frank-N-Furter, the mischievous, magnetic, stiletto- and corset-clad mad scientist who seduces the straight-laced Brad and Janet (Barry Bostwick and Susan Sarandon) on a fateful, stormy night. This is the image that Curry’s name has always conjured for me. Like several generations before me, singing along to Dr. Frank-N-Furter’s “Sweet Transvestite” at midnight Rocky Horror screenings has been somewhat of a tradition. Rocky Horror would also come to have a greater impact on my academic and professional life later on. Yet reflecting on the broader strokes of Curry’s career after news of his passing, I am reminded of the significance that even his lesser-known roles had played in my own life. The many faces of Tim Curry Kids are often captivated by Dickensian-style orphan tales, an obsession Annie cemented for me early on. Witches and magic were another fixation, and I’d direct anyone looking for a hit of ‘80s nostalgia to Curry’s musical number as The Grand Wizard in The Worst Witch (1986). These are the performances I connected to most. But reading through Curry’s extensive resumé, it would be difficult to overstate the number of “Oh, that was him too?” exclamations that occurred along the way. Curry voiced several cartoons I watched regularly, including FernGully: The Last Rainforest (1992) and The Wild Thornberrys (1998–2004) . He playfully satirized his Rocky Horror fame in the raunchy horror parody Scary Movie 2 (2001) , a clandestine viewing at my seventh-grade sleepover, and helped me pass the time at a babysitting gig or two in Clue and Home Alone 2: Lost in New York . A compilation of Tim Curry’s performances from WatchMojo. My inability to recognize Curry in some of these performances initially is not to imply that he was unmemorable. Rather, it speaks to his ability to immerse himself and disappear fully into his roles. I have little memory of Tim Curry the actor — or the person — growing up. But I do know that It ’s Pennywise terrified me, and I remember cheering as orphan Annie outwitted the schemes of Curry’s villainous Rooster Hannigan. The art of disappearing Curry himself aspired toward this status of absolute absorption for his characters. In his 2025 memoir Vagabond Curry wrote admiringly of fellow actor Alec Guinness, who prepared for roles by walking down busy streets in character with the goal of not being recognized. For Curry, acting was a way of disappearing or of hiding in plain sight. It might have been a contradictory state of being, but Curry, fittingly, saw contradiction as one of the most integral and fascinating aspects of human nature. Acting was a vehicle for exploring such contradictions; a way to understand the most paradoxical aspects of human emotion, as Curry suggested in his memoir: “Professionally, the lure of pursuing contradictions has drawn me toward complex characters or compelled me to make them more complex and nuanced.” 'Making the darkness sparkle’ Curry often played villains and antagonists: malicious characters who, on the surface, are difficult to root for, yet remain beguiling and charismatic. He intentionally infused a level of playfulness into even his most nefarious roles, a process he referred to as “mak[ing] the darkness sparkle.” His empathetic desire to explore even his most unlikable characters can be traced back to the most complex and challenging aspects of his own early life. Growing up modestly in the “dull, strange time” of post-Second World War England, Curry and his older sister Judy lost their father when he was 11 or 12. Curry described his mother as both emotionally distant and highly mercurial, traits that he, retrospectively, attributed to his mother’s own childhood neglect. In his memoir, Curry does not shy away from the pain these early experiences caused him, writing with a level of humility and vulnerability that lends an even greater depth to his surviving work. He also credits some of his key performance techniques to his mother. Her frequent, irate, outbursts became an acting masterclass emotional expression — experiences he would later draw on in his performances. Curry also recounts his time studying theatre and literature at the University of Birmingham and his eventual emergence onto the London theatre scene. Success did not always come easily, and he often took a scrappy, hardscrabble approach. One of his most memorable stories concerns his first major audition for the original London stage production of Hair . By the time the truth came out, he had already charmed the casting directors with his musical rendition of “Cool” from West Side Story . Connections made with Rocky Horror creator Richard O’Brien during the production of Hair would eventually lead to Curry’s casting in the ground-breaking 1973 London stage production . The Rocky Horror Picture Show is still among the most screened titles worldwide, and Curry’s central performance has undoubtedly been integral to its enduring popularity and definitive cult status. He continues to strut across midnight movie screens everywhere, adding a much-needed “sparkle” to the darkness. articles.description: Rocky Horror fans everywhere have been celebrating the life and work of actor and cult cinema icon Tim Curry, who passed away at the age of 80 at his home in Los Angeles . Curry brought distinctive charisma, energy and dramatic flair to countless films, including Annie (1982), Clue (1985), Legend (1985) and Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (1992). Children of the 1990s may remember him as the murderous, wisecracking clown Pennywise in the TV adaptation of Stephen King’s It (1990) . Curry was also a familiar face on Broadway and London’s West End, where he starred in many productions, including Amadeus (1979) and Spamalot (2005). An illustrious, nearly six-decade career notwithstanding, Curry remained best known for his 1975 screen debut as The Rocky Horror Picture Show ’s Dr. Frank-N-Furter, the mischievous, magnetic, stiletto- and corset-clad mad scientist who seduces the straight-laced Brad and Janet (Barry Bostwick and Susan Sarandon) on a fateful, stormy night. This is the image that Curry’s name has always conjured for me. Like several generations before me, singing along to Dr. Frank-N-Furter’s “Sweet Transvestite” at midnight Rocky Horror screenings has been somewhat of a tradition. Rocky Horror would also come to have a greater impact on my academic and professional life later on. Yet reflecting on the broader strokes of Curry’s career after news of his passing, I am reminded of the significance that even his lesser-known roles had played in my own life. The many faces of Tim Curry Kids are often captivated by Dickensian-style orphan tales, an obsession Annie cemented for me early on. Witches and magic were another fixation, and I’d direct anyone looking for a hit of ‘80s nostalgia to Curry’s musical number as The Grand Wizard in The Worst Witch (1986). These are the performances I connected to most. But reading through Curry’s extensive resumé, it would be difficult to overstate the number of “Oh, that was him too?” exclamations that occurred along the way. Curry voiced several cartoons I watched regularly, including FernGully: The Last Rainforest (1992) and The Wild Thornberrys (1998–2004) . He playfully satirized his Rocky Horror fame in the raunchy horror parody Scary Movie 2 (2001) , a clandestine viewing at my seventh-grade sleepover, and helped me pass the time at a babysitting gig or two in Clue and Home Alone 2: Lost in New York . A compilation of Tim Curry’s performances from WatchMojo. My inability to recognize Curry in some of these performances initially is not to imply that he was unmemorable. Rather, it speaks to his ability to immerse himself and disappear fully into his roles. I have little memory of Tim Curry the actor — or the person — growing up. But I do know that It ’s Pennywise terrified me, and I remember cheering as orphan Annie outwitted the schemes of Curry’s villainous Rooster Hannigan. The art of disappearing Curry himself aspired toward this status of absolute absorption for his characters. For Curry, acting was a way of disappearing or of hiding in plain sight. It might have been a contradictory state of being, but Curry, fittingly, saw contradiction as one of the most integral and fascinating aspects of human nature. Acting was a vehicle for exploring such contradictions; a way to understand the most paradoxical aspects of human emotion, as Curry suggested in his memoir: “Professionally, the lure of pursuing contradictions has drawn me toward complex characters or compelled me to make them more complex and nuanced.” 'Making the darkness sparkle’ Curry often played villains and antagonists: malicious characters who, on the surface, are difficult to root for, yet remain beguiling and charismatic. He intentionally infused a level of playfulness into even his most nefarious roles, a process he referred to as “mak[ing] the darkness sparkle.” His empathetic desire to explore even his most unlikable characters can be traced back to the most complex and challenging aspects of his own early life. Growing up modestly in the “dull, strange time” of post-Second World War England, Curry and his older sister Judy lost their father when he was 11 or 12. articles.content: In 2019, in the first episode of the Dolly Parton’s America podcast, Jad Abumrad asked Dolly Parton the question everyone eventually asked her: did she think of herself as a feminist? “No, I do not,” she said. “I think of myself as a woman in business.” She spent six decades refusing a label that fit her better than almost anyone else in country music. “I think that I just live my femininity,” she told Sky News , a deflection she gave, in one form or another, for 50 years. Parton passed away on Aug. 25 in Nashville, Tenn., at the age of 80. She may have been right that she never set out to be a feminist, but her career — the songs, the films, a lifetime of philanthropy — tells another story. I’ve spent much of my career reading artists’ legacies in the songs that charted and, just as often, in the songs that didn’t. Parton’s chart history tells the story of an artist who broke through a landscape stacked against women, and spent her final years as a featured artist on songs by women who came after her. Breaking into a male-dominated industry Parton’s national breakthrough came in 1967, when Porter Wagoner hired her as a regular co-host and performer on his popular television show — a launching pad that put her in front of an audience she could not have reached at that point. But the same platform set terms she’d spend years working against. For the first six years, Parton’s solo singles climbed modestly. “ Dumb Blonde ” peaked at 24 on the Billboard Hot Country Songs chart, and “ Something Fishy ” and “ Just Because I’m a Woman ” both peaked at 17. Meanwhile, her collaborations with Wagoner resulted in a string of Top 10 records. As a collaborator, the ceiling was higher than as a solo artist. As Parton recounted in her 1994 autobiography My Life and Other Unfinished Business , Wagoner produced her records, shaped her early RCA Victor output and owned a 49 per cent stake in her publishing company, Owepar. Other women, including Melba Montgomery, Loretta Lynn, June Carter and Tammy Wynette, likewise appeared in male-led collaborations during a decade when women accounted for a small fraction of the Billboard Hot Country Songs chart . Wagoner gave Parton national exposure, but it increasingly hemmed in her ambitions as a solo artist and songwriter. On her own terms The turn came in the early 1970s, as Parton began pulling away from Wagoner and the No. 1s for her solo efforts accumulated. “ Joshua ” reached the top in 1971; then, in 1974, “ Jolene ” and “ I Will Always Love You ” followed, the latter written as a farewell to Wagoner as she prepared to leave their professional partnership. Between 1971 and 1989, Parton logged 19 solo No. 1 singles and spent 27 weeks at the top — the sixth-most weeks at No. 1 by a solo female artist in the chart’s history — at a time when songs by women typically accounted for only 20 to 25 per cent of the chart. Breaking with Wagoner gave Parton something she had spent years working toward: a career increasingly on her own terms. By the end of the 1970s, she was pushing beyond the country industry that had made her a star, first into pop and then into film. In 1977, “Here You Come Again” crossed her into pop for the first time, spending five straight weeks at No. 1 on Hot Country Songs while climbing to No. 3 on the Hot 100. Her audience was no longer bounded by the country chart, but neither had she left it behind. As music journalist Jewly Hight recently put it , Parton insisted she was not leaving her country-ness behind, but bringing it with her. Writing women’s stories Parton’s country No. 1s continued as she crossed into pop stardom and, in the 1980s, made her film debut alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in 9 to 5 , a film rooted in the real-life organizing of women office workers for better pay, treatment and working conditions. She wrote and recorded “9 to 5” for the film, turning the fight over pay inequity, workplace power and working conditions into a No. 1 country and pop anthem. Later that year, she included the song on 9 to 5 and Odd Jobs , an album that widened its focus to labour and economic precarity, with songs about miners, migrants and the poor. These were not new concerns for Parton. On Dolly Parton’s America , she described writing about subjects that mattered to her, including abortion and adoption, even when other country songwriters avoided them. “Down from Dover,” recorded for her 1970 album The Fairest of Them All , is one example. Three years before Roe v. Wade , it follows an unwed mother whose baby is stillborn — a subject Parton told Abumrad her label would not release as a single because radio would not touch it . “People didn’t talk about unwed mothers, much less a child dying and all that.” The song left no chart trace, but it was part of Parton’s longstanding practice of telling women’s stories that were often overlooked. A legacy of giving back Parton’s philanthropy followed the same instincts. Her book-gifting program, The Imagination Library, distributed more than 300 million books worldwide . She donated millions to other causes, including disaster relief and COVID-19 vaccine research at Vanderbilt. She also used royalties from Whitney Houston’s recording of “I Will Always Love You” to buy property in a historically Black neighbourhood — a purchase sometimes recounted as an act of philanthropy, though the reality was more complicated : the property became home to Parton’s business operations. As her cultural and financial power grew, she used it on behalf of others, sometimes so quietly that the full extent of her generosity emerged only later. But the mythology that grew around her generosity could sometimes outrun the facts — something Parton herself seemed wary of. She was “addicted to giving,” she said , but didn’t want to be worshipped for it. A feminist in practice Parton’s final chart appearances brought the story back to where it began: with Parton’s name beside someone else’s. In 2024, she was featured on Beyoncé’s “Tyrant” and Post Malone’s “Have the Heart.” In March 2025, Sabrina Carpenter’s “Please Please Please” charted with Parton’s name beside hers . The young woman whose records once climbed higher with a man’s name beside hers was now the artist others sought to place beside their own. Parton called herself a woman in business, not a feminist, for 50 years. But her 60-year career left a trail: in the control she claimed over her work, the space she made for women’s lives and ambitions, and the path she opened for those who came after her. Near the end of the first episode of Dolly Parton’s America , Abumrad returned to the word Parton had resisted. “There were feminists in theory,” he said referring to journalist Sarah Smarsh , but there were also “feminists in practice.” “That’s me, that’s me,” she said. “I think that’s a good way of saying it, ‘I live it.‘ I work it. And I think there’s power in it for me.” Jada Watson receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.

articles.title: How Dolly Parton built a life and career on her own terms

articles.content: A couple of weeks ago, Netflix released The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare , a documentary revisiting the 2022 killings of four University of Idaho students — Ethan Chapin (20 years old), Kaylee Goncalves (21), Xana Kernodle (20) and Madison Mogen (21). The case, which seemed closed when Bryan Kohberger pleaded guilty in 2025 and was sentenced to life in prison, isn’t actually closed. Kohberger has since petitioned the court to withdraw that plea , arguing coercion and bad legal advice. The victims’ families are ready and unafraid to face him in court again. The three-part series, detailing the grisly mass slaying, is doing exceptionally well . In its first five days on the streamer, it had brought in 18.2 million views and outperformed other Netflix titles. And this has revivified ongoing questions about why this type of programming is so alluring. What does it say about us as a society when lurid content like this is so central to our cultural milieu? The psychology of fear Although true crime feels current, it is the fourth iteration of the genre under one name or another since the mid-19th century. In terms of explaining its appeal, no one explanation suffices. It may be best understood as a system of complex processes, with each of the following mechanisms operating simultaneously at different levels: individual psychology, moral reasoning and social belonging. Foremost among these is a phenomenon known as benign hedonic masochism . Masochistic behaviours, or enjoyment derived from self-suffering , can, in extreme forms, be pathological and even dangerous . But it’s the “benign” part that provides us the intellectual licence to enjoy content about murder and mayhem. The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare trades on exactly this: dramatized crime-scene reconstruction and survivor interviews, all consumed from the safety of a couch. Read more: The Gabby Petito case has been exploited by the media. We need to stop treating human tragedy as entertainment Drawing on Paul Rozin’s pioneering theory of hedonic reversal , benign hedonic masochism describes a paradoxical psychological condition through which people acquire pleasure from simulated aversive experiences that generate fear, anxiety and emotional discomfort, all while remaining fundamentally safe. The maladaptive and self-deprecating language that often surrounds true crime consumption, such as “binging,” “obsession,” “addiction” and being a true crime “junkie,” reflects a certain self-awareness of this reality. More than just a voyeuristic exercise, true crime offers controlled encounters with uncertainty, danger and moral disorder, while simultaneously reassuring audiences of closure and finality. In an era characterized by declining institutional trust and heightened perceptions of crime, the genre functions as an emotionally charged but socially acceptable means of indulging those same anxieties. Psychologists have a name for it: opponent-process theory . The theory proposes that intense emotional experiences trigger a secondary, opposing emotional response. Dread, tension and even revulsion can give way to relief; anxiety to reassurance. With repeated exposure, the negative reaction may weaken while the positive after-effect, or the high, becomes more predictable and prolonged. This is likely why true crime is especially prevalent on streaming and podcasting platforms that are built for continuous, immoderate consumption or “binging.” Didactic storytelling One of the other recurring explanations for true crime’s enduring popularity has to do with who’s actually consuming it. Adult women, in particular, are consistently identified as the target demographic for cable and streaming true-crime series, and the pattern holds even more strongly in podcasting . One explanation for that skew is that the genre serves a didactic function : it imparts factual and moral lessons. Rather than consuming crime narratives solely for entertainment, audiences may be using them as informal lessons in vulnerability, risk and survival. They watch series and listen to podcasts about sadistic psychopaths like Ted Bundy and Richard Ramirez to know how to spot them, how to thwart a possible kidnapping and how to avoid becoming a victim in a way the women in those cases so often couldn’t. Originally coined by communications professor George Gerbner as “mean world syndrome,” the theory holds that repeated exposure to mediated violence can cultivate heightened perceptions of danger, vulnerability and interpersonal threat. Audiences, in the grip of that same syndrome, may then use crime narratives to gradually build a repertoire of mental scripts regarding warning signs, predatory behaviour and situational risk. In this respect, consuming true crime resembles a form of low-stakes threat simulation, allowing the rehearsal of responses to hazards they hope to never encounter in real life. Whether these lessons are empirically valid or merely produce an exaggerated sense of danger remains subject to some debate . A true crime community There are certainly other theories, too, about the psychological undergirding of this current true-crime zeitgeist. Some researchers point to morbid curiosity . Others frame it as a form of boredom-induced sensation-seeking or what’s been called negative information seeking (an appetite for unsettling information for its own sake). And in some cases, the fascination with male offenders in particular has been linked to a disordered erotic interest known as hybristophillia . But the one thing these theories tend to converge on is that true crime, in its current form, provides a sense of community. The barriers to membership in this community are remarkably low. Listeners can move effortlessly from consumers to contributors through message boards, Facebook groups, TikTok communities and even their own DIY podcasts . In contrast to traditional media, true crime invites collective interpretation: armchair sleuthing, theory-crowdsourcing, shared meaning-making. It fosters a participatory culture in which audiences do not merely follow cases; they also actively help retell them. That the path to community, in an increasingly segmented and partisan reality, includes a road paved by serial killers and cold cases may say less about our fascination with death than it does about our enduring need to find one another through stories. That the path to community, in an increasingly segmented and partisan reality, includes a road paved by serial killers and cold cases may say less about our fascination with death than it does about our enduring need to find one another through stories. articles.content: Moving beyond traditional roles as communicators of established knowledge, science museums are engaging more and more with difficult societal issues. Despite the pressing importance of responding to mental health globally and locally, science museums are have rarely been connected to this topic. I argue, however, that science museums are increasingly becoming emotional sites where difficult issues, including mental health, can be approached. This affirmation is supported by research I conducted over the past 10 years in different countries, including Canada, Portugal, the United States and Finland . Key challenge of our time Mental health is a key challenge of our times. Research from the World Health Organization shows how governments around the world have been responding to growing levels of loneliness, social isolation and mental distress. In this scenario, social connection is increasingly recognized as a critical issue for public health and well-being. My research examines a challenging transformation in how science museums understand their roles and purposes through initiatives with a mental health focus, as across the world, science museums begin to join conversations and develop work about this theme. Finnish exhibit My research about hosting a mental health exhibition at a science centre talks about an exhibition originally developed by Heureka, the Finnish science centre . The exhibit engaged with mental health through personal narratives, immersive environments (such as a “schizophrenia room”), displays to help express emotions and scientific perspectives. The Finnish Central Association for Mental Health was part of the exhibition’s scientific advisory board (as well as psychiatrists), and through this body, organizers worked with “peer experts” — people with lived experiences of mental health problems who had support learning how to communicate what they’d been through. Organized around three main themes — “The Labeled,” “How does it feel” and “Go Crazy!” — the exhibit was intended to support visitors in safely talking about mental health and in developing empathy. Finnish versus American context In 2018, the exhibit was hosted by the Science Museum of Minnesota . At that time, I was part of a research team that studied how staff adapted the exhibit for the American audience. The research showed that the exhibition’s impact was not only on visitors, but also on the institution. In bringing the exhibit to the U.S., staff had to rethink content, representation and ethical responsibility. Based on interviews, we traced how museum professionals navigated adjustments across cultural contexts. We heard how they encountered moments of tension, uncertainty and what researchers in the Museum of Science in Boston call “ productive struggle .” For example, the original Finnish title of the exhibit was Heureka Goes Crazy , but the Minnesota staff rejected that wording because of its negative connotations. They call the exhibit Mental Health: Mind Matters . Similar to what happened in Finland, adjustments to the exhibit were informed by an advisory committee of mental health professionals from the National Alliance for Mental Illness and the Wilder Foundation in St. Paul, Minn. Advice also came from community members and museum staff living with mental health conditions. With this guidance, and through careful consideration, staff redesigned content and video testimonials to better reflect local racial and cultural diversity. Questions of representation, care These experiences show that exhibiting mental health is not simply a matter of content delivery. It is a relational, emotional and ethical process shaped by questions of representation, social inclusion and care. My research also showed that emotions are not external to museum practice but central to how exhibitions are designed, curated and experienced by staff. Moments of productive struggle have the potential to foster a shift in science museums. In preparing for and hosting the 2018 exhibition, U.S. staff struggled with issues of stigma, inclusion, diversity and the risks of misrepresentation. They had to rethink, in their own context, what it means for a science museum to publicly engage with a topic that is deeply personal, socially sensitive and unevenly experienced across communities . COVID-19 shifts in Portugal Mind Matters is not an isolated case. In another example from my current research related to science museums and the COVID-19 pandemic, mental health also emerged as an important area of museum work. The study focuses on how staff see the impact and lessons of the pandemic in their own museums. In 2024, as part of this work, a colleague and I visited the Museu Nacional de História Natural e da Ciência (National Museum of Science & Natural History) in Portugal. Interviews with staff revealed how the pandemic reshaped practices of care and relationships among colleagues, with visitors and also with non-visitors. It also reshaped staff perspectives about social inclusion and what this concept means in practice. The natural history museum’s education head described how, at the peak of the pandemic, the institution had to rethink its social role in relation to mental health. This topic had never before been part of the museum’s agenda. Since 2021, the museum became a participant in Portugal’s Social Prescription Project . This initiative involves health-care professionals recommending cultural and community activities as part of mental-health support. In this new context, the natural history museum and its botanical gardens have become spaces where people experiencing loneliness, isolation or mental-health challenges could be referred by doctors. At the museum, they could participate in activities that foster well-being, social connection and a sense of belonging. Impact beyond single exhibitions Taken together, these examples invite us to reconsider science museums as more than places that communicate established knowledge. They can be seen as sites where care, emotions and ethical responsibility are embedded in curatorial practice, and sites where societies negotiate how to talk about difficult and sensitive topics. This shift has impact beyond single exhibitions. It can permeate institutional values and broader practice. In this new context, science museums can play a more active role in public engagement than what is often acknowledged. They can help build the conditions for connection, understanding, empathy and collective well-being. Ana Maria Navas Iannini does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: As an artist who explores associations and disassociations of culture and nature, I am playing with sunlight in performance in the hot Montréal summer. This is an extension of a body of collaborative research creation work . My project this summer, Halo Event , thinks of sunlight as a material and as something that’s alive. This isn’t a new framework: the belief that natural phenonmena are alive, or animism, is as old as human culture, and has more recently been articulated in schools of contemporary philosophy . Creative efforts to shape sunlight are as old as human culture, evidenced in the variety of ancient structures built around solstices by Mayan, Druid, Indigenous and prehistoric populations. Our relationship to the sun, to ecological entities, matters. It matters because those relationships affect how we shape ecologies, how we consider our impact and how we respond to the increasingly real pressure of climate change. These are inherently cultural questions, which artists are uniquely equipped to address . Canada and climate change This summer has been particularly hot because of global warming. Canada is warming at about twice as fast as the global rate: a 2 C increase globally means a 3 to 4 C increase for Canada. The biggest contributors to global warming are major corporations and companies, many tied to fossil fuel industries, which operate internationally . Resistance to global warming takes particular forms in North America. Aside from provincial initiatives, like Québec’s 2021 ban on future fossil fuel projects, Indigenous resistance to fossil fuel infrastructure expansion has had a proven, consistent and dramatic effect. In Halo Event , I worked with sound artist Kathy Kennedy and performance artist Laurence Beaudoin Morin on a short piece in response to the sunlight passing through giant foyer windows at QUAI 5160, my local Maison du Culture , on the St. Lawrence River. The light is reflected and redirected by static and motorized mirrors in my own design, assisted by Kris Hodder. ‘Angles of Consequence’ Like many site-specific visual and conceptual artists, I don’t see location as a blank canvas or an empty stage, but an entity in dialogue with the performance, unfolding within it. Last summer, I invited six artists to create in response to sunlight and site, as part of a larger project called Angles of Consequence . Varied shiny objects in Angles of Consequence behave as scenographic pieces and performance props: they are meant to expand the space of the performance, articulating its themes and meanings . ‘Angles of Consequence’ artists’ panel discussion at Concordia University. In one project, in response to the legacy of Indigenous resistance, I invited artist Sabina Gamez to create a performance along the path of the cancelled Energy East Pipeline that would have run from Montréal to New Brunswick . Gamez, who is Colombian and works with themes of Indigineity and celestial forces, worked with designer Carolie Delisle and project research assistants to create a large apparatus to channel sunlight through a circular path. She wore this, with a ring hung in front and behind her, from a frame on her shoulders. Gamez orbited a remote location along the pipeline path, an area lush with birds and insects, reflecting sunlight through a lens at circles of fabric at standing mirrors. In post-show interviews after each performance, audience members remarked at the power of the sound, as well as the wonder and wildness of the remote site. They also expressed curiosity about the piece’s installation and costume design. One visitor said: “The sun made me feel happy, and the performance made me feel light and flickering.” Refinery as performance site In considering a negative form of climate impact, I invited dancer Lucy Fandel and performer-designer Isabella Leone to create a performance in response to a Suncor refinery in Montréal-Est . They spent weeks biking out to the remote location, creating a 40-minute dance piece performed in coveralls dyed to match the refinery infrastructure, wielding security mirrors and pocket reflectors. Again, the site played a major role: audience members remarked on how the site invited a contemplation of scale, and how difficult it was to access. “It kind of made you have that new perspective on how strange we’re acting … doing all these contortions to not look at what we’re doing to our planet,” said one audience member. Several visitors came away from the performance with an appreciation for petroleum as a precious, intense resource. Art in response to fossil fuel project ban In a creative interpretation of the role that site plays, I asked a group of three artists, Bastik , Oriana Confente and Mila Figuet , to choose a location and develop a performance there in response to the 2022 ban on fossil fuel projects in Québec. They chose a wild, unmanaged area next to a shipping yard, the Boise Steinberg park . Their project invited audience members to wander through a landscape of mirrors and poetic audio musings on the processing climate grief, through the lens of the popular notion of “seven stages of grief” and climate research. A visitor remarked: “It kind of gave us the opportunity to reflect on things we are going through. And just having that space to share it as a community but also share it ourselves …Definitely touching, and made me grieve in a deeper way … Just seeing how we are connected forever, in a way, without realizing.” Once having passed through the stages, the visitors were led by the artists through space as they reflected the landscape and people through mirrors. At the end of a path, the artists prompted everyone to lay down on giant cloths treated with cyanotype, and hung the resulting solar prints on a clothesline to dry. Audience members watched as their own silhouettes, captured by the sun’s rays, developed in front of them, and became part of the landscape. Manual for working with reflected sunlight The initial season of performances has resulted in a manual for working with reflected sunlight, including safety and care guidelines, overviews of material qualities and forms, instructions on how to work with reflective material and strategies for collective site-specific performance . Performances from the Angles season have gone on to be re-performed in other Montréal events , such as the Champs des Possibles FRAIStival . I’ve conducted sunlight reflection workshops based on the project at Scenofest at World Stage Design in Sharjah, United Arab Emirates, and screened videos of the performances online as part of Fall of Freedoms’ May Day Programming . The playing continues, in the hopes of keeping us connected to ecological forces. Meghan Moe Beitiks received funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Council of Canada. They work as an Assistant Professor at Concordia University, which has also funded this research.
